Three issues this PR perpetuates / misses, all the same bug class as #1611 (silent slug-mismatch → restore 409):

---

### 1. Windows colon-stripping actively disagrees with ground truth

`toClaudeProjectPath` does `\\` → `/` and then strips `:` before the main fold. Claude does no pre-processing — `:` and `\` are both just non-alphanumerics that get folded to `-`.

| Input | We produce | Claude actually produces |
|---|---|---|
| `C:\Users\dev` | `C-Users-dev` | `C--Users-dev` |

The "Windows drive letters keep their special handling" comment added in this PR is a reverse-engineered guess that disagrees with the actual implementation. The simplest correct version is just:

```ts
return workspacePath.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/g, "-");
```

Probably zero impact in practice if no Windows users hit Claude restore, but it's actively wrong and we should not be doubling down on the comment.

---

### 2. No 200-char truncation + hash — will hit #1611 again for long paths 🚨

Claude truncates encoded paths over 200 chars and appends a `simpleHash` (djb2). AO doesn't. Any AO workspace path whose encoded form exceeds 200 chars will compute a slug Claude never wrote → exact same cascade as this issue.

Likelihood is non-trivial. AO worktrees live at `/Users/<user>/.agent-orchestrator/<12char-hash>-<sanitized>_<10char-hash>/worktrees/<uuid>/`. With a long username and a moderately long project name, the encoded form can plausibly cross 200 chars. This is silent — there's no error, restore just fails to find the JSONL.

To match Claude byte-for-byte AO needs to port both the truncation and `simpleHash` (so the hash bytes agree). The current "verified against actual on-disk slugs" doc-comment is only true for short paths.

---

### 3. Drifted mirror in `core/src/migration/storage-v2.ts:869`

`encodeClaudeProjectPath` — explicitly documented as "Mirrors `toClaudeProjectPath` … kept in sync by hand" — was not updated. It still uses the old `[/.]` regex, so `ao migrate-storage`'s Claude-relink step (called from lines 1372 forward and 1661 rollback) will silently skip underscored projects and leave users without their Claude history after V1→V2 migration. Either update the mirror to match, or extract a shared helper to remove the hand-sync footgun.

---

### Recommendation

Land the underscore fix as-is — it's correct and unblocks #1611. File follow-ups for:

- (a) Update the `storage-v2.ts` mirror (or extract a single shared helper).
- (b) Drop the Windows pre-processing and add the 200-char truncation + djb2 hash, porting `sanitizePath` byte-for-byte from the leaked source.
- (c) Add a regression test for an encoded path > 200 chars.

Claude Code accepts a prompt as a positional argument and stays interactive — `-p` triggers exit, not the prompt itself. If that's right, this PR carefully fixes real bugs in code that shouldn't exist. ## What the codebase says about this path Two existing comments (not changed in this PR) tie the entire mechanism to Claude Code's `-p` flag. **`packages/core/src/types.ts:460-467`:** ```typescript /** * - "post-launch": prompt is sent via runtime.sendMessage() after the agent starts, * keeping the agent in interactive mode. Use this for agents where inlining * the prompt causes one-shot/exit behavior (e.g. Claude Code's -p flag). */ readonly promptDelivery?: "inline" | "post-launch"; ``` **`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:1422-1424`:** ```typescript // Send the task-specific prompt post-launch for agents that need it // (e.g. Claude Code exits after -p, so we send the prompt after it starts // in interactive mode). ``` And only Claude Code opts in: ``` $ grep -rn "promptDelivery" packages/ --include="*.ts" | grep -v __tests__ packages/core/src/types.ts:467: readonly promptDelivery?: "inline" | "post-launch"; packages/core/src/session-manager.ts:1428: if (plugins.agent.promptDelivery === "post-launch" && ...) { packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts:686: promptDelivery: "post-launch", ``` Codex, Aider, OpenCode all use the default `"inline"` — prompt on launch command. ## Where the inference breaks `-p` does cause one-shot exit (verified at `main.tsx:976` → `runHeadless` at `main.tsx:2829` in the published [Claude Code source](https://github.com/AprilNEA/claude-code-source/)). But the positional `[prompt]` is a separate code path: - `main.tsx:991` — `claude [prompt]` defined as positional - `main.tsx:857-883` — populates REPL `initialMessage` from positional/stdin - `screens/REPL.tsx:3028-3141` — submits `initialMessage` as first user turn after **interactive** REPL mounts `--print` routes to headless. L1 — bare CLI ``` $ claude -p "what is 2+2" 4 $ ← exits $ claude "what is 2+2" > what is 2+2 • 4 * Worked for 4s > ← interactive, "? for shortcuts" footer ```

```
❯ [Pasted text #1 +13 lines][Pasted text #2 +10 lines]…
```

…but it stays in paste-preview mode and never submits. AO reports `state: not_started, reason: spawn_requested` indefinitely.

**Workaround that works every time:**

```bash
tmux send-keys -t <session> Escape
tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter
```

`Enter` alone is treated as newline-insert in multi-line edit mode; `Escape` first dismisses paste-preview, then `Enter` submits.

## Diagnostic run results — original hypothesis falsified

55-minute capture on the diagnostic branch (`debug/pty-leak-instrumentation`), with the user actively navigating session terminals. PTY count grew from 0 → 86 while `terminals.size` stayed at 1 the entire run.

### Per-event FD deltas (n=82 spawn cycles)

| Event | Count | FD delta | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pty_spawn` | 82 | **+3.00** every time (100%) | one spawn opens 3 PTY-class fds |
| `pty_exit` | 82 | **−1.94** average | 77× −2, 5× −1 |
| `pty_kill_lastsub` | 70 | 0 | only signals, no fds released yet |
| **Net per spawn↔exit cycle** | | **+1 fd leaked** | deterministic |

82 cycles → +87 fds leaked → matches observed final ptys=82–86 exactly.

Extrapolated to the originally-reported incident: **486 fds = ~486 leak events**. At the observed ~50–70 cycles/hour of active dashboard use, that's exactly the 7–10 hour timescale that was reported.

### What this falsifies

My original "client doesn't send `close` → orphan terminals accumulate" hypothesis is **wrong**. The `terminals` map size never grew beyond 1 during the entire capture — every leaked fd happened despite the entry being properly cleaned up. The leak is per spawn↔exit cycle, not per orphaned terminal.

The `pty_reattach_counter_reset` instrumentation also fired 12 times during normal use (each `pty_reattach_try` was followed by a counter reset to 0) — confirms the suspected `MAX_REATTACH_ATTEMPTS=3` cap never engages, but this is a contributing amplifier, not the root cause.

### What it points to

Each `ptySpawn` opens **3 PTY-related fds** in the parent direct-terminal-ws process; each natural PTY exit releases only **2**. The third fd is unaccounted for — every cycle.

Top suspect: the **`mouseProc` / `statusProc` short-lived `spawn()` calls** in `mux-websocket.ts:254-263` that run right before each `ptySpawn`. On macOS, even short-lived tmux child processes can briefly hold or inherit ptmx-related fds. A real possibility: one of these is inheriting an fd from the parent that should have been marked `O_CLOEXEC`.

Less likely but possible: a known node-pty 1.1.0 cleanup quirk on macOS — the `/dev/terminal-test` page already calls out 1.1.0 stability issues.

### Next steps (in progress)

1. Add `/debug/pty/lsof` endpoint to the diagnostic branch so we can dump the full fd table for the leaking process at high PTY count and identify exactly which fd type leaks.
2. Create a fix-and-see branch that removes the `mouseProc` / `statusProc` spawn calls. If the +3 per spawn becomes +1, the source is confirmed and the fix is to either inline these into a single tmux invocation or run them via the attached PTY's tmux client.

Will post the snapshot data and result of the fix-and-see test once captured.

## Tighter Reproduction Path

Confirmed by reporter — the bug is more common than initially described:

1. `ao start` — spawns codex orchestrator, writes AO session metadata
2. **Never send a message** to the orchestrator — codex CLI never creates a session file in `~/.codex/sessions/` because it never received its first prompt
3. Exit (`Ctrl+C` or `ao stop`)
4. `ao start` again → restore fails permanently

**Why:** The codex session file (JSONL in `~/.codex/sessions/`) is only created when codex receives its first message. If the user exits before sending anything, `codexThreadId` was never generated in the first place — not "lost," but **never existed**.

This means the bug hits every time someone starts an orchestrator and exits before the first prompt. Not an edge case — a common workflow interruption.

## Self-review (`/pr-review`)

### Summary
Surgical fix to a real, system-impacting runaway loop, with both forward (cap engages) and backward (counter recovers after grace) regression tests. Clean rebase onto current `main` preserves both the bug fix and #1608's `=`-prefix exact-match changes.

### Code Quality
The closure guard `if (terminal.pty === pty)` is doing real work — it correctly prevents a stale timer from resetting the counter for a PTY that was replaced by re-attach or unsubscribed away. Combined with the `clearTimeout` in unsubscribe and at the top of `open()`, this is defense in depth: even if `clearTimeout` ever races and misses (callback already in the task queue), the closure guard catches it.

`terminal.resetTimer = undefined` inside the timer callback is correct — runs whether or not the pty match holds, so the field reflects reality after firing.

### Architecture & Design
The 5 s grace constant has a real rationale (`~40 ms doomed attach exit ≪ 5 s ≪ "PTY ran for hours"`) and the JSDoc captures it. The `~80 spawns/sec` and `~40 ms` figures in the inline comment are real measurements but won't survive code rot — the `Refs: #1639` link in the comment block is the durable pointer.

### Testing
Both halves of the contract are covered:
- `bounds re-attach attempts when tmux session dies mid-subscription` — counter does NOT reset on early crash → cap engages
- `retry budget recovers after PTY survives the grace period` — counter DOES reset after grace → loop still bounded on subsequent failure

The recovery test takes ~5.5 s because it uses the production grace constant. Acceptable for a critical-regression test, but worth a follow-up: parameterizing `REATTACH_RESET_GRACE_MS` via a `TerminalManager` constructor option (or `createMuxWebSocket` option) would let tests use 200 ms and stay sub-second. Not blocking — Vitest parallel scheduling absorbs the cost.

### Backward Compatibility
None. `TerminalManager` is unexported. Mux protocol unchanged. Behavior change for healthy PTYs: identical. Behavior change for crashing PTYs: bounded retries instead of an infinite loop — strict improvement.

### Boundary Verification
Same-process state machine within `mux-websocket.ts`. No IPC/serialization seam. All cross-component state (`reattachAttempts`, `pty`, `resetTimer`) lives on the same `ManagedTerminal` object accessed from one event loop. No boundary-bug-hunter findings to incorporate.

### Consumer Impact
Strict positive UX change. Pre-fix, when a tmux session was killed externally, the dashboard tab silently spun in the runaway loop until the user refreshed; the `"exited"` message was *never* emitted, so `MuxProvider`'s exit handler (the one that displays `\r\n[Terminal exited with code N]\r\n`) was effectively unreachable code. Post-fix, that path fires after ~150 ms — users get clear feedback, the affected terminal entry is removed from `openedTerminalsRef`, and the panel doesn't get re-opened on WS reconnect. No new fields, no removed fields.

### Edge Cases (walked through)
Recursive `this.open()` via re-attach, `open()` throwing partway, last subscriber leaving mid-grace (timer cleared), multiple subscribers with one leaving (timer survives), re-attach inside grace window (old timer cleared, new one scheduled), PTY exits exactly at the 5 s boundary (race resolves safely either way), `clearTimeout` racing the callback execution (closure guard catches it). All paths bounded by `MAX_REATTACH_ATTEMPTS=3`.

- `exactTmuxTarget = \`=${tmuxSessionId}\`` at line 278; consumed at lines 280, 286, 309

The only line removed-from-upstream-and-not-replaced is `terminal.reattachAttempts = 0; // reset on successful attach` — exactly what this PR is supposed to remove. Conflict resolution clean.

**Ship.** Critical-priority bug, correctly diagnosed, surgically fixed, both forward and recovery paths tested, CI green (10/10), prior reviewer comments addressed, rebase preserves both halves of the conflict.

## ⚠️ Still open: hook ordering race

@iamasx — could you trace this and confirm safety?

In the regular spawn path (`_spawnInner`), the order is:
1. `runtime.create()` at `session-manager.ts:1294` — Claude starts **with the task** as a positional arg
2. ~90 lines of post-launch work
3. `postLaunchSetup()` at `session-manager.ts:1387` → calls `setupHookInWorkspace` which writes `.claude/settings.json` with the PostToolUse hook

In the previous flow, this ordering was implicitly safe because the polling-then-send pattern acted as a barrier — Claude saw the task only *after* `postLaunchSetup` had completed. With inline delivery, Claude has the task on its first tick and may issue tool calls before step 3 lands.

Whether this is an actual regression depends on Claude Code's settings.json read behavior:
- If Claude reads `.claude/settings.json` **once at process start**, the hook never registers and PostToolUse never fires for the entire session — silently breaking dashboard PR/commit metadata tracking.
- If Claude reads/watches it **per tool call**, only the first few tool calls miss the hook (still a regression, but bounded).

Two ways to resolve:
1. **Move hook installation before launch** — call `setupWorkspaceHooks` (or the same `setupHookInWorkspace` body) in `preLaunchSetup` instead of `postLaunchSetup`, so `.claude/settings.json` exists before `runtime.create()` runs.
2. **Empirically verify** — spawn a session, check whether the PostToolUse hook fires for the *very first* tool call. If yes, no fix needed. If not, option 1.

I'd lean option 1 — it removes the timing question entirely with a one-line code move.

**Update:** while testing this branch end-to-end against a real Forgejo instance (15.0.0+gitea-1.22.0), I found that the orchestrator's `pollBacklog` flow never finds labeled issues on Forgejo. Root cause: Forgejo's repo-scoped `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues?labels=...` query parameter is silently broken — the swagger documents it as a comma-separated name list (matching what `tracker-forgejo` sends), but in practice it returns 0 results for any name and ignores any ID.

Forgejo's cross-repo `/repos/issues/search?owner=X&repo=Y&labels=...&type=issues` endpoint honors the same documented contract correctly. Pushed `be935c0a` to route `listIssues` through that endpoint when a label filter is set, and keep the existing repo-scoped path otherwise. Two regression tests added.

This is technically a Forgejo upstream bug, but `tracker-forgejo` needs to work with the Forgejos that exist today — so the workaround lives here, with an inline comment citing the Forgejo version where the bug was observed. Holding off on filing against Forgejo unless reviewers want to push that.

Folding this into #1674 follows the same pattern as the Greptile fixes — discovered during validation, narrow scope, regression-tested. Happy to split into a separate PR if reviewers prefer.

## Revised threat model — the original repro doesn't actually fire

While implementing #1707, I went back and traced the full flow. The "clone twice, `ao spawn` in each" repro in the body **does not fire on a properly-registered second checkout**. `ao project add` already auto-disambiguates prefixes via `deriveAvailableSessionPrefix` (`global-config.ts:610`):

- Checkout A → `sessionPrefix: ao`
- Checkout B → `sessionPrefix: ao2` (auto-derived because `ao` was taken)

Two clones of the same repo never collide on tmux names. Verified against my own config — I have two `agent-orchestrator` clones registered, with prefixes `ao` and `ao2`.

### The real surviving holes

The bug only fires when a config bypasses the global-registry's prefix-disambiguation:

1. **Local-only configs** — a project with an explicit `sessionPrefix` written into its local `agent-orchestrator.yaml` for a path not registered globally. `findSessionPrefixOwner` only checks the global config, so a purely-local config can pick a prefix another global entry owns.
2. **Hand-edited configs** that force a duplicate prefix. `addProject` throws on this, but only when both go through `addProject`. A direct YAML edit isn't validated until spawn.
3. **Migration / restoration flows** that resurrect a config without `addProject` (legacy data, manual recovery).
4. **Multi-machine / shared-home setups** (rare).

So this is a **rare-but-confusing** failure mode, not the everyday repro the body suggests.

### Repro that actually fires

```bash
ao project add /tmp/checkout-a       # gets sessionPrefix "int" automatically
# Hand-write a local config for B that pins the same prefix:
cat > /tmp/checkout-b/agent-orchestrator.yaml <<EOF2
projects:
  checkout-b:
    path: /tmp/checkout-b
    sessionPrefix: int               # ← duplicate, not caught by ao project add
EOF2
cd /tmp/checkout-a && ao spawn       # ✓ tmux session "int-1"
cd /tmp/checkout-b && ao spawn       # ✗ tmux: duplicate session "int-1"
```

### Fix options revisited (cost vs. completeness)

**A. Won't-fix.** Document that two configs sharing a `sessionPrefix` collide; `ao project add` is the supported registration path. Cost: zero. Leaves rare cases with an opaque tmux error.

**B. Pre-check at spawn (lightweight).** Before `tmux new-session`, call `tmux has-session -t {name}`. If owned by another config, throw:
```
tmux session "int-1" is already in use by another AO config.
Two projects appear to share sessionPrefix "int".
Run `ao project list` to inspect; change one project's prefix.
```
Cost: ~5ms per spawn. No naming change. Doesn't auto-recover orchestrator (fixed name) but tells the user *why* it failed.

**C. Validate at AO startup.** Walk global config on `ao start`, refuse to start if two registered projects share a prefix. Catches registration-layer holes; doesn't help purely-local configs.

**D. Hash discriminator on tmux names (currently in #1707).** `tmuxName` = `{8-hex-hash}-{prefix}-{num}`; `sessionId` stays bare. Robust to all of (1)–(4) by construction. Cost: 9 extra chars in tmux names forever, slightly noisier `tmux list-sessions`, two parser branches to maintain.

### Recommendation

Originally I went with **D** in #1707. After tracing the threat model, **B** may be the better trade — it solves the real user pain (a confusing error in a rare case) without paying ongoing UX cost on every tmux name. Open to either — happy to retarget #1707 if reviewers prefer B.

## Re-diagnosis: scrollback: 0 alone does NOT fix the clipping

User reports the right-side clipping is still happening after rebuild + daemon restart, with `scrollback: 0` confirmed in the shipped bundle. I dug in with Playwright on the live dashboard. The original RCA in #1677 was incomplete — there is a second, independent cause that this PR does not address.

### Findings

**1. `scrollback: 0` is loaded and FitAddon does the right thing.**
- `term.options.scrollback === 0` ✓
- FitAddon source (`@xterm/addon-fit@0.11.0`): `scrollback === 0 ? 0 : (overviewRuler?.width || 14)` — so FitAddon reserves **0 px**, exactly as intended.

**2. There is no actual scrollbar consuming layout space.**
- `.xterm-viewport`: `scrollHeight === clientHeight === 774`, `hasScrollbar: false`, `overflow-y: auto`.
- xterm's internal `.invisible.scrollbar.vertical` widget exists (14 px wide, positioned `right:0`) but `opacity: 0; pointer-events: none` — it's not the visual culprit.

So to answer the user's question — *we do not need to leave space for a scrollbar on the right.* There isn't one. The original premise was wrong.

**3. The actual root cause: font-metric drift between xterm's measure and render phases.**

Live numbers from the running dashboard (font-size 13 px, SF Mono):
| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| `term.cols` | 124 |
| `_renderService.dimensions.css.cell.width` | **7.83 px** |
| `cssCanvasWidth` (= cols × cell) | 971 px |
| `.xterm` container width | **974 px** |
| `.xterm-rows > div` width | **971 px** (`overflow: hidden`) |
| Actual rendered text width (Range.getClientRects) | **992 px** |
| **Drift** | **+21 px ≈ 3 chars clipped** |

Visually confirmed in the screenshot — lines ending in `(Chrome` show as `(Chr`, `FitAddon` shows as `FitAddo`, etc.

**4. Why the drift exists.**

In `packages/web/src/app/globals.css:432`:
```css
body {
  ...
  letter-spacing: -0.011em;
}
```
At the body's font-size of 16 px, that's `-0.176 px` and it inherits all the way down into `.xterm`.

xterm's DOM renderer measures char width inside that inherited context:
- natural SF Mono "M" width at 13 px ≈ **8.00 px**
- with body's `-0.176 px` letter-spacing applied → measured **7.83 px** → that becomes xterm's cell width

Then xterm puts an inline override on `.xterm-rows`: `letter-spacing: 0.174395px` (≈ +0.176 — clearly attempting to *cancel* the body's negative spacing). Net effective letter-spacing on row glyphs ≈ 0, so they render at their **natural 8.00 px** width.

So xterm allocates 7.83 px per cell (`width: 971px`) but every glyph paints at 8.00 px. Over 124 cols the cumulative drift is `124 × (8.00 − 7.83) ≈ 21 px`. Each row child div has `overflow: hidden`, which is what's chopping the rightmost ~3 chars.

In other words: **xterm's measure phase and render phase observe different `letter-spacing` values, and the size mismatch grows with `cols`.**

### Implications

### Clarification: PR association IS persisted in metadata; the bug is that detectPR overwrites it

Re-reading the on-disk metadata for the affected session (`~/.agent-orchestrator/projects/agent-orchestrator/sessions/ao-179.json`):

```json
"lifecycle": {
  "version": 2,
  "session": {
    "kind": "worker",
    "state": "working",
    "reason": "fixing_ci",
    ...
  },
  "pr": {
    "state": "open",
    "reason": "ci_failing",
    "number": 643,
    "url": "https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/pull/643",
    "lastObservedAt": "2026-05-07T21:12:45.949Z"
  },
  ...
}
```

`pr.number` is a **persistent** field in metadata. Originally `1723`. Now `643`. So somewhere in the post-merge / restore flow, the lifecycle manager is **rewriting** the persisted PR association — replacing the legitimate (now-merged) PR with whatever detectPR happens to return for the current `session.branch`.

This refines the bug:

1. **Primary bug**: lifecycle re-runs `detectPR` for a session whose original PR has already merged, and silently overwrites the persisted `pr.number` / `pr.url` with the new (wrong) result. Once a worker session's PR has merged, the session is effectively done — its PR field should be **terminal**, not subject to re-detection.

2. **Aggravating factor (already in the issue body)**: `detectPR` itself is too permissive (matches fork PRs by bare branch name), which is why the wrong PR is even available to overwrite with. Hardening detectPR (drop fork heads, refuse default-branch matches) is still the right thing to do, but the deeper fix is to stop running detectPR at all on a session whose PR is in a terminal state.

### Refined fix priorities

- **A. Don't run detectPR on terminal-PR sessions.** If `session.lifecycle.pr.state === "merged"` (or `"closed"`), skip detectPR and don't repopulate `pr.*`. The session should transition to `done` / `cleanup`, not "working / fixing_ci".
- **B. On restore, preserve PR terminal state.** If a session is restored after its PR has already merged, do not reset `lifecycle.session.state` to `working` or rerun detectPR. Either keep the merged record or refuse to restore (with a clear message: "PR is merged; nothing to resume").
- **C. (Same as before)** Harden `detectPR` to filter fork heads and refuse default-branch matches.

A + B together close the regression. C is a defense-in-depth that prevents similar misattributions if A/B are bypassed.

## Analysis Summary

The `npm warn deprecated prebuild-install@7.1.3` warning that appears during global installation (`npm install -g @aoagents/ao`) is **cosmetic and harmless**.

### Root Cause
`prebuild-install` is a transitive dependency used by two optional packages in our monorepo:
- **`better-sqlite3@^11.0.0`** (packages/core) — used for event database
- **`node-pty@^1.1.0`** (packages/web) — used for pseudo-terminal support

Both packages use `prebuild-install` to download pre-built native binaries instead of compiling from source.

### Investigation Results

**Tested solutions:**
1. ❌ **Update `better-sqlite3` to v12.9.0** — Still uses `prebuild-install`. Upstream maintainers show no plans to change this.
2. ❌ **Suppress with npm config** — No valid per-package deprecation filter exists in npm. Invalid config approaches like `npm-cli-audit.exclude` don't work and trigger new warnings in npm 11.2.0+.
3. ❌ **Update `node-pty`** — Latest stable is v1.1.0; v1.2.0 is still in beta.

### Why This Is Not a Problem

1. **Packages are actively maintained** — Both `better-sqlite3` and `node-pty` are well-maintained and work reliably.
2. **Unmaintained ≠ broken** — Despite `prebuild-install` being unmaintained, it continues to download and install pre-built binaries correctly across all platforms.
3. **No security risk** — The package functions as intended for our use case.
4. **No alternative** — npm provides no clean, per-package deprecation suppression mechanism.

### Recommendation

**Accept the warning as expected behavior.** Document in your installation guide that users may see this message, and that it's safe to ignore:

> "You may see: `npm warn deprecated prebuild-install@7.1.3: No longer maintained.` This is expected and safe — the packages using this dependency continue to work reliably."

### Conclusion

This is not a bug or a requirement to fix. The warning correctly informs users that `prebuild-install` is unmaintained, while reality shows that it poses no risk to the project's functionality.

## Research: How Modern Tools Handle Config Hot-Reload

### 1. Server Orchestration

| Tool | Mechanism | Granularity | Invalid Config Handling |
|------|-----------|-------------|------------------------|
| **Nginx** (`nginx -s reload`) | Signal-based (`SIGHUP`). Spawns new workers with new config, gracefully drains old ones. | Full reload | **Rejects reload entirely** if config validation fails. Old workers keep serving. Two-phase commit: validate → spawn → drain. |
| **Envoy Proxy** | File watching + xDS gRPC/REST API | **Per-resource granular** (each xDS type independently updateable) | NACKs invalid updates, continues with last-known-good config. Versioned updates prevent stale writes. |
| **HAProxy** | Signal-based (`SIGUSR2`). New process with new config, old drains. | Full (OSS). Enterprise has granular stats socket API. | New process fails to start on invalid config — old process continues. |
| **Kubernetes ConfigMap** | Kubelet sync loop (~60s polling). Atomic symlink swap. | Full file replacement | No built-in validation — app responsibility. Common pattern: Reloader controller triggers rolling update. |

### 2. Application Frameworks

| Tool | Mechanism | Key Pattern |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| **Vite** | `chokidar` file watching. Restarts dev server on `vite.config.ts` change. HMR for source files. | **50ms debounce** on watch events. Keeps previous server running if new config has errors. |
| **Spring Boot** (`@RefreshScope`) | Actuator endpoint triggers bean recreation. Only `@RefreshScope`-annotated beans rebuild. | **Selective rebuild** — unaffected beans stay live. `@Validated` properties enable bind-time validation. |
| **Go Viper** | Built-in `WatchConfig()` via `fsnotify`. Fires `OnConfigChange` callback. | Parse into temp struct → validate → swap. Clean minimal API. |
| **Rust config-rs** | `notify` crate for watching. `Arc<RwLock<Config>>` for concurrent access. | Reader-writer lock pattern. Deserialization errors → keep old config. |

### 3. Databases / Infrastructure

| Tool | Mechanism | Key Pattern |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| **PostgreSQL** (`pg_reload_conf()`) | `SIGHUP` signal. Only `SIGHUP`-context params reload; `POSTMASTER`-context params need full restart. | **Per-parameter reload levels.** Invalid params log error + keep old value. Partial-success: valid params apply even if one fails. |
| **Redis** (`CONFIG SET` / `CONFIG REWRITE`) | Pure API. `CONFIG SET` changes memory immediately; `CONFIG REWRITE` persists to disk. | **Split live vs persistent config.** Two separate operations give operator control. Never mutates on error. |

### 4. Agent / Orchestrator Precedents

- **Prefect**: Workers poll API for config on each heartbeat (~60s). No file watching.
- **Airflow**: Scheduler re-parses DAG files every ~30s. Invalid DAGs quarantined — don't affect running DAGs.
- **Nomad**: File watching (agent config) + RPC (job specs). Invalid specs rejected at submission.
- **AI Agent Frameworks** (LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen): **None support live config reload.** This is a gap and a potential AO differentiator.

### 5. File Watching Libraries

| Library | Platform | Used By |
|---------|----------|---------|
| **chokidar** | Node.js (inotify/FSEvents/ReadDirectoryChangesW) | Vite, Webpack, Nodemon |
| **fsnotify** | Go (inotify/kqueue/ReadDirectoryChangesW) | Viper, Hugo |
| **notify** | Rust (inotify/kqueue/FSEvents) | Paired with config-rs |

Common patterns: **debounce** (50-200ms), **atomic write** (write-to-temp + rename), **checksum comparison** before reload, **event type filtering** (ignore chmod/access).

## Recommended Architecture for AO

Based on these precedents:

| Aspect | Recommended Approach | Precedent |
|--------|---------------------|-----------|
| **Change Detection** | `chokidar` file watching (AO is Node.js) | Vite, Viper |
| **Atomicity** | Write-to-temp + rename (readers never see partial files) | K8s ConfigMap |
| **Validation** | Validate-before-apply; reject entire reload on failure | Nginx, Envoy |
| **Granularity** | Per-section reload levels (`hot` vs `restart-required`) | PostgreSQL (SIGHUP vs POSTMASTER) |
| **Rollback** | Keep last-known-good config; swap back on failure | Redis, Nginx |
| **Notification** | Event emitter pattern — subsystems subscribe to config changes | Viper (`OnConfigChange`), Spring (`@RefreshScope`) |
| **Debounce** | 100-200ms on file watch events | Vite, chokidar defaults |
| **Concurrency** | Atomic config swap (safe for concurrent reads) | Rust `Arc<RwLock<Config>>` pattern |

### Config Section Reload Classification

```yaml
# Sections safe to hot-reload (apply immediately):
- projects.*.labels
- projects.*.registry  
- plugins.*.settings (non-agent)

# Sections requiring session restart:
- projects.*.agent (model, provider changes)
- plugins.*.type (plugin swap)
```

### Minimal API Sketch

```typescript
configWatcher.watch("agent-orchestrator.yaml", { debounce: 100 })
  .validate(configSchema)
  .onChange((newConfig, diff) => {
    if (diff.requiresRestart.length > 0) {
      logger.warn("Some changes require session restart", diff.requiresRestart);
    }
    configStore.swap(newConfig);     // atomic swap
    eventBus.emit("config:changed", diff.hotReloadable);
  })
  .onError((err) => {
    logger.error("Config reload failed, keeping current config", err);
  });
```

**Analyzed against:** `a33b2ba` (origin/main, ahead of v0.6.0)

### Root Cause Confirmed (for v0.6.0)

Your analysis is correct against the **published v0.6.0** npm package. The `promptDelivery: "post-launch"` path relies on tmux `paste-buffer` which races against Claude Code's trust dialog. The success criterion (`tmux paste-buffer` exit code 0) is met regardless of whether Claude actually processed the input.

### Fix Already on `main` (unreleased)

[PR #1583](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/pull/1583) (`1981d471`) rewrote prompt delivery to use Claude Code's **positional `[prompt]` argument** instead of post-launch tmux paste:

```ts
// Current main — prompt is a CLI arg, not a tmux paste
if (config.prompt) {
  parts.push("--", shellEscape(config.prompt));
}
```

This eliminates the trust-dialog race entirely — the prompt is passed as a launch argument, not injected via keystrokes. The entire post-launch polling loop was removed.

### Release Gap

v0.6.0 was cut at `b9b20e19` and is **6 commits behind `main`**:

```
a33b2ba fix(workspace-worktree): restore re-attaches existing branch...
13c5a50 ci: drop windows-latest from typecheck matrix
0f5ae0b feat(windows): complete Windows support
be69a580 fix: reset stale worktree session branches
9bfd7656 fix(cli): refuse to spawn when daemon is not polling the project
1981d471 fix(core): deliver prompt inline via positional arg...  ← the fix
b9b20e19 chore: release 0.6.0  ← published
```

A `0.7.0` release from current `main` would close this issue.

### Suggested `preLaunchSetup`

Your `~/.claude.json` pre-trust idea is a good **defense-in-depth** measure — it prevents the trust dialog from firing at all, which is cleaner even with inline delivery. Worth keeping as a follow-up enhancement regardless.

### Workaround

Running from `main` instead of the npm package avoids this entirely. Or install from git:

```bash
npm install -g github:ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator
```

## Root Cause: `sendMessage` sends `Enter` into the bypass-permissions dialog

Traced this against v0.6.0 (`b9b20e19`, the published npm package). The session doesn't just "silently exit" — AO actively kills it. Here's the kill chain:

### Sequence

1. `ao spawn` → tmux launches `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`
2. Claude Code immediately shows the bypass confirmation:
   ```
   WARNING: Claude Code running in Bypass Permissions mode
   ❯ 1. No, exit        ← pre-selected by default
     2. Yes, I accept
   ```
3. After 3s (first backoff), session-manager calls `runtime.sendMessage(handle, prompt)` which does (`runtime-tmux/src/index.ts:129-168`):
   - `tmux send-keys C-u` — clear line (harmless)
   - `tmux send-keys -l "fix the bug..."` — prompt text typed into the dialog
   - `sleep(300ms)`
   - **`tmux send-keys Enter`** ← this presses Enter on **"No, exit"**
4. Claude Code exits. Session dead.

The `Enter` at the end of `sendMessage` is intended to submit the pasted prompt to Claude's `❯ ` input. But because Claude is sitting on the bypass dialog instead, that `Enter` selects the pre-selected option — "No, exit" — and kills the session.

### On current `main`

PR #1583 removed the post-launch `sendMessage` loop entirely (prompt is now a positional CLI arg), so the rogue `Enter` no longer fires. But the bypass dialog itself still shows — if the user doesn't manually accept, Claude still exits.

### The fix

Change the config default from `permissionless` to `default` in `packages/core/src/config.ts`:

```ts
// Current (v0.6.0 and main)
z.enum(["permissionless", "default", "auto-edit", "suggest", "skip"])
  .default("permissionless")

// Fix
  .default("default")
```

This prevents `--dangerously-skip-permissions` from being passed unless the user explicitly opts in, so the bypass dialog never fires for default-config users. One line, fixes the root cause.

`permissionless` is a terrible default for a config value most users never set — it silently spawns a confirmation dialog that kills the session if unattended.

## Root cause — confirmed

Traced this from the reporter's evidence to a concrete mechanism (checkout at `821cda64`, live sessions `agent-orchestrator-6`/`-7`/`-11`/`-12`/`-14`/`-15`/`-16`/`-17` all showing `no_signal` with `first_signal_at` NULL, `activity_last_at` clustered within ~5s of each other — a batch `MarkSpawned` from a `RestoreAll` pass, not the sessions' real prior activity).

The daemon's shutdown/startup cycle (`SaveAndTeardownAll` → `RestoreAll`, `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:833`) fully tears down and relaunches every live session's harness process on every daemon restart — it does not merely reattach to a still-running process. For Claude Code, the relaunch command is built by `GetRestoreCommand` (`backend/internal/adapters/agent/claudecode/claudecode.go:215`), which resumes via `claude --resume <sessionId>` **without resubmitting a prompt** — it only reopens the existing conversation and waits at the TUI prompt.

`MarkSpawned` (`backend/internal/lifecycle/manager.go:248`) unconditionally clears `FirstSignalAt` on every restore ("each spawn/restore must re-prove its hook pipeline"). But Claude Code's `SessionStart` hook carries no activity signal by design (`backend/internal/adapters/agent/claudecode/activity.go:19-34` — only `user-prompt-submit`, `stop`, `notification`, and `session-end` map to a state). Since restore never submits a prompt, **no qualifying hook can ever fire** for a session that was idle at the time of the restart, until the user manually sends it a new message. `deriveStatus` (`backend/internal/service/session/status.go:54`) then downgrades it to `no_signal` after the 90s grace and it stays there permanently — not a transient hiccup, but a dead end with no self-healing path.

This also means the severity scales with how often the daemon restarts: `~/.ao/data/hooks.log` in this environment shows daemon-down hook-delivery failures recurring almost daily over the past week, so most idle workers accumulate in `no_signal` between sessions.

**Fix direction:** either (a) have `GetRestoreCommand`/the restore flow treat `SessionStart` on a resume as a qualifying signal (it does prove the pipeline works, even without activity semantics), or (b) don't reset `FirstSignalAt` on a restore that resumes the same native session id (only reset it on a true fresh spawn), or (c) submit a lightweight no-op nudge on resume to force a real hook to fire.

**Confidence:** High — mechanism fully traced end to end and matches the reporter's DB fingerprint exactly.

## New Report — corroborating evidence

Hit this independently while triaging why workers in this environment never progress to In Review/Ready to Merge/Done and pile up instead of terminating.

Confirmed two more live instances of the exact same mechanism (checkout `821cda64`):

- `agent-orchestrator-6` — branch `ao/agent-orchestrator-6/root`, real open fork PR [AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator#2485](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/pull/2485) (head `mukesher4/agent-orchestrator:ao/agent-orchestrator-6/terminal-focus-fix`)
- `agent-orchestrator-15` — branch `ao/agent-orchestrator-15/root`, real open fork PR [AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator#2593](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/pull/2593) (head `mukesher4/agent-orchestrator:ao/agent-orchestrator-15/spawn-confirmation-name-fork`)

`sqlite3 ~/.ao/data/ao.db "select * from pr where session_id in ('agent-orchestrator-6','agent-orchestrator-15');"` returns 0 rows for both, matching the reported root cause exactly: `sessionRepo.headRepo` is hardcoded to the project's registered `origin` for every entry in the `scanRepos` loop (`observer.go:475`), so `candidatesForHeadRepo` (`observer.go:685`) never matches a fork-authored PR's real head repo and `discoverNewPRs` silently drops it before `matchSession` even runs — even though the branch-matching logic itself (`sessionBranchPrefixes`/`matchSession`) would correctly attribute these stacked branches to their owning session if it ever got the chance to run.

**Compounding effect:** because these sessions also never accumulate real activity signal after a daemon restart (see [#2604](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/issues/2604)), they show `no_signal` instead of any PR-derived status, and never terminate — both bugs together are why workers in a fork-based project pile up indefinitely instead of reaching `pr_open`/`review_pending`/`mergeable`/`merged`/`terminated`.

## Correction/nuance to my earlier comment

I said no qualifying hook can ever fire for an idle resumed session, but that's slightly imprecise. `notification` events with `notification_type: idle_prompt` ARE a qualifying signal (`activity.go:46` maps them to `waiting_input, true`) — Claude Code's CLI does have a built-in idle-notification timer for exactly this situation.

The more precise finding: empirically, `idle_prompt` is **not firing at all** for sessions relaunched via `--resume`. Checked `agent-orchestrator-6` live — idle since the last restore at `06:48:39 UTC`, still zero signal received at `07:27:24 UTC` (~39 minutes), well past whatever cooldown that notification normally uses on a fresh interactive launch.

So the actual gap is narrower than "no event type maps to a signal for this case" — it's "the `idle_prompt` notification hook never arrives after `claude --resume`, even though the event IS wired to be treated as a signal if it ever showed up." Worth having whoever picks this up check:
- Does Claude Code's idle-notification timer start at all on a `--resume` launch vs. a fresh launch?
- Is the hook config (which drives which native events get piped to `ao hooks claude-code notification`) actually still in effect after `--resume`, or does something about the restore path skip re-applying it?

This doesn't change the suggested fix direction from my prior comment (don't reset `FirstSignalAt` on a resume that reuses the same native session id) — that's still the more robust fix since it doesn't depend on Claude Code's own idle-notification behavior. But it's worth noting in case the assigned worker wants to also chase down why `idle_prompt` itself is silent on resume, as a secondary/defense-in-depth fix.

Requested change: make the generated-token workflow unavoidable in publish paths, and document the convention.

`package` and `make` are covered by `prepackage` / `premake`, but `publish` currently only runs:

```json
"publish": "npm run build:daemon && electron-forge publish"
```

The release and nightly workflows call `npm run publish` directly, so those paths can build from stale `src/styles/design-system.generated.css` if the generated output was not refreshed before publishing. For this PR’s new source-of-truth model, `publish` should also run the token generator, either via a `prepublish` script or by changing the script to include `npm run tokens` before `build:daemon`.

Can we also document the convention in the design-system docs or a short note near `src/styles/tokens.ts` / `src/styles/README.md`? Something like:

- edit token values in `src/styles/primitives.ts`, bridge mappings in `tailwind-bridge.ts`, and generated utilities in `utilities.ts`
- never hand-edit `src/styles/design-system.generated.css`
- run `npm run tokens` after token changes
- CI/publish paths verify or regenerate the generated CSS

That will make future token changes follow the new pipeline instead of drifting back toward direct CSS edits.

## Review: feature releases (per-PR installable prerelease builds)

**Strong design, well-tested, but one blocker that makes the feature unreachable, and one claimed capability that isn't implemented.**

Good separation of `channel` (home) from `feature` (overlay), migration-safe `coerceFeature`, real channel isolation defended by the guard job + the electron-updater predicate regression test, solid unit coverage.

### 🔴 Blocker: the Feature Releases picker is unreachable

`UpdatesSection.tsx` (`primaryValue`, `handlePrimaryChannel`, the `<Select>`, and the `{primaryValue === "feature" && ...}` gate):

```
const primaryValue = form.feature != null ? "feature" : form.channel;   // derived only
// handlePrimaryChannel("feature"): "just reveal the secondary select" -> sets NOTHING
<Select value={primaryValue} onValueChange={handlePrimaryChannel} ...>  // controlled
{primaryValue === "feature" && <FeatureBuildsSelect .../>}
```

The `<Select>` is fully controlled by `primaryValue`. Selecting "Feature Releases" calls `handlePrimaryChannel("feature")`, which updates no state, so `form.feature` stays `null`, `primaryValue` recomputes to `form.channel`, the dropdown snaps back to Stable/Nightly, and the picker never renders. The only thing that sets `form.feature` is `handlePinBuild`, which lives inside the picker. Chicken-and-egg: a user with no existing pin can never open it.

**Fix:** add `const [showFeature, setShowFeature] = useState(false)` (true in the "feature" branch, false in latest/nightly) and gate on `primaryValue === "feature" || showFeature`. Existing tests seed `feature` directly, so they mock past this interaction; add one that actually selects "Feature Releases" from the dropdown.

### 🟠 Claimed "Automatic fall-home" is not implemented

`desktop-release.md` step 5 and the PR body both state that if the pinned PR's build is retired, the app "detects the retirement on its next update poll, clears the pin, and falls back to the home channel automatically." There is no code that clears `settings.feature` on retirement; it is only ever nulled by `handleReturnToHome` (user click) or the opt-in defaults. When the `pr<N>` release is deleted, `autoUpdater.channel = "pr2270"` just 404s the feed and emits `error`; the pin persists across restarts (`startAutoUpdates` re-pins every launch). Manual recovery via the banner works, but the automatic path is documented-but-absent. Either implement it (on check: if `feature` is set and `listFeatureBuilds()` no longer contains that PR, write `feature: null` and reconfigure) or remove the claim from the docs and PR body.

### 🟡 Minor

- **Quota vs rebuild** (`feature-release.yml` guard): the quota counts all open-PR feature builds before the "delete prior build" step runs. Rebuilding a PR that already has a live build while 5 are active fails with "retire one first" even though the rebuild is net-zero. Consider excluding `inputs.pr` from the count.
- **Fork cleanup on close** (`feature-release-cleanup.yml`): `pull_request: closed` from a fork gets a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so `gh release delete` fails for fork builds on close. The daily `schedule` sweep covers them, so this is fine; worth a one-line comment noting the sweep is the real backstop for fork builds.
- **Duplicate parser**: `parseFeatureBuild` exists in both `feature-version.mjs` (strict, `\d{12}`) and `feature-builds.ts` (loose, `-pr(\d+)\.`). The comment acknowledges avoiding a cross-dir import; acceptable, but align the anchors to avoid drift.
- **Unrelated churn**: the ellipsis replacements in `UpdatesSection.tsx` (Saving, Downloading, Checking) are a style change unrelated to feature releases and add diff noise. Split out or drop.

### Over-engineering note

`feature-channel-resolution.test.mjs` re-implements electron-updater's `selectTag` predicate and tests the copy, not the library. Reasonable canary for a version bump, but it verifies your reproduction, not their actual `GitHubProvider`; keep it, just don't over-trust it.

The blocker and the fall-home gap are the two I'd hold the merge on.

Selecting "Feature Releases" sets `showFeature`, Stable/Nightly and "Return to home" clear it. Added a test that actually opens the dropdown, selects "Feature Releases", and asserts the picker mounts (empty state).

**🟠 Auto fall-home** — implemented (kept the capability rather than dropping the claim). @illegalcall 
Thanks for the review. The core change: **new-session shortcut detection now happens in the main process via `before-input-event`**, which is the application-level boundary flagged in the comments. That one change resolves both focus-related bugs and let me delete the fragile guard.

**# 1 — Dead in terminal-focused view (High)**
Root-caused to `isEditableTarget` classifying xterm's helper `<textarea>` as an editable field, so the shortcut short-circuited exactly where it mattered. The guard is **removed entirely** — detection now lives in `main/new-session-shortcut.ts` (`before-input-event` on the main window), which fires regardless of which element has focus, including the terminal. The main process forwards an `app:new-session` IPC to the shell renderer, which owns the routing (scoped project vs. create-project fallback). Note: editable-target suppression is intentionally gone, not just untested — the shortcut *should* work while the terminal (an editable element) is focused.

**# 5 — Doesn't cross the Browser-preview boundary (Medium)**
The same hook is now attached per preview `WebContentsView` in `browser-view-host.ts`, forwarding to the shell renderer. So the shortcut works with the native preview focused. Also guarded against key auto-repeat so holding the combo opens the dialog once.

**# 2 — Missing boundary coverage (Hard)**
Added tests across each seam: the shared matcher (`shared/shortcuts.test.ts`), the main-process `before-input` dispatch incl. keyDown-only / auto-repeat / non-match (`main/new-session-shortcut.test.ts`), renderer project scoping + no-project fallback (`renderer/lib/new-session-shortcut.test.ts`), and dialog opening + navigation on create (`GlobalNewTaskDialog.test.tsx`).

**# 3 — Single-use delegation components (Hard)**
`CreateProjectShortcutBridge` and `CreateProjectNonceListener` are **deleted**. The ⌘N "no project in scope" fallback now flows through an `openSignal` prop on the existing, always-mounted `CreateProjectFlow` — no pass-through components.

**# 4 — Duplicate task-creation completion path (Judgement)**
`GlobalNewTaskDialog` is now the **single owner** of the invalidate-then-navigate completion path. `ShellTopbar` and `SessionsBoard` both route their "New task" buttons through `requestNewTask`, and their local dialogs/handlers are removed.

## UI/UX Audit cross-reference — AO-01 (P0)

This issue is the primary existing tracker for **AO-01: External file changes are not reflected until the project is reopened** from the [UI/UX Audit](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/issues/2728) (15 July 2026).

The audit elevates the severity framing: stale file views during concurrent agent activity can cause users to make decisions on information that is no longer accurate — a **P0 trust/correctness** issue.

### Audit acceptance criteria
- Creating, editing, renaming, or deleting a tracked file updates the relevant AO view without reopening.
- Simultaneous agent activity does not leave the board, preview, or diff view stale.
- Refresh failures explain what could not be updated.
- The user can see the last synchronization time or current sync status.

**Tracking epic:** #2728

Valid issue, but a few corrections are needed:

- `localControlRequest` does **not** allow loopback origins, it rejects any request with an `Origin` header. The config endpoint simply isn’t protected by it; it uses the global CORS middleware, which allows loopback origins.
- Electron’s sandbox and disabled Node integration do not disable ordinary browser JavaScript. Raw `<script>` content in the preview still executes and can call the same origin daemon API.
- I’d rate this **medium severity**, not high: it requires attacker controlled workspace content to be loaded in the desktop preview and `postCreate` executes during a subsequent spawn. Impact is lower when the agent already has unrestricted shell access, but it can bypass approval-gated workflows.
- Validating `postCreate` alone is not sufficient because arbitrary shell commands are its intended behavior. Preview isolation plus stricter API origin controls/CSP is the stronger fix.
- The symlink escape appears valid but should be tracked separately as an arbitrary file read issue.

> ## Review Summary
> I reviewed this implementation against AO's existing GitHub observer flow and GitLab's REST API behavior. Using REST exclusively for GitLab is acceptable and is not a blocker by itself. The provider abstraction, GitLab authentication support, and reuse of AO's existing SCM domain are directionally correct.
> 
> However, the implementation is not ready to merge because transient API failures can corrupt durable state, project changes trigger excessive MR refreshes, current GitLab mergeability values are mapped incorrectly, and rate-limit instructions are ignored. There are also correctness problems around provider isolation, repository identity, approvals, and pagination.
> 
> ### 1. Transient failures can overwrite durable SCM state
> `FetchPullRequests` records an error but returns a keyed `Fetched=false` observation with a nil batch error. The observer does not reject `Fetched=false`, so that placeholder can proceed to persistence. Pipeline, job, and approval failures are also converted to `unknown`, empty checks, or `none`, while the final observation remains `Fetched=true`.
> 
> A timeout, 429, 5xx response, or malformed payload can therefore replace previously valid MR metadata, CI, review, and mergeability facts. Failed retrieval must preserve the last durable state and must not advance ETags or refresh cursors.
> 
> ### 2. A project ETag change refreshes every MR
> The project guard requests only the latest open MR with `per_page=1`. When its ETag changes, AO paginates through every open MR, marks every tracked MR in that project as a refresh candidate, and executes approximately four additional REST requests for each tracked MR.
> 
> A change to one MR in a project containing 50 tracked MRs can produce approximately 252 requests. GitLab supports `updated_after` on project MR listings, so ordinary synchronization should request only MRs updated since the last successful cursor. Use `state=all` to include opened, closed, and merged MRs, retain an overlap window to avoid timestamp races, advance the cursor only after successful processing, and reserve complete listings for startup and periodic reconciliation. This would reduce the same one-MR update to approximately 56 requests under the current pipeline-guard design.
> 
> Reference: [GitLab project merge-request listing](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/merge_requests/#list-project-merge-requests).
> 
> ### 3. Current mergeability values are mapped incorrectly
> `effectiveMergeStatus()` prefers `detailed_merge_status`, but the mapper expects legacy values such as `can_be_merged` and `cannot_be_merged`. Current GitLab values include `mergeable`, `conflict`, `checking`, `preparing`, `need_rebase`, and `requested_changes`. Consequently, a mergeable MR can be reported as blocked, and a conflicting MR may not be reported as conflicting.
> 
> Tests must populate `DetailedMergeStatus` and cover current values while retaining legacy aliases for older GitLab installations.
> 
> ### 4. GitLab rate-limit instructions are discarded
> A 429 is reduced to a generic `ErrRateLimited`. AO ignores `Retry-After`, `RateLimit-Reset`, and remaining-quota headers and continues polling every 30 seconds. The adapter should expose structured retry information, apply a provider-level cooldown with bounded backoff and jitter, and use a finite HTTP timeout. Conditional 304 responses still consume request capacity.
> 
> References: [GitLab.com limits](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/gitlab_com/#rate-limits-on-gitlabcom) and [rate-limit headers](https://docs.gitlab.com/administration/settings/user_and_ip_rate_limits/#response-headers).
> 
> ### 5. One provider failure suppresses the other provider
> The multi-provider dispatcher processes provider groups sequentially and returns immediately on the first error. A GitLab timeout can discard successful GitHub observations or prevent GitHub from being called, depending on map iteration order. Provider failures must remain scoped to their own references, and healthy-provider results should continue through persistence.
> 
> ### 6. Repository identity is not preserved end to end
> Claim validation compares owner and repository but ignores provider and host. Repositories with identical names on GitHub and GitLab can therefore pass validation incorrectly. Nested GitLab namespaces are parsed inconsistently, and self-managed hosts can be recognized while API traffic still uses `https://gitlab.com/api/v4`.
> 
> The provider, host, complete namespace, REST base, and credential host must be derived from one canonical repository identity. Either support self-managed GitLab end to end or explicitly scope this change to GitLab.com.
> 
> ### 7. Approval state and persistence are unreliable
> The approvals endpoint is requested twice during review refresh. The implementation compares `len(approved_by)` with `approvals_required`, but `approved_by` can contain approvals that do not satisfy the applicable rules. Use `approved`, `approvals_left`, or the REST approval-state endpoint.
> 
> Generated review summaries also need stable IDs; otherwise multiple approvers use the same empty persistence key and overwrite one another.
> 
> ### 8. Jobs and discussions are truncated
> Only the first 100 pipeline jobs and first 100 discussions are fetched. Later failed jobs and unresolved review threads can remain invisible indefinitely. Follow GitLab pagination links or explicitly represent bounded responses as partial without deleting previously persisted data.
> 
> ## API Consumption
> For 50 active sessions, stable polling is approximately 102-200 requests per minute, moderate activity is approximately 150-300 requests per minute, and cold synchronization is approximately 400-500 requests. Large failed-pipeline bursts can add hundreds of job-trace requests. This makes incremental discovery and rate-limit recovery important for the REST-only design.
> 
> ## Conclusion
> The REST-only direction is acceptable, but the blocking areas above need to be addressed before merging: durable-state preservation, incremental MR discovery, current mergeability mapping, rate-limit recovery, provider isolation, repository identity, and approval correctness.
> 
> The package documentation should also describe REST as a deliberate compatibility and raw-trace decision rather than claiming that GitLab GraphQL does not support pipelines or approvals. Once these issues are resolved with focused tests, the implementation can be reassessed for merge readiness.

Thank you for the thorough review. All eight blocking findings plus the documentation concern have been addressed. Build and vet are clean, 333 tests pass with `-race`. Changes are split into one commit per finding for reviewability.

## 1. Transient failures preserve durable state

`FetchPullRequests` propagates the first sub-fetch error as a non-nil return and leaves a `Fetched=false` placeholder. `fetchCI` and `fetchApprovalDecision` return `(value, error)` instead of silently degrading. The observer rejects `!obs.Fetched` observations — no persistence, no ETag or cursor advancement.

**Tests:** `TransientFailureReturnsError` (500), `PipelineFailureReturnsError` (502), `ApprovalFailureReturnsError` (503), `Poll_RejectsFetchedFalseObservation`.

## 2. Incremental MR discovery

`ListPRsByRepo(ctx, repo, updatedAfter)` sends `state=all` + `updated_after` when a cursor exists; first poll is a full listing. `LastSyncCursor` advances only after successful persistence. 5-minute overlap window absorbs clock skew. Reduces the 50-MR scenario from ~252 to ~56 requests.

**Tests:** `IncrementalDiscovery_OnlyUpdatedMRsRefreshed`, `IncrementalDiscovery_CursorNotAdvancedOnFailure`, `ListPRsByRepo_UpdatedAfterAndStateAll`, `ListPRsByRepo_FirstPollFullListing`.

## 3. Current mergeability values mapped correctly

`mergeabilityFromMR` handles all current `detailed_merge_status` values (`mergeable`, `conflict`, `checking`, `preparing`, `need_rebase`, `requested_changes`, `not_open`, `merge_request_blocked`, etc.) with legacy aliases retained for older self-managed instances.

**Tests:** `MergeabilityFromMR` (24 cases), `FetchPullRequests_DetailedMergeStatus` (end-to-end).

## 4. Rate-limit recovery

`RateLimitError` exposes `RetryAfter` and `ResetAt` parsed from 429 headers. Observer applies per-provider cooldown (30s–10min, bounded, with jitter). HTTP client uses 30s timeout. Provider calls skipped during cooldown, resume after expiry.

**Tests:** `ClassifyError_RateLimitRetryAfter`, `ClassifyError_RateLimitResetHeader`, `NewClient_DefaultHTTPTimeout`, `Poll_RateLimitCooldown_SkipsProviderCalls`, `Poll_RateLimitCooldown_ResumesAfterExpiry`.

## 5. Provider isolation

`multi.FetchPullRequests` partitions by provider, processes independently, returns partial results with nil error if any group succeeds. Error returned only when all groups fail.

**Tests:** `OneProviderFailsOthersSucceed`, `AllProvidersFail`.

## 6. Repository identity end-to-end

`splitOwnerRepo` handles nested namespaces. `requireSameRepo` compares host, not just owner/repo. Per-host client map with `clientForHost` deriving `https://<host>/api/v4` for self-managed instances.

**Tests:** `ParseRepository` (nested + self-managed), `FetchPullRequests_SelfManagedRESTBase`, `RequireSameRepoGitLab` (cross-provider and cross-host mismatch).

## 7. Approval state and persistence

`approvalDecision` trusts the `approved` bool, not `len(approved_by)`. Approvals fetched once and reused. Review summaries get stable IDs (`approval:<username>`).

**Tests:** `TrustsApprovedField`, `NotApproved`, `SingleApprovalsCall` (hit exactly once), `StableReviewIDs`.

## 8. Full pagination for jobs and discussions

`doGETPaginated` follows `Link rel=next`, capped at 10 pages, returns a `truncated` flag. `Partial` is set from actual truncation, not item count.

**Tests:** `PipelineJobsPagination` (150 jobs across 2 pages), `DiscussionsPagination` (130 threads, `Partial=false`), `DiscussionsTruncated` (1000 threads, `Partial=true`).

## 9. Package documentation

`doc.go` rewritten: REST as a deliberate choice for raw trace access and API compatibility, not a GraphQL limitation.

## Known non-blocking items

1. Periodic full reconciliation (~30 min) deferred — `LastSyncCursor` infrastructure supports adding it later.
2. Pagination cap at 10 pages is a safety valve; `Partial=true` only when the cap is hit.

Adding a macOS data point with the **same symptom** (launcher exits cleanly, nothing stays up; direct launch works) but a different root cause — useful in case there is a shared "launcher vs direct launch" surface worth generalizing.

## Environment

- OS: macOS Sequoia (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64)
- Self-built `.app` from a fork: `npm run package` → deployed via `ditto` over an existing `/Applications/Agent Orchestrator.app` (adhoc / linker-signed, not Developer ID)
- Launcher: `~/.local/bin/ao start`

## Symptom (matches the OP)

`ao start` prints its launcher banner and returns, but **no window opens and no daemon binds** — `ao status` stays `stopped`, no `agent-orchestrator` process appears, nothing on `127.0.0.1:3001`. `open "/Applications/Agent Orchestrator.app"` behaves the same — `exit 0`, silent, no process.

Unlike the Linux case, the child is not dying orphaned here — it is **never started** by LaunchServices at all.

## Root cause (macOS)

After a `ditto` deploy over the existing `.app`, the code signature becomes inconsistent. `spctl --assess` reports:

```
code has no resources but signature indicates they must be present
```

and `codesign --verify` fails. `open`/LaunchServices then refuses to launch the bundle **silently** — no error, no crash report, nothing in `log show`. The `com.apple.provenance` xattr is also present and is not removable on Sequoia (`xattr -cr` is a no-op for it), but re-signing is what actually unblocks the launch.

## Workaround (macOS)

1. Re-sign adhoc: `codesign --force --deep --sign - "/Applications/Agent Orchestrator.app"` — `codesign --verify` then reports `valid on disk` (`spctl` still says `rejected`, which is expected and harmless for adhoc).
2. If `open` is still silent after re-signing, launch the binary directly, bypassing LaunchServices:

```bash
"/Applications/Agent Orchestrator.app/Contents/MacOS/agent-orchestrator" &
```

Both bring the app + daemon up; `ao status` → `ready` in ~5–8s.

## Where this overlaps with the OP

Both cases reduce to: **the app is healthy when launched directly, but the "official" launcher path does not bring it up** — on Linux because the child is not detached, on macOS because the (self-built) bundle fails LaunchServices' signature check. If `ao start` is reworked to daemonize/detach per the suggested fix, it would be worth confirming whether the macOS launcher path can also surface *why* the launch failed (today it is fully silent) — a non-zero exit or a stderr line from the launcher would have saved the tracing here. (Not claiming this is the same bug — just a sibling symptom on a different OS.)

### Live evidence

Every `/docs*` URL returns an **HTTP 307 that redirects to itself** → infinite loop:

| URL | Status | Location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/docs` | 307 | `/docs` (self) |
| `/docs/architecture` | 307 | `/docs/architecture` (self) |
| `/docs/plugins` | 307 | `/docs/plugins` (self) |
| `/docs/changelog` | 307 | `/docs/changelog` (self) |
| `/docs/installation` | 307 | `/docs/installation` (self) |
| `/docs/cli` | 307 | `/docs/cli` (self) |

Control cases: `/` → **200**, `/install` → **404**. So **only** `/docs*` loops; the rest of the site routes normally.

### Why this is not a code bug

The docs app lives at `frontend/src/landing/` (Fumadocs + Next.js). I traced the full redirect surface:

- `app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx` — no `redirect()` call; calls `notFound()` on missing pages (would 404, not loop).
- `app/docs/layout.tsx` — no redirects.
- `next.config.mjs` — trivial: `createMDX()({})`. No `trailingSlash`, no `i18n`, no `redirects()`.
- **No `middleware.ts`** anywhere in the landing app.
- No `vercel.json` / `_redirects` / `_headers` in the repo.

A 307 self-redirect scoped *exclusively* to `/docs*` with zero redirect logic in the codebase is the signature of a **misconfigured redirect/forwarding rule at the CDN/hosting layer** (aoagents.dev is fronted by Cloudflare). The repo cannot fix this — whoever controls the deployment needs to check the Cloudflare Redirect Rules / Page Rules (or wherever the edge config lives) for a pattern matching `/docs*`.

### Minor: footer targets that don't have a page

Even after the redirect loop is fixed, several footer links point to pages that don't exist in `content/docs/`:
- `/docs` (Overview) — no root `index.mdx`
- `/docs/changelog` — no `changelog.mdx`
- `/docs/cli` — no `cli.mdx`

These would 404 (via `notFound()`), not loop. Worth resolving as a follow-up once the redirect is unblocked.

### Notes on the report
- Reporter's cited paths (`app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx`, `content/docs/*`) exist — they omit the `landing/` prefix. Actual paths are `frontend/src/landing/app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx` and `frontend/src/landing/content/docs/`.
- No assignee, no comments, no related open PRs as of now.

**Update — the `--issue` path has the same problem, and it points at the real root cause.**

I initially framed this around the freeform `--prompt` path, but the architecture intends workers to be spawned **on an issue** (`ao spawn --issue <N>`), not on an inline prompt. So I checked whether the `--issue` path hands the full issue to the worker. It does **not** — it truncates too:

`backend/internal/observe/trackerintake/observer.go`:

```go
// maxIntakePromptLen mirrors the session HTTP prompt limit. Intake uses the
// session service directly, so it must enforce the same boundary itself.
maxIntakePromptLen = 4096

intakePromptTruncationNotice = "\n\n[Issue content truncated to fit the session prompt limit. Open the linked issue for the full details.]\n"
```

and `capIntakePrompt()` slices the issue body down to ~4 KB and appends the truncation notice. So even the "correct" path is **lossy**: a detailed issue gets truncated, and the worker is told "open the linked issue for the full details" — i.e. the worker is expected to re-fetch the very issue AO already fetched.

## The actual architectural smell

AO models a worker task as a **prompt string with a size ceiling**, then inlines the issue body into that string and truncates to fit. The deeper fix is the inverse: **the task is a reference to a source the worker reads itself**, not an inlined blob. For `--issue`:

- pass the issue ref (owner/repo/number, plus a resolved API endpoint / cached snapshot path), and
- let the worker fetch/read the full issue (it already can — it has the tracker credentials and is told to "open the linked issue" today), instead of AO trying to fit the body into a 4 KB prompt budget.

That removes the truncation entirely for the `--issue` path, and for the freeform `--prompt` path the same idea applies (spill to a workspace file, pass a pointer) rather than inline-and-truncate.

## So the suggestion generalizes

The pre-flight size check from the original post is still useful for the `--prompt` case (fail fast with "too long, use --issue or --prompt-file"). But the `--issue` case shouldn't have a size problem at all — it should pass a reference, not a truncated body. Both reduce to: **stop inlining task content into a length-capped prompt; pass a reference and let the worker read the source.**

(Not changing the issue title since both paths are in scope — happy to split into two if a maintainer prefers `--issue`-truncation as its own bug.)

## New Report — full local repro, with two additional findings
**Reported by:** maintainer (local desktop app) | **Date:** 2026-07-19 | **Analyzed against:** `dec77c61b` | **App:** nightly channel, daemon `dev` on :3001 (app-owned, pid 4688)

Reproduced end-to-end with session `agent-orchestrator-4` (codex worker, spawned 2026-07-13). Its PR [#2807](https://github.com/AgentWrapper/agent-orchestrator/pull/2807) (`ao/agent-orchestrator-4/update-landing-video`) merged at `2026-07-18 21:58:02Z`; the merge observation landed at `21:58:00Z` (`pr` row: `pr_state=merged, is_merged=1`) and the lifecycle reaction marked the session terminated ~4 min later (`updatedAt 22:02:31Z`).

State captured immediately after, confirming the leak:

- **API/DB:** `isTerminated: true`, `activity.state: "exited"`, `status: "merged"`
- **Runtime:** tmux session `agent-orchestrator-4` still alive (created Jul 17), **codex agent process still running inside it**
- **Disk:** worktree `~/.ao/data/worktrees/agent-orchestrator/agent-orchestrator-4` present, branch still held; no `session_worktrees` row for this session (pre-dates that table's population)

### Finding 1: it's not just the worktree — the runtime and agent process leak too
The doc comment on `MarkTerminated` (`backend/internal/lifecycle/manager.go:465`) says it terminates "without tearing down external resources", and the merged-PR reaction (`backend/internal/lifecycle/reactions.go:152-157`) calls exactly that. So every merge-terminated session leaks a **live tmux session + agent process**, not only a worktree. This is what makes the UX confusing: the terminal pane still renders a live, responsive agent, so the session *looks* not-terminated — while the Kill button is hidden because `sessionIsActive()` (`frontend/src/renderer/types/workspace.ts:285-286`, `status !== "merged" && status !== "terminated"`) gates the topbar kill control (`frontend/src/renderer/components/ShellTopbar.tsx:185`).

### Finding 2: the backend Kill path works fine on merge-terminated sessions — the gap is UI-only
`ao session kill agent-orchestrator-4` on the already-terminated session succeeded (exit 0), killed the tmux session, and reclaimed the worktree. So no backend change is strictly required to *recover*; the CLI is a full workaround. The fix space is therefore:

1. **Best:** merged-PR reaction performs full teardown (reuse `Kill`'s path incl. dirty-worktree preservation) instead of flag-only `MarkTerminated`, or schedules cleanup;
2. **And/or:** UI keeps a cleanup/kill affordance for terminated sessions whose runtime is still alive (a "Clean up" button instead of hiding Kill entirely).

Thanks for the thorough review, @illegalcall. I've worked the design through and I'm confident in the direction. Here's the plan. It's **5 PRs**, and this PR (#2819) becomes PR 2.

2 decisions before starting implementation:

- **I reuse the existing `session_updated` CDC event** for both the finalizer wake and the live-UI nudge, rather than adding a new `event_type`. Adding one would force a `change_log` CHECK-widen rebuild that recreates every trigger — which would collide with, and silently revert, my own open PR #2798 (session-rename adds `display_name` to `sessions_cdc_update`). Reuse avoids the rebuild entirely: the facts-table trigger emits `session_updated` with a `{id}`-only payload, `WHEN`-guarded to exclude the retry-bookkeeping columns so it can't self-wake the reconciler, and the live-wake path filters on `isTerminated` and never immediate-retries (retries stay on `next_attempt_at`).
- Designing this surfaced **two pre-existing bugs on `main`** that I'm handling explicitly: the AO reviewer pane leaks today, and legacy/backlog terminal rows can reach cleanup with an unresolvable runtime handle (#1458).

**PR 1 — Storage foundation (no behavior change).** A cleanup-facts table (`workspace_disposition` ∈ `pending`/`removed`/`preserved_dirty`/`failed`/`not_applicable`, `runtime_released_at`, `attempt_count`, `next_attempt_at`, `failure_code`; no stored display status) plus a monotonic `sessions.cleanup_generation` column, sqlc + store. Migration `0024`, coordinated with #2798 — whichever lands second rebases to `0025`. The facts-table trigger reuses `session_updated`; no `change_log` rebuild.

**PR 2a — Reviewer runtime teardown (pre-existing-bug fix, stacked on #2800).** The AO reviewer runs in the worker's worktree as a separate pane `"review-"+workerID`, but `Cancel` only interrupts it — so a cancelled reviewer leaks the pane today (the #2715 family). Since my open #2800 (reviewer-harness-respawn) already introduces the reviewer `Destroy` seam, PR 2a stacks on it and adds an idempotent `Launcher.Teardown` + `Engine.TeardownReviewer(workerID)`, wired into `Cancel` so the pane is destroyed rather than merely interrupted. (The harness-change supersede case is already handled by #2800's destroy-on-spawn.) Independent of the reclaim work; it lets PR 2 safely reclaim a worker's worktree without corrupting an in-flight reviewer's cwd.

**PR 2 — Finalizer + reconciler (this PR).** Removes the callback seam (lifecycle back to fact-only, which also breaks the construction cycle). Extracts one low-level release core — runtime-first (abort + retry if runtime destroy fails; don't treat a nil `Destroy` on an unrouted handle as success, #1458), safe child-first worktree removal, dirty preserved, and clean multi-repo children reclaimed even when a sibling is dirty (per-repo state stays in `session_worktrees`) — reused by `Kill`, bulk `Cleanup`, and the new `FinalizeTerminalSession`. The finalizer takes a per-session keyed lock, re-checks terminal + no *restorable* marker + generation, and tears down + awaits any live reviewer (via PR 2a) before the worktree phase. The reconciler wakes on `session_updated` (non-blocking subscriber), runs a **sessions-driven** boot scan (`sessions LEFT JOIN facts`, so it heals the pre-existing leaked backlog — not just rows that already have facts), and retries transient failures with capped backoff plus a capped attempt count → `failed`. Boot reorders so adoption/restore reconciliation completes, the CDC subscription registers, then observers start. The Restore→Terminate reset is atomic by construction: `MarkSpawned` bumps `cleanup_generation` in the same `UPDATE` as `is_terminated=false`.

**PR 3 — Per-session cleanup API.** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/cleanup` (idempotent, terminal-only, returns refreshed facts, preserves the error envelope), bulk cleanup delegates to the same primitive, and the session read model exposes the facts so the UI can derive presentation at read time.

**PR 4 — Frontend recoverability.** Cleanup state + retry affordance on the Done/Terminated card, keyed off the raw `is_terminated` fact (so merged sessions get it too, not just terminated ones); the primary Merged/Terminated label stays unchanged.

Mapping to your 8 steps: (1)(2)(3)(7) → PR 2, (4) → PR 1, (5) → PR 3, (6) → PR 4, (8) tests throughout — including an end-to-end test that flips `is_terminated` and asserts convergence through the real `session_updated` → reconciler → finalizer chain, not just the primitive in isolation. All the useful teardown work and tests from this PR carry over (dirty-worktree handling, the extracted per-session helper, the real-SQLite/git-worktree integration harness — the latter moves to awaiting async finalization).

To set expectations on when the leak closes: PR 2 lands automatic reclaim of clean worktrees + live runtime for every terminal path plus capped-backoff retry of transient failures; preserved-dirty and exhausted-failure cases are safely preserved at PR 2 but only become user-recoverable at PR 3–4.

**Six remaining blockers:**

- **Incremental polling** (bf81060) — `selectRefreshCandidates` now fetches only MRs in the updated set once a `LastSyncCursor` exists; the cursor advances only after successful persistence.
- **Terminal-state observation** (bf81060) — new `reconcileTerminalGitHubPRs` pass issues detail fetches for tracked-open GitHub PRs absent from the `state=open` listing, so merged/closed transitions are no longer permanently missed. GitLab is excluded because its `state=all` listing already retains terminal MRs.
- **Cooldown acknowledgement** (bf81060) — refs skipped under cooldown now call `markRepoRefreshFailed`, so the repo ETag and `LastSyncCursor` do not advance without an observation.
- **Fork identity** (7763adf) — fork MRs fetch the source project's `path_with_namespace` and set `HeadRepo` accordingly; failure propagates so the head repo is never falsified.
- **Credential isolation** (7d934a7, 3b11060) — `isGitLabHost` replaced with an explicit `AllowedHosts` allowlist; `SCMCredentialsAvailable` returns the first real error so `CheckCredentialsOnce` retries instead of disabling until restart.
- **Numeric issue handling** (d6d3bb2) — `githubRepoForTracker` returns false when the origin is a non-GitHub provider, so `ao spawn --issue 42` on a GitLab project no longer falls through to the GitHub tracker.

**Six inline findings:** nested namespaces (593692e), cross-provider display identity (8d4489f), pagination trust (56f526a), log memory bounds (a1ff90b), job completeness (ebe4c97 + 16ce0cb), mixed-provider error propagation (2017bb3).
