Hi @neversettle17-101,
I'd like to pick up this issue. Can I get assigned?

## Measured the replay path — the root cause above needs one correction, and the fix follows from it

I built a probe that runs the real xterm 5.5.0 we ship, in real Chromium, and samples `buffer.active.viewportY` on **every animation frame** during ingest. Distinct consecutive values = the scroll positions a user actually saw painted. That turns this from an argument into a number.

```
payload   98,528 bytes (1000 lines)   grid 200×50

  delivery              writes  frames  positions   ingest  max block   offsets painted
  32KB chunks, 0ms gap       4       8          1    129ms      0.1ms   [951]
  32KB chunks, 4ms gap       4       9          2    150ms      0.1ms   [948 → 951]
  8KB chunks, 0ms gap       13      11          4    183ms      0.2ms   [450 → 699 → 948 → 951]
  8KB chunks, 4ms gap       13      12          5    200ms      0.1ms   [201 → 367 → 616 → 865 → 951]
  4KB chunks, 0ms gap       25      14          7    233ms      0.1ms   [284 → 408 → 533 → … → 951]
  4KB chunks, 8ms gap       25      22         15    367ms      0.1ms   [0 → 76 → 159 → … → 951]
  4KB chunks, 16ms gap      25      33         25    550ms      0.1ms   [0 → 35 → 76 → … → 951]
  one concatenated write     1       8          1    133ms      2.2ms   [951]
```

### Correction: xterm does not split writes into ~15KB batches

The issue body attributes the scroll to xterm chopping large `write()` data into ~15KB internal chunks. It doesn't do that, and the measurement shows it: **a single `write()` of 98,528 bytes painted exactly 1 position.** If it split at ~15KB it would have painted ~7.

Confirmed in the source (`@xterm/xterm@5.5.0`, `src/common/input/WriteBuffer.ts`): `_writeBuffer` holds **one entry per `write()` call**, and `_innerWrite` calls the parser on a whole entry atomically. `WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS = 12` is only checked *after* an entry finishes parsing, to decide whether to yield before the **next** one. There's no size-based splitting anywhere in the file.

### Actual mechanism

The batch granularity is exactly our WebSocket frames.

`attachment.go:182` reads the PTY in 32KB slices → each becomes a WS frame → `useTerminalSession.ts:221-225` does one `terminal.write()` per frame → each lands in its own event-loop turn → the browser paints between turns → each paint shows a further-scrolled state.

Severity is `frame count × inter-frame gap` and nothing else. Same bytes, same terminal: **1** painted position at 4 back-to-back frames, **25** at 25 frames spaced 16ms. That's why some sessions look fine and others look broken — it tracks the PTY read pattern, not the scrollback size directly.

### On the multi-session / renderer-thread theory

Worth ruling out explicitly since it's come up: only **one** `TerminalPane` is ever mounted. `SessionView.tsx:415` renders a single `CenterPane` → single `TerminalPane` for the selected session (tabs switch which one, they don't mount N). `ShellTerminalsView.tsx:106` renders only the active shell tab, and `/terminals` is a separate route. On unmount, `attach()`'s cleanup runs `teardownMux()` → socket closed.

So there's never an A/B/C fan-in of concurrent terminal streams in the renderer. The single-stream case reproduces the bug on its own, which is also what the repro steps in this issue describe. Main-thread saturation is real and worth its own issue for the resize/switching/preview lag — but it isn't this.

### Also: gating on `attached` is too early

`attachment.go`'s run loop calls `setPTY(p)` — which fires `onOpen` → `msgOpened` → frontend `state = "attached"` — and only **then** calls `copyOut(p)`. So `attached` arrives before the first replay byte exists. Extending `showEmptyState` to cover `state === "connecting"` (recommendation 1 in the body) would uncover before the replay starts and change almost nothing on its own.

---

## Proposed fix

**Concatenate the replay into one `write()`, behind a cover, revealed on the write callback.** Concatenation is what removes the cause — measured 25 positions → **1**, for **2.2ms** of main-thread block (one dropped frame at worst, not the UI freeze it's been assumed to be). The cover exists only because you can't concatenate bytes that haven't arrived over the network yet.

**1. Expose xterm's write callback** — `XtermTerminal.tsx:727`

```ts
write: (data, cb) => term.write(data, cb),   // second arg is currently dropped
```

It fires exactly when that chunk finishes parsing — a deterministic reveal signal instead of a timing guess.

**2. Buffer-then-flush during the gate** — `useTerminalSession.ts:221-225`

Open the gate at `connect()`, not at `onOpened` (see above). While gated, `onData` pushes bytes into an array instead of writing. A quiescence timer (~60ms, tuned from a real capture) ends the burst → concat → one `write(all, cb)` → on callback, reveal and switch to passthrough for the rest of the session.

**3. Cover** — `TerminalPane.tsx:365`

`showEmptyState = !handleId` becomes `!handleId || !replaySettled`. Plain `bg-terminal`, no text — the current overlay's *"Starting session / Preparing the worker terminal…"* card would flash on every session switch. Show a message only if the open exceeds ~120ms.

**4. Suppress the resize re-assert while gated** — `useTerminalSession.ts:92, 277-281`

`RESIZE_REASSERT_MS = 250` deliberately re-sends the resize, the backend answers every resize frame with an explicit SIGWINCH, and tmux repaints. That lands ~350ms after the grid settles — after any quiescence gate would have revealed — so without this you get a repaint flash right after the reveal.

(Related: the body's "up to 20 re-fits, each sending a backend Resize" is overstated. `MAX_REFITS = 20` caps *committed* re-fits, xterm only fires `onResize` on an actual grid change, and `RESIZE_DEBOUNCE_MS = 100` collapses bursts — realistically 1–2 SIGWINCHes.)

### Why the cover needs concatenation to be safe

A cover with a hard timeout cap, on its own, reintroduces the bug in the worst case: biggest scrollback → slowest replay → cap fires → uncovers mid-walk. With concatenation, hitting the cap means *flush what you have as one write* — one jump instead of 25 steps. The failure mode degrades to a blink rather than the original bug.

### Edge cases that decide whether this ships clean

- `exit` / `error` during the gate → flush and reveal immediately; never leave a stuck cover
- Generation guard on the quiescence timer (`isCurrentAttachment()` already exists) — a stale connection's timer must not reveal a newly-selected session
- Empty session with no data → the quiescence timer never starts; needs a fallback timer from gate open
- Re-attach: gate resets per generation, `clear()` first, then buffer
- Live output after the gate must be pure passthrough, never buffered

### Verification

The probe asserts the right invariant directly: `positions === 1`. There's also a companion capture script that speaks the mux protocol (`ws://<daemon>/mux`, plain JSON, base64 payloads — no Electron needed), attaches to a live session handle, and records every data frame's actual bytes and arrival time. Replaying that capture through the probe places production exactly on the table above, and the recorded inter-frame gaps are what the quiescence value should be tuned from.

Worth noting the tmux case specifically: `tmux attach-session` replays an alt-screen repaint with cursor addressing rather than 1000 appended lines, so it may scroll quite differently from the conpty ring path. The capture run would show that rather than assume it.

Happy to land the probe under `frontend/e2e/` as a regression test and pick up the implementation.

<sub>Probe limits, so nobody over-reads the numbers: headless Chromium uses the DOM renderer, not WebGL — paint *scheduling* is identical (writes → refresh → rAF) but draw cost differs — and the sweep payload is synthetic. The capture stage removes both.</sub>

## New Report — live orchestrator-side evidence: the idle nudge is not just noisy, its delivery logic is buggy in three distinct ways
**Reported by:** maintainer + orchestrator session logs | **Date:** 2026-07-28 | **Daemon:** app-owned :3001, running post-#2836 build (worker_idle_outbox / migration 25 present; note the checkout at `dec77c61b` predates it, so line refs omitted)

Observed from a single orchestrator session's inbox over 24h:

1. **Delivery to the orchestrator AFTER the worker was terminated.** Session `agent-orchestrator-52` was killed at ~its 13th minute; the "[AO] Worker agent-orchestrator-52 has gone idle" nudge arrived *after* the kill (daemon confirmed `terminated: true` on inspection). The outbox appears to enqueue on the idle transition and deliver later with no terminal-state check at delivery time.

2. **Duplicate deliveries with no state change in between.** Sessions `-63` and `-64` (completed workers, status `review_pending`) each produced two identical nudges minutes apart; session `-40` produced at least four over ~3h on 2026-07-27. Either the outbox lacks ack/dedup, or every observation re-queues.

3. **Re-arming on human interaction with long-done workers.** Session `-32` has been finished and `review_pending` for 8 days; the maintainer typed one message into it ('preview localhost:5173'), the activity flapped active→idle, and the orchestrator got nudged about it twice — as if the week-old worker had just finished. A `review_pending`/`done` session going idle after a human poke is not a signal the orchestrator needs.

**Suggested tightening (if these nudges are kept at all rather than removed as this issue proposes):**
- check `IsTerminated` (and arguably `review_pending`/terminal board zone) at *delivery* time, not just enqueue time;
- dedup by (session, completion-generation) with an ack once delivered — not one nudge per idle transition;
- suppress for sessions whose idle is caused by inbound human/orchestrator messages (the interaction itself proves someone is already looking at it).

Also: the repeated nudges materially pollute the orchestrator's context/attention — each one triggers an inspect cycle (session get + pane capture), which at 2-4 dupes per worker across a 10-worker fleet is real overhead.

## Self-review pass on the replay gate

Reviewed this branch against `origin/main` and pushed fixes in c56ce3f. Full renderer suite green (1155 tests, 89 files), `tsc --noEmit` clean.

No defect was found that produces an incorrect outcome — the strand analysis is complete, and the two paths that are easy to miss (socket dying before `opened`; teardown with no reconnect) are both genuinely handled. What follows is one behavioural gap and two comments that documented mechanisms the code does not have.

### The mechanism this PR relies on is real — but #3160's root cause is wrong

Worth recording, because the PR is unusable if the issue is right. #3160 says xterm "splits it into chunks, rendering each chunk before processing the next" in ~15KB batches. If that were true of xterm 5.5.0, concatenating the frames would change nothing.

It isn't. In the installed `_innerWrite`, the drain loop hands **one whole queue entry** to the parser in a single synchronous call and only then tests its 12ms budget:

```js
for (; buffer.length > offset; ) {
  parse(buffer[offset]);                 // whole entry, uninterrupted
  callbacks[offset](); offset++;
  if (Date.now() - start >= 12) break;   // check is BETWEEN entries
}
if (buffer.length > offset) setTimeout(drain);   // yield -> browser may paint
```

The yield sits between entries, never inside one. So N writes can paint between them; one write cannot, at any size. The PR's own comments describe this correctly — only the issue text is wrong. Also means the 1MB byte cap doesn't reintroduce the scroll; it only bounds main-thread block time, which is what its comment claims.

### 1. A pane that replayed nothing stayed covered for the full cap — fixed

The quiet window was armed only from an incoming data frame, so with no data nothing triggered an early flush and the 750ms cap was the only path. The user got a blank cover for 750ms with `Loading latest output…` from 120ms, on a pane with nothing to show. Before this branch they'd have seen the empty terminal immediately.

The `flushReplay` empty-chunks branch claimed otherwise — "reveal immediately rather than holding the cover for the full cap" — but only reveals immediately *once something calls it*, and here the only caller was the cap. The existing test couldn't catch it: it advanced exactly 750ms and asserted settled, which passes either way.

Fix is `REPLAY_FIRST_BYTE_MS = 250`, armed at `opened` alongside the cap. The important part is that it **lifts the cover without ending the gate**. The naive version — arming the quiet timer at `opened` — is actively harmful: `opened` fires from `setPTY` *before* `copyOut`, so a 60ms timer can expire before the first replay byte exists, flush an empty buffer, clear `replayBuffering`, and leave the real replay to arrive frame by frame with the bug fully intact and no cover over it. Same trap the cap-anchoring comment already warns about. There's a regression test that fails if this ever becomes a flush.

### 2. A test credited the cap for a case the cap cannot cover — fixed

`lifts the cover when the attachment is torn down with no reconnect scheduled` said "The cap timer is what guarantees the cover still lifts — it is deliberately shorter than OPEN_TIMEOUT_MS". That test never emits `opened`, and the cap is armed from `opened`, so it never runs. `teardownMux` is what settles. The implementation comment in `connect()` says this correctly, so the test contradicted the code fifteen lines away — on precisely the risk class this design is most exposed to.

Reworded, and now pins the timing: not settled at 2999ms, settled at `OPEN_TIMEOUT_MS`. That fails if either replay timer is ever moved back to `connect()`.

### 3. The resize deferral's rationale was inverted — comment corrected, behaviour kept

The comment justified deferring the re-assert as avoiding a repaint that "would land just after the cover lifts and flash". Deferring *guarantees* that repaint:

| | Fire mid-burst | Defer to flush (ships) |
|---|---|---|
| Repaint bytes go | into the buffer, absorbed into the single write — invisible | onto the revealed pane — visible |

The real benefit is a **shorter cover**: added frames restart the 60ms quiet window, so not injecting more bytes lets the burst go quiet sooner. That's a good reason, just not the one the comment gave. Behaviour unchanged; comment now states the actual trade.

The latent bug the timer split fixes — debounce and re-assert sharing one slot, letting a stale grid land after a newer one — is real and correctly handled.

### Verified and holding

- **Buffering frame references is safe.** `base64ToBytes` allocates a fresh `Uint8Array` per frame, so nothing is reused underneath.
- **No strand path.** Enumerated all of quiet / cap / byte-cap / exit / error / socket-closed / user-input / teardown; every terminal state has a live settle path.
- **No write to a disposed xterm.** `AttachedTerminal` is keyed by handle, so a session switch remounts the subtree and React runs the parent's flush before the child disposes. The one path unmounting xterm alone is the init-failure early return, where `onError` fires from the `catch` around construction — before `onReady`, so no attachment exists.
- **Byte accounting at the 1MB trip** — tripping chunk is pushed before the check, so it's included: no loss, no double write.
- **Decoder ordering** — joined buffer decoded once, before later live chunks.
- **The measurement claims are internally consistent.** "~2ms parse" and "~44KB/ms" only agree if the burst was ~88KB over ~25 frames, i.e. ~3.5KB each. That follows from `copyOut` forwarding whatever a read yields; 32KB is the ceiling, not the frame size.

### Accepted residuals

- Replays over 1MB keep the walk for the tail once the byte cap trips. Right call — a multi-MB single parse would freeze the main thread.
- One blank frame is possible at the reveal, since the cover's removal goes through React while xterm's paint goes through its own scheduler. Blank, never a scroll.
- The reattach path is uncovered by design (state gate). Still gets the single write, so one jump rather than a walk.

Thanks for offering to take this on — please go ahead, it's yours. Your plan is the right shape, and the instinct not to broaden Enter nudges to harnesses that can't safely report blocked states is exactly the correct call.

We prototyped this locally to confirm the diagnosis before filing, so the specifics below are verified rather than theoretical. Passing them along so you don't have to re-derive any of it.

**Root cause.** In `backend/internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/tmux.go` (the chunk loop, around line 411), when a `POST /api/v1/sessions/{sessionId}/send` is cancelled mid-paste — HTTP client disconnect, renderer re-render, network blip — the loop short-circuits on the cancellation error *before* the post-paste pause and the trailing Enter fire. The chunks tmux already accepted stay in the pane as an unsubmitted draft. The GUI clears its input box on the 200 response, so it looks sent, but the worker never received a prompt. A later send then appends more chunks to that same input box and fires a single Enter, submitting both messages together — that's the "flush" behaviour people notice, and why the symptom looks intermittent.

**Approach that works.** Once the first chunk has been accepted, run the rest of the chunk loop, the pre-Enter pause, and the Enter itself on a context detached from the caller's — `context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), enterDelay + a small margin)` — reusing that same detached context for all three. That yields:

- cancel *before* the first chunk is accepted → abort cleanly, nothing stranded (unchanged from today)
- cancel *after* the first chunk is accepted → loop, pause and Enter continue on the detached context, so the partial draft submits instead of stranding
- cancel after all chunks are written → unchanged (that pause + Enter path was already detached)

**On the regression test.** The one that earns its keep is a negative control: cancel the caller ~50ms in, then assert `SendMessage` returns nil *and* that the second command issued carries the Enter args. Pre-fix that returns `context.Canceled`, so the test fails if the fix is reverted — which is the property you want. A complementary test pinning that post-first-chunk writes go through the detached context is worth having alongside it. One caveat: a strict cancel-mid-command race isn't practical to assert directly, because the post-run `ctx.Err()` check conflates success with cancellation.

**Your scoping question:** keep the confirmation-budget increase separate. This issue is a correctness bug; the budget values (`sendConfirmAttemptDeadline`, `sendConfirmMaxAttempts`) are a timing tunable with a different risk profile. Bundling them makes the correctness fix harder to review and harder to revert on its own if it ever needs to be.

The WARN-on-exhausted-confirmation-budget you proposed is genuinely wanted — `Send` currently returns 200 silently when confirmation gives up, which is what makes this whole class of failure invisible. Also unclaimed if you'd like it: the `confirmActive` rescue loop is skipped for harnesses that don't implement both `EmitsSubmitActivity` and `EmitsBlockedActivity` (see `adapters/agent/codex/codex.go:44`).

Happy to review whenever you open it — and thanks again for picking this up.

## Root cause (pin only — fix not included)

The silent substitution is not a backend bug in the strict sense: there is no AO-side model registry and no AO-side validation. The model string is persisted only on the **project's** `AgentConfig.Model` (and the role override), never on the session row. Both spawn and restore derive the model via `effectiveAgentConfig(...)` and forward it unchanged to the agent CLI's `--model` flag. The actual substitution is performed by the agent CLI itself (the upstream binary), which has its own allow-list and its own fallback-to-default behavior. The "transcript note" you observed is the CLI's stdout warning printed into the tmux pane — AO buffers that output for the terminal UI but does not parse it.

### Where the stored string is read on restore

- `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:1040` — `agentConfig := effectiveAgentConfig(rec.Kind, project.Config)` (restore path; mirrors line 381 for spawn).
- `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:632` — `effectiveAgentConfig` merges `cfg.AgentConfig.Model` with `roleOverride(kind, cfg).AgentConfig.Model` (set wins).
- `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:1046` — `agentConfig` is passed into `restoreArgv(...)`, which threads it into `agent.GetLaunchCommand(...)`.

### Where it is "resolved" against the model set

There is **no** backend resolution. The string is forwarded verbatim:

- `backend/internal/adapters/agent/claudecode/claudecode.go:172-174` — appends `--model <trimmed>` on launch.
- `backend/internal/adapters/agent/codex/codex.go:377-380` — same pattern via `appendModelFlag`.
- Same shape in `cline`, `copilot`, `qwen`, `pi`, `kiro`, `kimi`, `auggie`, `goose`, `autohand`, etc. — `strings.TrimSpace(cfg.Config.Model)` then append the flag.

Domain-level validation in `backend/internal/domain/agentconfig.go:41` (`AgentConfig.Validate`) checks `Permissions` only; the `Model` field is deliberately unconstrained.

### Where the actual substitution happens

Inside the agent CLI itself — outside the daemon's process. The CLI prints a warning ("...not available, falling back to …") into the pane and starts the session with its configured default. AO never observes the substitution; no error is returned to `Manager.relaunchSession`, no sentinel is raised, and `RestoreSessionResponse` / `ResumeAgentResponse` return 200 with `restoreMode: native|saved_prompt|fresh` regardless.

### Why the note never reaches API/UI

- The agent CLI's stdout is what AO surfaces as the live terminal (via `runtime.GetOutput`); it is not parsed for warnings.
- `backend/internal/httpd/controllers/dto.go:133` `SessionView` does not include any model field. The model is not stored on `domain.SessionRecord` (see `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/queries/sessions.sql` — columns are `id, project_id, num, issue_id, kind, harness, display_name, …`). The only durable copy is `ProjectConfig.AgentConfig.Model`.
- No error path produces an API envelope, so the CLI/HTTP surface has nothing to refuse on.

### Callers reaching the same fallback

`effectiveAgentConfig` is reached from every relaunch path, so this is not restore-only — it affects spawn and in-place resume too:

- `Manager.Spawn` (`manager.go:381`)
- `Manager.RestoreWithMode` → `relaunchRestoredSession` → `relaunchSession` (`manager.go:1040`)
- `Manager.ResumeAgentWithMode` → `relaunchSession` (`manager.go:1040`)
- `Manager.RestoreAll` → `relaunchRestoredSession` (boot-time reconcile, `manager.go:1442`)

A more interesting subtlety: `backend/internal/adapters/agent/copilot/copilot.go:154` already documents that `GetRestoreCommand` deliberately does NOT forward `cfg.Config.Model` (see #2895) — so the copilot adapter is the one adapter where this bug does not manifest on restore. Every other adapter that takes `--model` is affected.

## What a fix would need to touch

Any of these would close the gap; each has a trade-off.

1. **Backend-side allow-list per adapter.** Add a `KnownModels(ctx) ([]string, error)` method (or extend `ConfigSpec.Field[model].Enum`) on `ports.Agent`, validate at `effectiveAgentConfig` time in `Spawn`/`Restore`/`ResumeAgent`/`RestoreAll`, return a typed sentinel (e.g. `ErrUnknownModel`) that maps to a 400/409 in the API. Storage implication: the model should also be snapshotted onto `domain.SessionMetadata` (or a new `SessionSnapshot` table) at spawn time, so restore can compare "what we asked for" vs. "what the project says today" and surface a drift error instead of silently following the project's current (possibly already-substituted) value.

2. **Detection post-launch.** Have the agent adapter's `SessionInfo` (or a new optional capability) parse the CLI's startup output for the "falling back to …" warning and surface it on the session row + API. This is the smallest blast-radius change but couples every adapter to a specific upstream warning string, which is fragile.

3. **Refuse + prompt.** Surface the substitution in `RestoreSessionResponse` as a warning field, and require an explicit confirmation to proceed. Aligns with the issue's "proposed behavior" but only works if the API/UI grows a confirmation path; today there is none.

## Main risk to flag (point 4 of the ask)

If the fix is option (1) — a strict allow-list — it will **break forward-compatibility by design**. Today the model field is unconstrained precisely so a new model shipped by an upstream CLI between AO releases does not require an AO release to be used. Any adapter whose CLI accepts models AO does not yet know about (which is all of them today — see claudecode.go:113-116, the `model` config field has no `Enum`, only a `Description` example) will start refusing valid spawns after the fix lands. Mitigations to consider alongside the strict path:

- Add an explicit `model_allowlist_override` config (opt-in escape hatch) for operators running on a newer CLI than AO.
- Treat "unknown" as a warning at spawn (log + API warning field) but only error at restore when the stored model was previously valid (i.e. keep a "last-known-good" set on the session row).
- Keep the unconstrained model on the `ConfigSpec` field but add an optional second, stricter `ConfigSpecStrict` used only by the restore path.

The copilot adapter's deliberate choice to drop `--model` on restore (#2895) is precedent for an adapter deciding that the field is unsafe to forward in a restore context; that decision lives in the adapter, not in a shared validator, and would not be affected by a backend-side allow-list (the allow-list would simply not apply to copilot on restore).

cc maintainers: I'd suggest option (2) (post-launch detection) as the lowest-risk first step, with option (1) on a per-adapter opt-in basis once each adapter's stable-model surface is known.

Thanks for filing. I traced this end-to-end on the public fork. There are two distinct defects in the `ao session cleanup` path. I'll describe them in terms of the three outcomes the issue already lists.

## (1) Counter counts "no error from Destroy", not "actual removal"

The session-manager loop runs:

> `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:1985` — `(*Manager).Cleanup`
> iterates `m.cleanupRecords(ctx, project)` (terminated sessions) and, for each
> row with a workspace path, calls `m.workspace.Destroy(...)`. Only the return
> value of `Destroy` decides which bucket the session lands in:
>   - `err == nil` → `result.Cleaned = append(result.Cleaned, rec.ID)` (line 2028)
>   - `err != nil` → `result.Skipped = append(...)` (line 2022)
>
> Nothing else touches the count. The counter therefore reports "no error
> returned from the worktree adapter", not "filesystem teardown actually
> happened."

The error-swallow site that produces the false success is in the worktree adapter:

> `backend/internal/adapters/workspace/gitworktree/workspace.go:258` —
> `(*Workspace).Destroy`. Line 270 runs `git worktree remove <repo> <path>` and
> captures the exit into `removeErr`. `removeErr` is then **only re-inspected**
> inside the `if _, ok := findWorktree(records, path); ok { ... }` branch
> (line 278).
>
> When the directory is already gone on disk (the case from this issue):
>   1. `git worktree remove` fails (path missing) → `removeErr` is set but
>      **silently discarded** for the "dir gone" path.
>   2. `git worktree prune` (line 271) succeeds and removes the stale
>      registration.
>   3. `findWorktree` returns `false` (path no longer registered).
>   4. `os.RemoveAll(path)` (line 299) returns nil because the path doesn't
>      exist — `os.RemoveAll` is documented to return nil on missing paths.
>   5. `Destroy` returns `nil` → Cleanup's counter increments by one.
>
> Nothing was actually removed on disk. The teardown "succeeded" because the
> code conflates "the worktree adapter returned no error" with "the workspace
> was present and is now gone."

## (2) DB-row leak — there is no deregistration path

Even if `Destroy` returned an error for the missing-dir case, the loop still
wouldn't free the row:

> `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:1985-2031` — `(*Manager).Cleanup`
> never calls `store.DeleteSession` (or any equivalent) inside the loop.
> The store's only hard-delete entry point, `(*Store).DeleteSession` at
> `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/store/session_store.go:114`, is gated to
> seed-state rows and explicitly leaves fully-spawned / terminated rows alone
> (per the docstring on line 95).

     Real success. Currently counted correctly.
  b. **Dir already absent, only DB deregistration needed** — `git worktree
     remove` fails on a non-existent path, `git worktree prune` clears the
     registration, the path was never on disk to begin with. Today's code
     lumps this into (a), counting it as "cleaned" without ever touching the
     DB row.
  c. **Removal genuinely failed** — dirty worktree, locked worktree, post-prune
     the path is *still* registered, etc. These go into `Skipped` today
     (see `cleanupSkipReason` at line 2037 and `ErrWorkspaceDirty` handling in

1. Spawn provisioning path (Go backend)

   Entry point:
   - backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:292 — `Manager.Spawn(ctx, cfg)`
     `CreateSession` writes a seed row, then `createSessionWorkspace`
     (manager.go:492) calls `workspace.Create` (manager.go:499). For a
     workspace-project spawn, each child repo's worktree is registered in
     the DB inside `createSessionWorkspace` via `store.UpsertSessionWorktree`
     (manager.go:539). `runtime.Create` follows (manager.go:432), and the
     session is marked live by `lifecycle.MarkSpawned` (manager.go:451,
     `lifecycle/manager.go:796`) — that `UpdateSession` write is the point
     after which a worker can be observed as running.

   Where the worktree directory and checkout land:
   - backend/internal/adapters/workspace/gitworktree/workspace.go:121 —
     `Workspace.Create`. For an existing local branch it shells out via
     `worktreeAddBranchArgs` (`commands.go:13` →
     `git worktree add <path> <branch>`). For a new branch it uses
     `worktreeAddNewBranchArgs` (`commands.go:17` →
     `git worktree add -b <branch> <path> <baseRef>`).
   - For workspace projects, `Workspace.CreateWorkspaceProject`
     (workspace.go:152) loops per repo and runs `git worktree add` via
     `createWorkspaceProjectRepo` (workspace.go:764, same args).
   - `existingWorktree` (workspace.go:647) decides reuse from
     `git worktree list --porcelain` only — no HEAD, status, or index probe.

2. Non-atomic window

   The DB registration (`UpsertSessionWorktree`, manager.go:539) and the
   `git worktree add` checkout are not in one transaction:

   - `CreateWorkspaceProject` (workspace.go:152) commits each repo's
     worktree via `git worktree add` inside `createWorkspaceProjectRepo`
     (workspace.go:776). The session-manager `createSessionWorkspace`
     loop (manager.go:538-550) then runs `UpsertSessionWorktree` AFTER
     the worktree add already succeeded. If the process is interrupted
     between `add` returning and the `UpsertSessionWorktree` write, the
     directory is registered with git's main repo (`git worktree list`
     shows it) but no row exists for it in `session_worktrees`. A later
     spawn finds the path in `git worktree list --porcelain` and reuses
     it without re-checking whether a usable checkout is present.
   - In the multi-repo case, the loop in `CreateWorkspaceProject`
     commits each child repo to git BEFORE moving to the next. On a
     later failure mid-loop the rollback (workspace.go:207-210) calls
     `forceDestroyPath` on already-created siblings, but again nothing
     reverts git's bookkeeping if the daemon dies between the add and
     the rollback.
   - If the daemon, shell, or `git worktree add` process is interrupted
     between `mkdir`/link and the checkout finishing, the directory is
     left registered in `.git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir` with a `locked`
     `initializing` marker. A later spawn calls `existingWorktree`
     (workspace.go:647), finds the path in
     `git worktree list --porcelain`, and returns success without
     checking whether the checkout completed. The session row is then
     marked active and a worker is launched into a directory whose
     index and working tree are inconsistent — the stall observed.

   I reproduced this shape locally by killing `git worktree add`
   mid-checkout on a branch that uses a slow smudge filter. After the
   kill, `git worktree list --porcelain` shows the path with `locked`
   and the reason `initializing`, the directory contains a `.git` file
   plus the staged files, and `git status` reports them as both
   deleted-from-index and untracked — exactly the husk pattern.

3. HEAD validation on the spawn path

   None. `existingWorktree` (workspace.go:647) and `Workspace.Restore`
   (workspace.go:605) both trust `findWorktree(records, path)` and
   return without probing `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` or `git status`
   on the worktree. `revParseHeadArgs` exists (`commands.go:90`) but is
   only used inside `StashUncommitted` (workspace.go:433) to support
   unborn-HEAD preservation — it never gates spawn eligibility or
   re-adoption. `worktreeRecord.Locked` is parsed from porcelain
   (parse.go:59-62) but no caller checks it before reusing the path.

4. Reaper / cleanup coverage

   - The LCM reaper (backend/internal/observe/reaper/reaper.go:123)
     probes runtime liveness via `runtime.IsAlive` only. It never
     inspects the worktree, so a husk with a runtime alive on top of it
     is reported healthy forever.
   - `Manager.Reconcile` (manager.go:1314) and `reconcileLive`
     (manager.go:1247) adopt a session if its runtime is alive,
     regardless of worktree state.
   - `Manager.Cleanup` (manager.go:1985) iterates terminal sessions
     and calls `workspace.Destroy` per row; `Destroy` (workspace.go:258)
     refuses a dirty worktree and surfaces `ErrWorkspaceDirty`, but
     never classifies a locked/initializing registration as
     reclaimable.
   - `saveAndTeardownOne` (manager.go:1182) and
     `saveAndTeardownWorkspaceProject` (manager.go:1630) only run for
     sessions whose row already has a `removed` marker — a husk that
     was never carried past the spawn's `MarkSpawned` step is invisible
     to them.

5. Interaction with #3219

   These compound. #3219 reports that `ao session cleanup` returns
   optimistic counts even when `git worktree remove` fails because the
   directory is already gone. The husk scenario is the inverse failure:
   the directory IS present (so remove proceeds) but the registration
   is locked/initializing, so `git worktree remove` either errors on
   the lock and Cleanup skips the session (manager.go:2016), or
   succeeds at the file level while leaving git's bookkeeping
   half-formed. Either way, a future spawn reuses the husk because the
   DB row still has `State="active"`. The combined effect: cleanup does
   not free disk and does not break the husk, and the next spawn
   reliably lands a worker in the broken state.

   Suggested direction (not implemented): make the worktree row's
   terminal state atomic with the `git worktree add` outcome — either
   commit both or roll back both on interrupt — and have
   `existingWorktree` / `Restore` refuse a registered path whose
   `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` fails, whose
   `.git/worktrees/<name>/locked` is set, or whose `git status` shows
   an inconsistent index, forcing the caller to clean up rather than
   reuse it.

On a slow attach that spends the whole 750ms cap on the handshake, flushes an empty buffer, and leaves `replayBuffering` false for the rest of the attachment — so the replay then lands frame by frame with the scroll bug fully intact, behind a cover that achieved nothing. `main` also lacks the byte ceiling, the teardown flush, and the split re-assert timer.

Landing this PR fixes all of that on `main`. No action needed here, but the packaging is worth someone's attention — a landing-page PR carrying five terminal files past review is the kind of thing that should probably trip a CODEOWNERS or diff-scope check.

### 1. A manual check that hits a manifest 404 now shows the user nothing at all

Both new check-404 paths (`auto-updater.ts:381` and `auto-updater.ts:510`) broadcast `{ state: "idle" }`. The renderer does not render that state:

- `UpdateActions.showStatus` (`UpdatesSection.tsx:318-325`) lists every state *except* `idle`, so the whole status row unmounts.
- `UpdateStatusLine` (`UpdatesSection.tsx:369-392`) has no `idle` case and falls through to `return null`.

So the sequence for a user who clicks "Check for updates" is: spinner appears → spinner disappears → nothing. No message, no error, no "you're up to date". That is the exact regression @Pulkit7070 raised in the first round ("the user clicks 'Check for updates' / 'Download' and on any failure sees nothing at all, arguably worse than the scary dialog"), and @illegalcall's follow-up asked for "a neutral terminal state **or friendly indeterminate result**". `idle` is terminal and neutral, but it isn't a result — nothing reaches the screen.

Suggested fix: emit something the renderer actually renders, mirroring what you already did for the download path — e.g. `{ state: "error", message: "Couldn't check for updates — the update information wasn't found on the server." }` — or, if `idle` is the state you want, add an indeterminate rendering for it to `showStatus` + `UpdateStatusLine` in this PR so the path has a visible outcome.

Also worth syncing the prose: the PR description still describes the original unconditional suppression ("logs errors instead of broadcasting", "26/26 tests"), and comment #2 item 2 says manual checks broadcast `"not-available"`, but commit `2b5ae99` changed that to `idle`.

### 2. The 404 branch drops a staged "Restart & install" build out of the UI

The comment above the handler (`auto-updater.ts:313-315`) states the invariant this relies on: a transient `checking` state is acceptable because "the available / not-available handlers below restore the enriched downloaded status right after". `update-not-available` honours that explicitly:

```ts
autoUpdater.on("update-not-available", () => {
  broadcastUpdaterStatus({ state: "not-available" });
  if (stagedAtMs !== undefined) broadcastUpdaterStatus(stagedDownloadedStatus());
});
```

The new manifest-404 branch broadcasts and returns without that restore, so `lastStatus` is left at `idle` while a build is still staged and installable. The sidebar restart row keys on `status.state !== "downloaded"` (`Sidebar.tsx:720`, `Sidebar.tsx:754`), so a user who already has an update downloaded and then runs a manual check on a channel with a missing manifest loses the "Restart to update" affordance until the 30-minute escalation tick rebroadcasts `stagedDownloadedStatus()`. ## Adversarial security / tenancy audit

I reviewed the full PR diff plus the surrounding `backend/internal/cloud` and touched `httpd` event code. This is intentionally focused on ways to break tenant isolation and auth, not feature completeness.

### Critical

1. **Unauthenticated device approval can mint tokens for an arbitrary known user id**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/server.go:94-99` registers all `/auth/*` routes outside the tenancy middleware.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/handlers.go:133-142` accepts `userId` directly from the request body for `/auth/device/approve`.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/auth_store.go:140-145` writes that arbitrary `userID` into `devices.approved_user_id` with no authenticated actor check.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/handlers.go:154-171` then lets the holder of the matching `deviceCode` exchange it for an access token and refresh token for that approved user and all of their orgs.

   **Exploit scenario:** an attacker calls `/auth/device/code` to get their own `{ deviceCode, userCode }`, then POSTs `/auth/device/approve` with `{"userId":"<victim-user-id>","userCode":"<attacker-user-code>"}`. If the victim user id is known or leaked, the attacker can immediately poll `/auth/device/token` with their `deviceCode` and receive bearer/refresh tokens scoped to the victim's org memberships. No victim session, Google login, or org membership check is involved in approval.

   **Minimal fix:** `/auth/device/approve` must authenticate the approving browser/user through Google/session/JWT and derive the user id server-side from that authenticated principal. Do not accept `userId` from the request body. The store update should also require the code to be unapproved (`approved_at IS NULL`) and should return the approved authenticated user only.

### High

2. **Refresh-token rotation is replayable under concurrent use**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/auth_store.go:104-109` selects a usable refresh token.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/auth_store.go:116` revokes it in a separate statement without atomically claiming the row.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/handlers.go:76-93` issues a new token pair after `ConsumeRefreshToken` returns `ok`.

   **Exploit scenario:** if a refresh token is stolen, the attacker can race the legitimate client. Under PostgreSQL read-committed semantics, both transactions can read `revoked_at IS NULL` before either update commits; both then update the same row and both receive fresh access and refresh tokens. That defeats one-time refresh-token rotation and lets a replayed token become a persistent session.

   **Minimal fix:** consume refresh tokens with one atomic statement, e.g. `UPDATE api_tokens SET revoked_at = $now WHERE token_hash = $hash AND kind = 'refresh' AND revoked_at IS NULL AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > $now) RETURNING user_id`, then load the user/orgs only if the update returned a row. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` with a recheck before returning `ok` is also acceptable.

### Medium

3. **CDC store has an unscoped fallback that leaks all orgs if any caller misses tenancy context**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/changelog_store.go:17-35` uses `currentOrg(ctx)` and falls back to `WHERE seq > $1` across the entire `change_log` table when no org scope is present.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/changelog_store.go:58-66` does the same for `LatestSeq`.
   - Current HTTP wiring mitigates this for `/api/v1/events`: `backend/internal/cloud/server.go:111-118` installs an org filter and mounts `api.Register` under `tenancy.Middleware`.

   **Exploit scenario:** the present cloud HTTP route appears protected, but the store itself does not fail closed. Any future streaming/admin/debug handler, background subscriber, or test helper that calls `store.EventsAfter(context.Background(), ...)` with the cloud store will receive every org's events. Because `change_log` includes project/session ids and event payloads, this is a cross-tenant data leak if one route forgets the middleware or context propagation.

   **Minimal fix:** make the cloud `EventsAfter`/`LatestSeq` store methods require `tenancy.OrgIDFromContext(ctx)` like the project/session/worktree stores. If a truly global admin stream is needed, add a separate explicitly named admin method/interface instead of overloading the tenant store path.

4. **Request-time org authorization is based only on org ids embedded in the access token**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/tokens.go:81-88` embeds `OrgIDs` at issue time.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/tenancy/middleware.go:39-59` verifies the token and checks only `slices.Contains(claims.OrgIDs, orgID)` for `X-AO-Org-ID`.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/postgres/auth_store.go:202-209` lists memberships during token issuance/refresh, but there is no DB membership check in middleware.

   **Exploit scenario:** if a user's org membership is revoked, or if a token was minted with an org membership that should no longer apply, the bearer token remains authorized for that org until access-token expiry. That creates a revocation window for tenant data reads/writes. It is bounded by the current 15-minute default, but it is still not a request-time membership authorization check.

   **Minimal fix:** have the tenancy middleware call an authz store method such as `IsOrgMember(ctx, subject, orgID)` before setting scope, or add token/session versioning that invalidates existing access tokens when membership changes. Keep the store-level `org_id` predicates either way.

5. **JWT and Google ID-token validation lack audience checks**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/tokens.go:119-125` has no `aud` claim, and `backend/internal/cloud/auth/tokens.go:141-165` verifies signature/issuer/expiry but not audience.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/google.go:94-115` relies on Google's `tokeninfo` status and then accepts `sub/email/name`; it does not check the returned `aud` against `GoogleConfig.ClientID` (nor does it explicitly validate issuer/email_verified in this code).

   **Exploit scenario:** an AO Cloud access token minted for another audience/environment can be accepted here if it uses the same issuer/secret. For Google, I am not asserting `tokeninfo` fails open, but this code does not enforce that the ID token belongs to this configured OAuth client, so the guarantee is external and untested.

   **Minimal fix:** add an audience config/claim to AO Cloud JWTs and require it in `VerifyAccessToken`. For Google, either use Google's ID-token verifier library with audience set to `ClientID`, or parse the `tokeninfo` response and require `aud == cfg.ClientID` plus issuer/expiry/email verification as appropriate.

6. **OAuth `state` is generated but never validated**

   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/handlers.go:45-50` generates a `state` for Google login.
   - `backend/internal/cloud/auth/handlers.go:53-63` handles the callback using only `code`; it does not read or validate `state`.

   **Exploit scenario:** this permits login CSRF/account-confusion flows where a callback initiated for one browser context can be completed without proving it matches the login request that started in that context. This is less direct than the device-code issue because the callback currently returns token JSON, but it is still a broken OAuth invariant.

   **Minimal fix:** persist a one-time state nonce server-side or in a secure/httpOnly SameSite cookie and require callback `state` to match before exchanging the code. Consume the nonce on success/failure.

### Notes / not findings

- I did not find raw SQL injection in the new cloud store code. Queries are parameterized; the concatenated SQL fragments I saw are constant local `WHERE` fragments, not user input.
- Implemented project/session/worktree/PR read paths generally enforce `org_id` at the store/query layer via `tenancy.OrgIDFromContext(ctx)` and `WHERE org_id = $1` predicates. The migration also uses composite `(org_id, id)` primary keys/foreign keys for the tenant-owned domain tables.
- `X-AO-Org-ID` spoofing is blocked in the current middleware for REST/SSE routes because the selected org must be present in the token's org list.
- The current `/api/v1/events` cloud route is mounted under tenancy middleware and also has an event filter; the issue above is specifically the store's unscoped fallback if any caller bypasses that route shape.
- Secrets custody is mostly schema/port skeleton in this PR. The migration stores `ciphertext`, `nonce`, `key_id`, and `algorithm`, and I did not see a plaintext credential API response/log path. However, `backend/internal/cloud/server.go:50` constructs and discards the `SecretsManager`; I do not see credential persistence wired through encryption yet, so encrypt-before-persist is not proven by this PR.

### Verification run

- `cd backend && go test ./internal/cloud/... ./cmd/ao-cloud` passed.

### Verdict

I would not merge this as a multi-tenant control-plane skeleton yet. The project/session store scoping is in the right direction, but the unauthenticated device approval path is a blocking account/org takeover bug, and refresh-token rotation is replayable under race. I would block merge until at least those two auth issues are fixed, and I would strongly prefer the CDC store to fail closed on missing tenant scope before more routes build on it.

Two corrections to my comment above, one to my own claim and one to the issue's premise. The second changes what this issue should do.

## Retracting the cause I described

The scope-clarification paragraph asserted that Gatekeeper performs an online notarization-ticket lookup against `api.apple-cloudkit.com` at first launch, and that a blocked request explains the "developer cannot be verified" dialog. That is not supported. As pointed out in https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/3261, `xcrun stapler validate -v` reaching that endpoint is stapler's own validation path, and it performs the lookup whether or not a ticket is already stapled, so it says nothing about the launch check. Stapling exists so first launch works offline. Retracted; the cause of that separate first-install report is unknown and tracked in https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/3260.

The `Contents/CodeResources` finding stands, and so does the conclusion that the packaging change cannot affect notarization.

## app-builder-lib 26.x does not use ditto

This is the part worth acting on. The premise that `electron-builder` builds mac zips with `ditto` is not true of the version pinned here.

In `app-builder-lib` 26.15.3, `ArchiveTarget.build` sets `preserveSymlinks: isMac`, which routes mac zips to native `zip` in `out/targets/archive.js`:

```js
// macOS native zip: -y preserves symlinks (required for .framework bundles)
const args = ["-q", "-r", "-y"]
```

`grep -rn "ditto" node_modules/app-builder-lib/out/` returns nothing.

So approach 1 as written cannot work: delegating to `app-builder-lib` produces a `zip -y` archive, not a ditto archive, and `zip` writes no AppleDouble entries either.

## Measured comparison

I built the same signed bundle three ways and extracted each with `ditto`, which is what ShipIt does:

| method | `._*` entries | `__MACOSX` | signature after extract | symlinks | `daemon/ao` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `zip -q -r -y -7` (what electron-builder 26.x actually runs) | **0** | 0 | valid, ticket stapled | 14/14 | present |
| `ditto -c -k --keepParent` | 275 | 0 | valid, ticket stapled | 14/14 | present |
| `ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc --keepParent` | 275 | 376 | valid, ticket stapled | 14/14 | present |

Three consequences:

1. electron-builder's own mac zip contains **zero** AppleDouble entries, so "match electron-builder's format" and "preserve AppleDouble" are contradictory goals.
2. Their absence breaks nothing. The `zip -y` archive has none and still extracts to a bundle passing `codesign --verify --deep --strict` with the ticket intact and all 14 framework symlinks preserved.
3. The bundle carries no resource forks. The xattrs present are `com.apple.cs.CodeDirectory` / `CodeSignature` / `CodeRequirements` on 65 entries, plus `com.apple.provenance`, which macOS adds locally rather than at build time. The `._*` files ditto writes are carriers for those, and the signature validates without them.

A ditto-based maker would add roughly 470 KB of `._*` files and change nothing measurable.

## What this suggests about #3034

The error output there names `._icon.png__`, `._app.asar__`, `._electron.icns__`. The trailing `__` is not a valid AppleDouble filename. Garbled entry names plus one genuinely missing real file (`daemon/ao`) is what extracting a **corrupted archive** produces, which is what a bad blockmap differential download yields. That is hypothesis 2 in #3034, and https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/3151 already removes it by forcing full downloads on mac.

## Suggestion

Descope or close this in favour of confirming #3151 resolved the reported failure, which needs one real auto-update cycle.

If a maker is still wanted, the version with a rationale is one matching electron-builder's actual output (`zip -y`, or delegating to `ArchiveTarget`), on the theory that maker-zip's pure-JS archive differs structurally from what `app-builder-lib`'s blockmap generator expects. That would target safely re-enabling mac differential updates rather than AppleDouble. I have not attempted it, since it cannot be verified without a real sign, publish, and auto-update cycle, and I would rather not put unverified code in the path of every macOS download.

Happy to be wrong on any of this if someone can reproduce the ShipIt failure against a full (non-differential) download. That would put AppleDouble back in play and I would withdraw the suggestion.

Thanks for picking this up. Before the two scoping questions, there is context that should probably shape the whole design.

**The mirror of this mechanism shipped and was then removed.** The worker-idle to orchestrator nudge was built (#2836) with a durable outbox and a just-in-time guard re-read, hardened after misfires (#3215), and then deleted wholesale (#3257). The recorded reasons were not design flaws in the delivery path. They were misfires on the underlying fact: nudges delivered after a worker had already been killed, sessions nudged repeatedly with no state change in between, and a session re-armed because a human typed a single message into it.

That matters here because #3245 proposes the same loop in the other direction. Whatever gets built should be able to answer, explicitly, why it will not end the same way. My read is that the delivery mechanics were never the problem. The problem was that "idle" was treated as evidence of "needs work", and it is not.

**v1 scope: `idle` only, not `waiting_input`.**

`waiting_input` means a human decision is outstanding. Injecting there creates a specific failure: a session blocked pending approval receives an automated message and proceeds as though the block were resolved. The message does not need to say "go ahead" for this to happen. Arriving at all can read as resolution.

This is not hypothetical. In sustained multi-agent operation we have seen sessions receive automated notification events carrying no payload whatsoever, where the correct behavior was to decline to treat them as approval for anything pending. That should not depend on each agent's judgment being sound in the moment.

There is a second, mechanical reason. Automated delivery into a session holding unsent input can flush that input as a side effect, which means automation can execute an instruction no human reviewed. #3231 closed the specific race; the general principle stands.

Usefully, the primitives already exist. `ActivityState.NeedsInput()` is the persisted predicate for "human decision outstanding", and `lifecycle.cannotNudge()` already encodes guard conditions from the previous nudge implementation, so this should reuse them rather than invent a parallel notion of eligibility. Worth knowing that the richer "needs attention" classification lives only in the frontend presentation layer today, so any server-side eligibility beyond those two will have to be added rather than read.

Your own constraint already implies idle-only: `waiting_input` *is* pending user input. It is also the safely expandable choice. Shipping narrow and widening on evidence is recoverable; shipping wide and narrowing after an incident is not.

**Cooldown: exponential backoff with a hard terminal state, not an open-ended ladder.**

- First re-engagement after a threshold comfortably longer than a normal turn, so ordinary think and tool time never trips it.
- Exponential backoff per attempt, with a cap.
- A hard ceiling of a few consecutive re-engagements, after which the loop **stops** and the session is flagged for a human.
- The counter resets only on genuine activity that produces work, never on the nudge itself, or the ladder never advances.

The ceiling matters more than the interval. If several re-engagements produced no work, the session is not idle in the interesting sense. It is stuck, waiting on something a nudge cannot supply, or finished. Continuing converts that into recurring cost and noise, which is precisely the complaint that ended the last mechanism. The terminal state should be "tell a human", not "keep trying".

**Two things worth building in that you did not ask about.**

*1. Mark the re-engagement as synthetic, and say in-band that it is not authorization.*

If a session is idle precisely because it awaits a human decision, and it receives something instruction-shaped, the failure is: nudge arrives, agent reads it as a go-ahead, agent performs the gated action. The payload should be unmistakably machine-attributed and should state that it does not constitute approval for anything pending. More generally, a session cannot currently distinguish a human instruction from an automated one, since everything arrives on the same path as keystrokes. If that distinction is not representable today, this feature is a good reason to introduce it, stamped by the daemon rather than claimed by the caller.

*2. Idle is not done, and the difference needs to be a first-class outcome.*

A session can be idle because it correctly finished. Given an open-ended "anything left to do?", a language model will tend to find something, because producing an answer is the default behavior. At fleet scale that turns finished sessions into generators of unnecessary work, which is worse than leaving them idle.

We have watched exactly this: an orchestrator with a bounded goal drifted into adjacent unrequested work, and only corrected when asked directly what the right thing to do was. A re-engagement loop would have accelerated the drift rather than caught it.

So the nudge needs an explicit "I am done, stop re-engaging" response that durably suppresses further attempts, with completion treated as a normal successful outcome rather than a failure to find work. And prefer a prompt that grounds the session in its own durable state ("re-read your ledger, then either act on a concrete open item or declare done") over an open-ended "continue", which invites confabulation.

Your other constraints all look right: durable state, de-duplication across restarts, visible logging, and staying linked to the original session rather than replacing it. That last one also avoids the #2501 failure mode, where an orchestrator is terminated mid-turn and replaced by an unlinked session with no notification.

Thanks for the review. All seven findings are real and none are dismissed. Merging this as the base and carrying every one of them into an immediate follow-up PR rather than churning this branch, per the requester's call to keep PR count against this repo low.

Threads resolved here only to mark them as triaged into that follow-up; full text is preserved in the follow-up's description. Carried forward:

P1
1. `maker-dmg.ts`: `dir` is the Forge package directory, not the `.app`. `buildForge` treats it as prepackaged, producing a nested `Agent Orchestrator.app/Agent Orchestrator.app`. Pass `path.join(dir, \`${appName}.app\`)` plus a layout-level maker test.
2. `sealDmg`: partial credentials fail open (identity without notary creds warns and returns success). Throw on every partial combination; allow only the zero-credential local case.
3. `forge.config.ts` postMake: seals the dmg but never runs the canonical verifier. Extend `verify-mac-artifact.sh` to accept `.dmg` (with `spctl -a -t open --context context:primary-signature`) and invoke it after `sealDmg`.
4. `mac-update-e2e.yml`: the N-1 baseline predates the sentinel, so the first run waits forever. Needs a sentinel-capable baseline or external staging observation, and a fail-fast capability check.
5. `mac-update-e2e.yml`: cannot be a stable-promotion gate while N and `latest-mac.yml` must already be public. Either test against an isolated candidate feed and promote after success, or document it as post-release monitoring.

P2
6. `dmg-builder@26.15.3` defaults `writeUpdateInfo` on, so a `.dmg.blockmap` is generated before postMake rewrites the dmg bytes. Set `writeUpdateInfo: false` and assert no dmg blockmap is emitted.
7. `e2e-mac-update.mjs`: `--state-dir`/`--run-file` never reach the app (neither launch passes `AO_DATA_DIR`/`AO_RUN_FILE`). Propagate both through both launches and constrain the deleted run-file path.

Heads up that the three workflow runs on this PR (Go, CLI E2E, gitleaks) are all currently in the `action_required` state — that's why no checks show up and the PR is showing `mergeable_state: blocked`.

`action_required` is the state GitHub assigns to workflows queued for first-time-contributor approval; it clears as soon as an approving maintainer approves the run. Nothing in the diff needs to change for this to resolve — purely a run-approval gate.

## Same pattern affects project removal — and it's worse

Reported separately by @nikhil: **Remove project** traps the user behind the same undismissable modal, for the entire teardown of **all** sessions in the project.

### Frontend — identical lock
- `Sidebar.tsx:600` renders the same `ConfirmDialog` with `busy={isRemoving}`.
- `handleConfirmRemove` (`Sidebar.tsx:465`) sets `isRemoving=true` → `await onRemoveProject(workspace.id)` → only then `setConfirmOpen(false)`.
- `onOpenChange` (`Sidebar.tsx:602`) only allows close when `!isRemoving` — same hard-lock as the session case.
- `onRemoveProject` (`_shell.tsx:336`) does `DELETE /api/v1/projects/{id}` — a single synchronous HTTP call.

### Backend — synchronous loop over *every* session
- `Service.TeardownProject` (`backend/internal/service/session/service.go:547`) loops over all non-terminated sessions and calls `Kill(ctx, rec.ID)` **sequentially** (L552-558), then `Cleanup(ctx, project)` (L560).
- Each `Kill` is the same expensive synchronous teardown from the original report (runtime destroy → shell-terminal gate → workspace destroy → MarkTerminated).
- So for a project with N active sessions, the modal is locked for the **sum** of all N teardowns + cleanup — potentially very long.

### Fix surface (shared)
Both bugs are the same class: **`ConfirmDialog` + synchronous blocking HTTP op**. A single fix that makes these destructive ops non-blocking (optimistic close + inline progress) resolves both. The session path (`SessionsBoard`/`SessionInspector`) and the project path (`Sidebar`) should be handled together.

Posting this as a primitive, not a competing design. The durable reconciler is the right seam, and the reclaim-vs-preserve debate is settled in favour of your architecture (the 2026-07-19 review on #2819).

One thing that might help inside the reconciler's decision: an objective `safe-to-reclaim` predicate.

```
preserve iff:
  (rev-list --count <branch> --not --remotes > 0)
  OR (status is non-clean: staged, unstaged, or untracked)
  OR (worktree is locked)
  OR (workspace path no longer resolves)
```

**The honest limit.** `rev-list --count <branch> --not --remotes` answers "commits on this branch that no remote ref has." It does NOT answer "uncommitted edits, index entries, or untracked files in this worktree" — those require `git status --porcelain` alongside it. The four-term predicate is what covers the failure modes in the cluster: merge path, kill path (uncommitted), spawn-timeout (unborn-HEAD husk), archived-project (path unresolvable), and locked-worktree recovery.

**Four wrong detectors worth ruling out before this lands.**

| detector | why it fails |
|---|---|
| `rev-list --count <branch> --not @{u}` (single-upstream form) | Returns 0 whenever the branch has no upstream tracking ref. In a measured set of 1,541 branch heads, 431 (28%) had no upstream set; in those cases the detector falsely claims "safe to reclaim" with no signal at all. |
| `status --porcelain` empty => safe | A clean working tree can still carry unpushed commits. Reclaiming on `status == clean` alone destroys local commits the user thought were backed up by a push that hadn't run yet. |
| `rev-list --count <branch> --not --remotes` at repo scope (cwd=repo, not worktree) | The count is per-repo, not per-worktree. Every worktree of the same repo reports an identical number, so the reconciler cannot disambiguate this worktree's history from a sibling's. The predicate must run with the worktree as cwd, not the repo. |
| `stash list` non-empty => preserved, empty => safe | Stashes are user-managed -- empty/applied/dropped state tells you nothing about work-in-progress that hasn't been stashed. A user with an in-progress edit and an empty stash list would be reclaimed. |

The four-term predicate is the only one I can find that holds across the failure modes in the cluster; the wrong-detector table is what I'd want pinned as a test-fixture set so the reconciler can't regress to any of them.

## Root Cause Analysis

After investigating the codebase, here is what I found:

### The AO `PROMPT_TOO_LONG` check (4096 bytes)

The only place AO itself rejects with `"PROMPT_TOO_LONG"` is `backend/internal/httpd/controllers/sessions.go:186-187`:

```go
const maxPromptLen = 4096

if len(in.Prompt) > maxPromptLen {
    envelope.WriteAPIError(w, r, http.StatusBadRequest, "bad_request", "PROMPT_TOO_LONG", "prompt is too long", nil)
    return
}
```

This check is on `in.Prompt` -- the **task prompt** field of the spawn request. A 25-line prompt is well under 4096 bytes, so this check should NOT fire.

### The real issue: system prompt passed as a CLI argument

For Codex, AO passes the entire system prompt as a command-line argument:

```go
// backend/internal/adapters/agent/codex/codex.go:120
cmd = append(cmd, "-c", "developer_instructions="+codexTOMLConfigString(cfg.SystemPrompt))
```

The orchestrator system prompt is assembled from multiple pieces:
1. `orchestratorSystemPrompt()` -- role, operating rules, core commands, coordination workflow, review workflow, project context (~1700+ bytes)
2. `OrchestratorRules` -- project-specific rules (variable)
3. `systemPromptGuard()` -- confidentiality block (~1100 bytes)
4. `workspaceProjectPrompt` -- workspace repos list (variable)
5. `aoSkillPointer()` -- CLI pointer + browser instructions (~700 bytes)

Total base size: **~3500-4000+ bytes** of system prompt, before any project-specific rules or workspace context.

This system prompt is inlined as a `-c` TOML config override on the command line. Combined with:
- 4 session-hook `-c` flags (each with JSON command strings)
- `projects` trust `-c` flag
- `check_for_update_on_startup` and `hide_rate_limit_model_nudge` `-c` flags
- `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, `--no-alt-screen` (Windows)
- `--model` flag
- The task prompt after `--`

The total command line could easily exceed limits. On Windows, `CreateProcess` has a 32,768 character limit, but the Codex CLI itself may impose its own limit on `-c` config value sizes before the OS does.

### No system prompt size check exists

There is **no validation** on the system prompt size anywhere in the codebase. The `systemPromptBytes` is measured for reporting only:

```go
// backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go:414
systemPromptBytes := len(systemPrompt)
```

It is never checked against any limit. A project with large `orchestratorRules`, `agentRules`, or many workspace repos could push the system prompt well past any reasonable `-c` argument size.

### What likely happens

1. User spawns an orchestrator with Codex
2. AO assembles the system prompt (~4000+ bytes) and passes it as `-c "developer_instructions=\x27<4000+ bytes>\x27"`
3. Codex CLI tries to parse the `-c` override and either:
   - Hits a Codex internal limit on config value sizes
   - Hits the Windows command line length limit (especially with all the other `-c` flags)
   - The TOML parser chokes on the inlined system prompt
4. Codex reports an error that surfaces as "prompt too long" to the user
5. The orchestrator agent dies

The worker (Claude) spawns fine because Claude Code gets the system prompt via a **file** (`cfg.SystemPromptFile`), not as an inline `-c` argument. Codex does not use the file path unless `cfg.SystemPrompt == ""` -- and since AO always generates a system prompt, the inline path is always taken.

### Fix options

1. **Always use `model_instructions_file` instead of inline `developer_instructions`** -- write the system prompt to a temp file and pass the path via `-c model_instructions_file=<path>`. This is what the code already does as a fallback when `cfg.SystemPrompt == ""`.
2. **Add a size check on the system prompt** before it is inlined as a `-c` argument, and fall back to the file path when it exceeds a threshold.
3. **At minimum, log the assembled system prompt size** so users can debug this instead of getting a cryptic error from the Codex CLI.

Option 1 is the cleanest -- the system prompt file is already being written (via `prepareSystemPromptFile`), but the Codex adapter prefers the inline `developer_instructions` over the file. Switching the priority so the file is preferred would eliminate the command-line length issue entirely.

## Additional observation: orchestrator worktree disappears after /quit

**Reproducible pattern** (confirmed 2 times in local testing):

1. Start an orchestrator session (e.g. `srouter-114`, kind=orchestrator).
2. Inside Claude Code within that session, execute `/quit` (clean CLI exit).
3. Attempt to re-enter via `claude -c` → `ENOENT: process.cwd failed`.
4. Worktree path `~/.ao/data/worktrees/<project>/orchestrator/<project>-orchestrator` is **empty/missing**.
5. Git `worktree list` shows no entry for it — it was removed.
6. **But**: the DB still shows the session as `activity_state=idle, is_terminated=0`, and the tmux session `srouter-114` remains alive (attached).

**Recovery:** `git worktree add ... ao/<project>-orchestrator` restores it (branch `ao/<project>-orchestrator` is intact in git), but this shouldn't be necessary.

**Open question:** What component/condition triggers `git worktree remove` after `/quit` without updating `sessions.is_terminated`? Daemon logs unavailable locally to trace the call site.

**Potential investigation directions:**
- Add logging to `reconcileLive` / `reconcileReap` paths to capture worktree teardown decisions.
- Check if orchestrator sessions have special cleanup logic on CLI agent exit that differs from workers.
- Examine whether `/quit` should mark orchestrator sessions `terminated` (vs `idle`) to prevent ambiguous "zombie" state.

This appears separate from the naming issue but related: orchestrator sessions don't have a stable identity, so when their worktree disappears, they're hard to locate/recover without DB lookup.

Yes — still observing this post #2947, and #2947 does not touch the three constants the issue actually rests on. Leaving the issue open.

**Our number is post-2947, not pre-2947.** The 956 MB / 976 MB reading was taken 2026-07-29, one day after #2947 merged on 2026-07-28, on a build that already contained #2947. So this is not a stale measurement.

**#2947's files (commit `fcb984ae`, via PR diff):**
- `backend/internal/adapters/telemetry/posthog.go` — modified
- `backend/internal/cli/root.go` — modified
- `backend/internal/httpd/cli_telemetry_reservoir.go` — **new**
- `backend/internal/httpd/router.go` — modified
- `docs/telemetry.md` — modified
- frontend telemetry files

It did **not** touch:
- `backend/internal/adapters/telemetry/localsqlite.go` (the SQLite-sink retention/prune code)
- `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/queries/telemetry.sql` (the prune SQL)
- anything with `VACUUM` (repository-wide code search returns zero matches)

**Current state of the three constants on today's `main`** (sha `63f10c54`, post-#3342) in `backend/internal/adapters/telemetry/localsqlite.go`:

```go
localRetention       = 30 * 24 * time.Hour   // line 18 — still hardcoded
localPruneEvery      = time.Hour             // line 19
localPruneBatchLimit = int64(1000)           // line 20 — still 1000 rows/cycle
```

`maybePrune` (lines 113-124) is still the only prune caller and still passes `localPruneBatchLimit` as the delete `LIMIT`. So all three halves of the issue — configurable retention, prune-keeping-up, and `VACUUM` — are unchanged on main.

**Fresh measurement today, 2026-07-30**, on the same machine running the post-#2947 build (`telemetry_cli_daily.json` reservoir is present, confirming the new code path is live):

- Database file size: **1,022,140,416 bytes (~975 MB)**
- `PRAGMA page_count` × `page_size`: **249,546 × 4096 = ~975 MB**
- `PRAGMA freelist_count`: **244,707 pages** = ~960 MB of free-but-not-returned pages
- `dbstat` sum across all tables (live data): **~14 MB**
- `telemetry_event` row count: **4,713**
- Rows ingested in last 24h: **318**
- Telemetry date range: 2026-07-09 → 2026-07-30

The current 975 MB file size with only ~14 MB of live data is the same shape as the 976 MB / 956 MB reading reported in the issue: the file is dominated by unallocated SQLite pages that no `VACUUM` has ever returned. Even at ~300 rows/day ingest, #2947's volume cuts cannot shrink this — the space is already held by freed pages from earlier rows, and nothing compacts them back to the filesystem.

So all three of the issue's asks still stand:
1. Retention is still hardcoded.
2. The prune batch cap is still 1000 rows/cycle.
3. There is still no `VACUUM` anywhere in the repository.

Happy to close as duplicate if #2947 (or any merged-since PR I missed) is now also addressing retention or compaction, but I have not found one.

# AO Token Usage Validation Report ## Result **Token tracking: PASS** For the tested AO session, the exact token totals stored by AO match the final usage reported in the native Codex rollout. All compared token fields have a difference of zero, confirming that AO token collection and display are working as expected. The ChatGPT Profile view was not used for the exact comparison because it is not refreshed in real time and updates on an unspecified interval. The session-level Codex JSONL record was used for the verification. **Monetary cost tracking: NOT VALIDATED** The AO interface displayed `Coming soon` for total cost, so this test validates token usage only. It does not establish the accuracy of monetary cost calculation. ## Test objective Validate whether Agent Orchestrator (AO) correctly tracks the tokens consumed by one Codex session by comparing: 1. Token usage displayed and persisted by AO. 2. The exact final token usage recorded by Codex for the session. ## Test environment | Item | Value | |---|---| | Date | 30 July 2026 | | Time zone | Asia/Kolkata (IST, UTC+05:30) | | AO session ID | `agent-orchestrator-180` | | Codex session ID | `019fb303-51e9-7411-b3bc-2aa95dc8d060` | | Codex source | `cli` / `codex-tui` | | Codex session started | 18:02:48 IST | | Final Codex usage event | 18:12:00 IST | | AO parser | `codex-rollout/v1` | | AO token confidence | `parsed_jsonl` | ## Evidence 1: usage reported by AO AO displayed the following rounded values for the tested session: | AO field | AO display | |---|---:| | Total tokens | 8.6M | | Input tokens | 8.5M | | Cache-read tokens | 8.2M | | Cache-write tokens | 0 | | Uncached input tokens | 315.1K | | Output tokens | 19K | | Reasoning tokens | 4.9K | ## Evidence 2: exact Codex usage The final cumulative `token_count` event in the native Codex rollout reported: ```json { "input_tokens": 8532952, "cached_input_tokens": 8217856, "output_tokens": 18979, "reasoning_output_tokens": 4859, "total_tokens": 8551931 } ``` The source rollout is: ```text /Users/nikhilachale/.codex/sessions/2026/07/30/rollout-2026-07-30T18-02-47-019fb303-51e9-7411-b3bc-2aa95dc8d060.jsonl ``` The Codex totals are internally consistent: ```text Total tokens = Input tokens + Output tokens = 8,532,952 + 18,979 = 8,551,931 Uncached input tokens = Input tokens - Cache-read tokens = 8,532,952 - 8,217,856 = 315,096 ``` Cache-read tokens are a subset of input tokens. Reasoning tokens are a subset of output tokens. They must not be added to the total a second time. ## Exact AO-to-Codex comparison The AO SQLite usage ledger was queried for `agent-orchestrator-180`. Summing its parsed usage events produced the following exact values: | Token field | Codex rollout | AO persisted aggregate | Difference | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Input | 8,532,952 | 8,532,952 | 0 | | Cache read | 8,217,856 | 8,217,856 | 0 | | Cache write | 0 | 0 | 0 | | Uncached input | 315,096 | 315,096 | 0 | | Output | 18,979 | 18,979 | 0 | | Reasoning | 4,859 | 4,859 | 0 | | **Total** | **8,551,931** | **8,551,931** | **0** | AO's UI values are the expected human-readable rounding of these persisted values: ```text 8,551,931 -> 8.6M 8,532,952 -> 8.5M 8,217,856 -> 8.2M 315,096 -> 315.1K 18,979 -> 19K 4,859 -> 4.9K ``` ## Validation conclusion The tested AO session passed token-usage validation: - AO identified the correct Codex rollout. - AO parsed the Codex usage events with `parsed_jsonl` confidence. - AO persisted exact aggregates equal to the final Codex totals. - AO displayed correctly rounded versions of the persisted values. - No double-counting of cached-input or reasoning tokens was observed. ## Recommended procedure for future tests 1. Stop other Codex activity to prevent unrelated account usage. 2. Start a new AO session and record its AO and native Codex session IDs. 3. End the session normally and wait for AO collection to complete. 4. Extract the last cumulative `token_count` object from each associated Codex rollout. 5. For sessions with subagents or multiple rollouts, include each distinct rollout exactly once. 6. Compare AO's unrounded persisted aggregate with Codex field by field. 7. Confirm that `total_tokens = input_tokens + output_tokens`. ## Reproduction command The final Codex usage object for this test can be extracted with: ```bash jq -s ' [ .[] | select( .type == "event_msg" and .payload.type == "token_count" and .payload.info.total_token_usage != null ) | .payload.info.total_token_usage ] | last ' /Users/nikhilachale/.codex/sessions/2026/07/30/rollout-2026-07-30T18-02-47-019fb303-51e9-7411-b3bc-2aa95dc8d060.jsonl ```
