# Terminal input readiness — investigation + gate fixes

**TL;DR** — The objection holds up. Chasing it surfaced two real bugs in the gate itself, both now fixed. On the readiness signal: a real one exists for tmux (and probably for Claude Code), but **not** for ConPTY — so the timer becomes the fallback rather than disappearing.

---

## 1. Two bugs found in the current gate

Both traced to the same root cause: the gate was keyed to a **pane**, when it should have been keyed to an **agent launch**.

### Bug A — resume left already-attached clients open

`ResetInputGate` only deleted the map entry, so the *next* attach minted a fresh gate. But a tmux restart **keeps its clients attached**: those attachments never reattach, so they never re-read the gate. They kept the `inputReady` they earned from the process that just exited and fed the replacement TUI exactly the keystrokes the gate is supposed to hold.

Issue #3023 therefore reproduced on every resume, not just on first launch.

The earlier test missed it because it closed and reopened the client — which is not what a resume does.

### Bug B — standalone shells were delayed too

The gate was created lazily for any pane id the mux ever opened. A plain shell has no agent TUI booting and nothing to protect, but still ate the full grace window on its first keystroke. Pure regression for shells.

### Fix

Holding is now **opt-in per launch**:

| before | after |
|---|---|
| `ResetInputGate(id)` — drop entry | `ArmInputGate(id)` — mint gate + re-arm live attachments |
| called on resume only | called on **every** launch (`Spawn` and resume/restart) |
| gate auto-created for any pane | gate exists only if armed; unarmed panes immediate |
| next attach picks it up | already-attached clients re-blocked too |

Timer start is now conditional on attachment state:

- **Live PTY** (resume) — timer starts at arm time, because no later `setPTY` will start it. Without this the gate would never open and input would hang.
- **No PTY yet** (fresh spawn, armed before any client attaches) — the first successful publish starts it, so a slow attach can't burn the window before the pane is even up.

### Tests

Two regressions, each verified to fail with its fix reverted:

- `TestServeArmInputGateReArmsLiveAttachmentOnResume` — client never detaches (deliberately, since detaching is what hid this).
  Reverted → `input reached the replacement TUI before its own grace window elapsed`
- `TestServeUnarmedPaneAcceptsInputImmediately` — unarmed pane types at once.
  Reverted → `condition not met within 100ms`

Plus `TestSpawn_ArmsInputGateForNewPane`: with opt-in holding, a missing arm on the spawn path would silently disable the guard for new sessions.

---

## 2. Readiness signals — per platform / agent

### Claude Code `SessionStart` — plumbing exists, unused

Already installed by AO at `claudecode/hooks.go:38` under the `startup` matcher, and it reaches the daemon today. `claudecode/activity.go:11` explicitly treats it as metadata-only with no signal, so wiring it to open the gate is a small change.

**Unverified:** whether it fires before or after raw-mode entry. Claude Code runs hooks from its own process after session init, so *likely* after — but "likely" is exactly what we're trying to get away from, and it can't be confirmed on a Windows dev box.

*Proposed experiment:* run Claude in a Linux/macOS pane, have the hook stamp a timestamp, poll `stty -a` on `pane_tty` in parallel, compare which crosses first.

### Codex — dead end, as you said

`SessionStart` fires at first turn, far too late. Any general fix must cover Codex some other way.

### tmux `#{pane_tty}` + termios — strongest option

Cheaper than expected: `tmux/commands.go` already uses the `display-message -p -t <id> #{...}` helper shape (for `pane_pid`, `pane_current_path`), so `#{pane_tty}` is the same pattern. Then open the tty and check `ICANON` / `ECHO` via `x/sys/unix`.

- Agent-agnostic — covers Codex and every future adapter with no per-agent work
- Tests the **actual** failure condition, not a proxy
- Cost: a short poll loop. The tty path is stable per pane, so resolve once and re-stat.

### ConPTY — the real gap

No termios. The Windows analogues (`ENABLE_LINE_INPUT` / `ENABLE_ECHO_INPUT`) live in the **child's** console, and `GetConsoleMode` does not read another process's console — there's no equivalent of a tty path to open.

Searched the runtime adapters: **no console-mode surface exists today at all.**

Honest answer: on Windows there is no readiness signal I can find. It stays timer-only unless the agent itself supplies a hook.

---

## 3. Coverage summary

| platform / agent | signal available | fallback |
|---|---|---|
| Claude + tmux | hook and/or termios | timer |
| Codex + tmux | termios | timer |
| any + ConPTY | **none found** | timer |

**Implication:** the timer can't be removed — it demotes from *mechanism* to *fallback*. Worth naming explicitly, since "replace the timer with a real signal" isn't fully achievable on Windows.

---

## 4. Open questions

1. **Termios first, or hook first?**
   Termios covers more (all agents, one code path) and doesn't depend on hook-timing behavior we haven't confirmed. The hook is less code but Claude-only and unverified.
   *Leaning termios, with the hook as an optional early-open layered on top.*

2. **Fallback timeout value.**
   Once a signal exists, the timer only fires when the signal never arrives — so it can be longer and more conservative than 500ms without hurting the common path.

3. **Ship order.**
   Keep the current 500ms on `main` meanwhile so the reported bug stays fixed, or hold the whole change until the signal lands?

---

## Exact-base vs exact-head desktop restart A/B

This is the differential visual proof that the earlier after-only recording was missing.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5fba0da3-06a2-4a39-9177-112428aa14ea

### Exact problem being fixed

Restarting the AO desktop app does **not** stop the underlying Chat/PTY/tmux workloads. The broken behavior is that the base build publishes its listener and lets the board read durable `Exited` facts **before startup recovery has reconciled those facts with the still-live workloads**. That creates a false `Exited` frame; some sessions repair later, while historical runtime cohorts can remain wrong.

The PR changes startup into a barrier: state-bearing API/UI reads stay gated while Chat and TUI ownership is recovered, live activity is reconciled with exact workload identity, and only then does the first usable board render. It also prevents a planned Chat-controller detach from publishing a false terminal activity signal, fixing one source of stale Chat state as well as the startup exposure.

### Controlled, identical scenario

Both packaged runs use a fresh isolated AO data directory and the same six real live cohorts:

- Chat
- native PTY
- released protocol-v2 PTY
- historical private-socket tmux
- named-socket tmux
- default-socket tmux

The recording first shows the healthy board. The harness then creates the affected precondition deterministically by writing stale `Exited` activity through AO's production activity endpoint while leaving every workload alive, quits **only** the desktop app, and relaunches it. This is intentionally controlled: it tests whether stale durable state can leak to users before recovery, independent of timing luck.

### Observed result

| Revision | Startup/API observation | First stable board | Workload proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Before — exact PR base `f16f31c3759e36b0c4ce82be14d59587d03bed25`** | `0` recovery gates; HTTP `200` exposed all six sessions as `Exited` | Five TUI cards visibly remained `Exited`; Chat had repaired asynchronously by the held board frame | Chat controller plus both PTY hosts and all three tmux workloads were still alive |
| **After — exact PR head `9e0f32e45a7998d6a3765adbefedc04f4b3311b2`** | `58` sampled `startup_recovery_in_progress` gates, then `0` invalid `200` responses | `0` `Exited` cards and `0` DOM `Exited` sightings | All six identities survived; five terminal input/output round trips passed; state stayed correct through a reaper interval |

So the before recording proves the actual contradiction: AO says `Exited` while the exact workloads are alive. The after recording proves the PR does not merely repaint the cards later—it prevents the false state from being observable at either the API or UI boundary.

Both recordings capture only AO's renderer and synthetic fixture names. No normal AO data or other desktop content was recorded.

### E2E verification Verified this PR locally at commit `95d40cdb9` in the actual Electron app, using an isolated AO data directory. **Confirmed regression — stopped controller** 1. Open a persisted Cursor chat while its agent controller is stopped (capabilities are unavailable). 2. The UI still exposes **Edit user message** on the first provider-backed prompt. 3. Submitting the edit reaches the backend and returns HTTP `409` with `CHAT_CONTROLLER_NOT_READY`. This is a safe failure (I saw no data corruption), but it is a user-visible false affordance: the UI offers an operation that cannot succeed. **Control case — live Cursor controller** After restoring the same controller to `ready`, the first-prompt edit worked as intended: the request returned `202`, created a conversation branch, rendered the edited prompt, and started the new turn. The likely cause is that `can(snapshot, "fork") === false` currently represents two different states: - a live provider that has reported it does not support anchored forks (the intended Cursor case), and - a stopped controller with no capabilities available. The first-turn exception should only apply when controller/capability state is authoritative, rather than treating absent capabilities as proof that the provider simply lacks `fork`. A focused regression test for a stopped controller would cover this boundary. **Stopped-controller failure:** **Live-controller success:**

Correction to my earlier review: after tracing the current release architecture end-to-end, there is still a blocking integration issue.

The entitlement change is mechanically correct, but it is wired into the wrong signing path:

- The public [`build-artifacts.yml`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/9f9a0f4326a9fa089e83b19582b4d571022729c2/.github/workflows/build-artifacts.yml#L4-L12) deliberately runs Forge **unsigned** and never supplies `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` or `CSC_LINK`.
- Canonical releases are signed, notarized, and packaged afterward by the private release conductor, as documented in [`desktop-release.md`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/9f9a0f4326a9fa089e83b19582b4d571022729c2/frontend/docs/desktop-release.md#L13-L44).
- Therefore this PR's `osxSign.optionsForFile` callback never signs the artifact that is ultimately published, and its signed-ZIP `postMake` branch is also skipped.
- The conductor owns a separate final-artifact verifier; changing the public `frontend/scripts/verify-mac-artifact.sh` does not change that publication gate.

As a result, the canonical downstream signer can still re-sign the bundled x64 Node with `@electron/osx-sign` defaults, omit `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`, and reproduce #3879 even after this PR merges. The focused tests pass, but they validate the unused/local signed-Forge path rather than the production release seam.

There is also an architecture-selection problem to avoid when moving the fix: `@electron/osx-sign` calls `optionsForFile(filePath)` with one argument, so this PR's default selector is `process.arch`. The conductor processes both arm64 and x64 artifacts from one signing host, so the policy must key off the artifact currently being signed (or inspect the Mach-O), not the host architecture.

Required before `Closes #3879` is accurate:

1. Add a paired change to the private conductor's downstream `signApp` invocation so only the x64 ACP Node receives both `allow-jit` and `allow-unsigned-executable-memory`.
2. Extend the conductor-owned final-artifact verifier to inspect the nested Node and execute the final x64 ZIP on a native Intel runner before publication; retain the arm64 verification as well.
3. Keep the public verifier changes only as the local diagnostic counterpart, and document that distinction.
4. Remove the unrelated `AgentModelCombobox` locale-formatting commit from this PR.

The narrow per-file entitlement policy and trust-before-execution ordering are good and should be preserved; the blocker is that neither currently reaches the canonical release path.

## Root cause (traced to exact lines)

Analyzed against `46741a59a` (fork of recent `main`; the lines below verified identical on `origin/main`). macOS 26.6 arm64, packaged daemon, Homebrew **tmux 3.6b**.

The deadlock comes from the tmux output classifiers not recognizing how **modern tmux** reports "no server". With no tmux server at all, tmux 3.6b prints:

```
error connecting to /private/tmp/tmux-501/default (No such file or directory)
```

`backend/internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/tmux.go` classifies outputs like this:

- `serverNotRunningOutput()` (~line 1188) only matches the **older** tmux text `no server running`
- `transientServerFailureOutput()` (~1203) matches `error connecting` → treated as **transient / inconclusive**
- `migrationSocketAbsentOutput()` (~1197) matches `error connecting` + `no such file or directory`, but it is only consulted when deciding whether to fall through from the private socket to the legacy default socket

Two consequences:

1. **`socketForSession()` legacy fall-through (~line 957)** checks only `sessionMissingOutput(legacyOut) || serverNotRunningOutput(legacyOut)`. With tmux 3.6b the legacy probe returns the `error connecting … (No such file or directory)` text, which matches neither — so it returns `ErrRuntimeProbeInconclusive`, forever. Annotated log line (session names anonymized):

   ```
   level=DEBUG msg="reaper: probe error reported as failed fact" session=<orchestrator-a> err="tmux runtime: probe session <orchestrator-a>: runtime: liveness probe inconclusive: system tmux \"/opt/homebrew/bin/tmux\" could not inspect legacy default-socket session <orchestrator-a>: exit status 1: error connecting to /private/tmp/tmux-501/default (No such file or directory)"
   ```

   That exact line repeated **15,701 times in ~3 hours** on my machine while the sessions stayed `isTerminated=false`.

2. **`IsAlive()` (~568–579)** likewise maps `error connecting` via `transientServerFailureOutput` to inconclusive; only `no server running` is treated as conclusive server absence.

So the full deadlock is: probe inconclusive → reaper never concludes death → `kill` 500s (`Destroy()` ~504 aborts on the same inconclusive probe; this is the [#4481](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4481) signature) → `restore` refuses with `SESSION_NOT_RESTORABLE` because the session is not terminal.

## Why the workaround needed *both* sockets on the private-socket migration path

On my machine, a dummy server **only on the default socket was not enough** (code-traced; I did not test it standalone): once the legacy probe answers `can't find session <id>`, `socketForSession()` returns the **private** socket name, and `IsAlive()`'s final probe then hits the absent private server → `error connecting` → inconclusive again. I had to create sentinel servers on **both** `tmux -L ao` (the daemon runs with `AO_TMUX_SOCKET_NAME=ao`) **and** the default socket. Then:

- both probes answer `can't find session <id>` → `sessionMissingOutput` → conclusive `(false, nil)`
- the reaper accepts the death; `ao session kill <id>` succeeds (a missing session on a live server is already handled generously by `killSessionMissingOutput()`)
- `ao session restore <id>` then relaunches with native resume, history intact

On the Linux repro above, default-only sufficed — plausibly an older tmux there still prints `no server running`, which the classifiers do recognize.

## Also affected: `ao session restart-all`

The bulk recovery tool is blocked by the same kill failure. After a reboot with 9 live sessions (7 orchestrators on tmux-runtime records, 2 workers on the new pty-host runtime), `restart-all` reported `restarted 3 of 9` — the pty-host workers recovered, every tmux-runtime session failed with `kill: INTERNAL_ERROR`. Only after the sentinel-socket workaround did per-session `kill` + `restore` bring all 7 back with `--resume` transcripts.

## Fix direction

Treat `error connecting … (No such file or directory)` as **definitive server absence** (equivalent to `no server running`) rather than transient:

- include the socket-absent pattern in the legacy fall-through check in `socketForSession()` (~957);
- in `IsAlive()`, classify that text as `ErrRuntimeUnavailable` instead of `ErrRuntimeProbeInconclusive`, so recovery may reconcile/recreate per the doc comment, instead of retrying forever.

This stays inside [#3475](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/3475)'s safety boundary: it is socket-level evidence (the socket file does not exist ⇒ no server can be reached there), not per-session death — per-session death still requires `can't find session`. Whether "runtime unavailable ⇒ mark archivable" belongs in the reaper is a policy call for maintainers, but *something* needs to conclude eventually: today the loop never ends, and neither the reaper nor `kill`/`restore`/`restart-all` can break it.

Confirmed, and it was worse than the read suggests. The captured target for a context menu was the menu element itself, not an unrelated control: the capture ran in a microtask after the content attached, and by then Radix had already moved focus into the menu. That element is detached by the time there is anything to hand back, so the hand-back silently did nothing and focus was left on `document.body`. I reproduced it before changing anything, right-clicking a project row from a chat session and pressing Escape on the dialog.

Dropdowns were unaffected because they never use that fallback: the trigger is found through the `aria-controls` link.

Fixed in c32873321. The fallback is now read synchronously as the content attaches, while the element the user was actually on still holds focus, and anything inside the menu is refused outright. The trigger lookup stays in the microtask, because `aria-controls` only exists once the commit that opened the menu has landed, and it overrides the fallback only when a trigger is found.

That makes the intended behaviour explicit rather than incidental: a context menu hands focus back to whatever held it when the menu opened, which is the same element Radix restores to. A dropdown still goes back to its trigger.

On the coverage gap you named: there is now a unit test that reproduces Radix taking the caret during the open and asserts the return target survives it, which fails on the previous code, and an e2e that opens and closes the sidebar context menu instead of only opening it. The e2e alone would not have caught this, since that path does not always reach the suppressed branch and Radix's own restore masks it.

The earlier P2 about the pending hand-off is fixed in 8712ef017. The pending entry now records the surface that borrowed the caret rather than the element inside it, which separates the two cases the old check ran together: focus moving within that surface is the user working inside the dialog, and focus moving outside it means the caret has a home, so the hand-back is abandoned and the listener removed. The fallback clears the entry whichever way it decides, and a focus drop while the surface is still open keeps waiting rather than spending the hand-back on it.

Reviewed this against the daemon side as well. The fix is correct in substance — the readiness poll is the right shape and the reason-code set, cadence, and copy do match desktop's `nativeSessionReadinessPoll`. What needs work is how the poll is bounded and how the tap path awaits it.

### 1. The readiness poll is unbounded and not gated on app state

`useInterfaceTransition.ts:71`

The comment above `nativeSessionReadinessCodes` concedes that a `--resume` relaunch stays `NATIVE_SESSION_UNVERIFIED` (#4122). For those sessions this is 1 request/second, indefinitely, for as long as the screen stays open. Pre-PR it was zero at idle, so this is new steady-state load rather than a slower version of something that already ran.

It is also not gated on `appActive`. The route sits under `presenceMiddleware` (`backend/internal/httpd/api.go:183`), so a backgrounded phone keeps ticking the roster and holds the desktop's live dot on — directly against the intent stated in `lib/appStatePoll.ts`:

> The poll is also the daemon's liveness signal, so stopping it is what makes the desktop's live dot go dark when the app is backgrounded.

Desktop is not equivalent here: react-query leaves `refetchIntervalInBackground` false, so `refetchInterval` pauses when the document is hidden. Nothing on mobile does.

**Needed:** gate the readiness interval on the same `shouldPoll(AppState)` predicate the board poll uses, and bound it — a capped attempt count or a backoff after the first several seconds. Given #4122 means the code provably never clears for a whole class of sessions, "poll until it resolves" has no terminating condition.

### 2. `setInterval` does not wait for the previous request

`useInterfaceTransition.ts:74`

`REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` is 12s (`lib/api.ts:262`). An unreachable daemon returns no status, so `shouldKeepPolling(undefined)` is `true` and the interval keeps firing every 1s while each request hangs for up to 12. That stacks ~12 concurrent requests and stays there. Out-of-order resolution can also revert a `supported: true` status back to unsupported, since `setStatus` is unconditional.

**Needed:** replace `setInterval` with a self-scheduling `setTimeout` loop that awaits `refresh()` before scheduling the next tick, and drop responses from a superseded request.

### 3. The tap awaits up to 12s with no busy state or re-entrancy guard

`TerminalSessionScreen.tsx:1023`

The refresh-on-tap is a good idea, but the press handler is now an unbounded await. On a flaky link the chat icon does nothing for 12 seconds where it used to respond instantly, repeated taps each start their own request, and the alert can land on a screen the user already navigated away from.

**Needed:** show the existing busy affordance while the recheck is in flight, ignore taps while one is pending, and bail out if the screen has unmounted before it resolves.

### 4. A failed recheck is reported as an unsupported agent

`TerminalSessionScreen.tsx:1032`

`refresh()` returns `undefined` on failure and writes the message to state, but the running closure still reads the `interfaceSwitch.error` it captured at render. So a connectivity failure during the tap surfaces as "This agent has not declared a compatible native conversation handoff."

**Needed:** have `refresh()` hand back the failure to its caller (or return a discriminated result) so the alert can distinguish "could not ask" from "asked, and the answer is no."

### Not blocking

- `shouldKeepPolling` only stops on auth and rate-limit, so a session deleted while the screen is open 404s once a second until the user leaves. Same rule the board poll already applies, so this is consistent rather than wrong — but it falls out for free once (1) is bounded.

### Checked and withdrawn

I initially flagged the shared `pollable` flag as freezing the pre-existing 300ms transition poll. It does share the flag, but `auth.go:196` is the only 429 in the daemon and it fires solely from the failed-auth lockout, so `pollable` can only go false when the password is rotated — a state where every request is already 401ing and the transition poll would stall regardless. Pushed `ba1d7b3a9`. All four addressed.

1. **Bounded and gated.** The readiness poll now runs behind the same `shouldPoll(AppState)` predicate as the board poll, and is capped per readiness state rather than running until it resolves. The budget lives in a ref keyed on session + phase + reasonCode, not in the effect closure, because `appActive` is in the dep list and would otherwise have made app-switching the way to restart a spent window.
2. **No stacking, no reordering.** `setInterval` is gone; the loop awaits each request before queueing the next, so one request is open at a time. A superseded response is dropped for state, for `settledRef`/`onSettled`, and for both counters.
3. **Tap path.** It has a re-entrancy guard, an unmount bail, and a spinner in place of the icon — dimming was no good since the recheck only runs while the icon is already faint. The busy flag is owned by the screen rather than the hook: the poll calls the same `refresh()`, so a hook-wide flag let a poll tick disable the user's own button and swallow the tap. I also widened `disabled` to match what the button announces as busy — a tap during the start POST was firing a duplicate and getting a 409.
4. **Failure vs verdict.** `refresh()` returns a discriminated result carrying the HTTP status, so the alert splits auth / rate-limited / answered-with-an-error / unreachable through `classifyConnectionFailure` instead of blaming the agent. `undefined` (no config yet) is its own case for the same reason.

On the non-blocking note: it does not fall out for free, and this was the sharpest thing the change surfaced. The readiness path is fine — a 404 leaves the reason code alone, so the attempt cap ends it. But a 404 arriving while an **active transition** is the last known status re-armed the 300ms poll indefinitely, since a failed request never advances `status` and `interfaceTransitionPollInterval` takes the active branch unconditionally. Kill a session mid-drain and it was 3.3 req/s forever. Failures now have their own capped budget with backoff, independent of the readiness window — which is also what retries a first fetch that never landed, a case the old code left with no poll scheduled at all.

Not changed: the poll still stops only on auth and rate limit; the bounds are what terminate everything else. The desktop's readiness poll stays unbounded — deliberate divergence, happy to revisit if you would rather they match.

## Fix: browser proxy HTTP 422 (your friend's ChatUI→browser error)

### Root cause
The Cloud browser proxy dispatches `kind='browser.fetch'` into `ao_worker_requests`, but **no migration ever added that kind to the `ao_worker_requests_kind_check` constraint**. The error chain:

`INSERT kind='browser.fetch'` → Postgres check violation (`23514`) → `normalizeConstraintError` → `ErrInvalid` → `writeStoreError` → **HTTP 422 `validation_error`** (`cloud/internal/httpapi/transport.go:73`).

Two contributing facts:
- A previous commit (`4d4f08300`, by Pritom14) fixed this with migration `00032` — but that commit was **lost during the PR conflict resolution**, so fresh databases never got the kind.
- Migration `00035` (interface transitions) rewrites the constraint wholesale and re-omitted `browser.fetch`, so even a schema that had it patched lost it again.

**When it occurs:** every browser-proxy request (Browser tab page loads, iframe fetch/XHR) on any database migrated purely from migrations — fresh Docker E2E, the friend's test env, new sandboxes. Staging did not hit it because it carries a hand-patched schema (documented in the original `4d4f08300` commit message).

### Fix (pushed, head d5e5f3e17)
- **Restored `00032_browser_fetch_worker_requests.sql`** — adds `browser.fetch` to the allowlist. Its Up list also carries the `interface.*` kinds so environments that already applied old `00035` re-run only `00032` without breaking in-flight interface handoffs.
- **`00035` Up + Down lists now include `browser.fetch`** so the final schema state keeps it.
- **Regression test** `TestWorkerRequestKindConstraintCoversDispatchedKinds` parses the migrations and asserts the highest-numbered constraint rewrite allows every kind the code dispatches (would have caught this class of bug).

### Verification
- Ran the full migration chain `00001..00036` against a scratch Postgres: applies cleanly.
- Confirmed the final constraint contains all 14 kinds and that `browser.fetch` and `interface.start` INSERTs succeed against the migrated schema.
- `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass in `cloud/`.

Your friend should re-run migrations (a fresh DB or `ao-cloud-migrate` on their existing env will pick up `00032`), and the browser proxy will stop 422'ing. If they already ran old `00035`, applying `00032` is sufficient — it re-adds `browser.fetch` while preserving the `interface.*` kinds.

## Second commit: the gate now sees the resolved child environment, and the reviewer is gated too

Head `e85a182`. Both additions come from a live measurement on a running install rather than from reading the code, and the first one is a gap in what I proposed in the opening commit.

### The measurement

The operator's home Claude state recorded `hasTrustDialogAccepted: true` for the **exact** session worktree paths. The live reviewer child's environment carried `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` pointing at a different root, whose state file had none of those entries.

Every surface said the trust existed. The child still stopped at the prompt that trust was meant to answer.

### 1. A gate could not have caught that

`PreLaunchRequest` did not carry the child environment. A gate would have had to assume the default root, write there, and return a green preflight for a file the child never reads — reproducing the incident inside the tool meant to prevent it.

`PreLaunchRequest` now carries `Env`: the resolved child environment as it stands immediately before creation. It is a copy, so a gate still contributes only through its decision, and a test asserts a gate cannot reach the child by mutating what it was handed.

The worker-side regression **is** the reported condition: a config root inherited through project env must reach the gate. Deleting `Env: copyEnv(env)` — the pre-fix state — fails it.

### 2. The reviewer was on a different path entirely

`review.Launcher` creates the reviewer child itself, not through `Manager.Spawn`. A gate wired only into the worker seam would have left the reviewer able to strand while the session it reviews looked healthy — which is exactly the live-reviewer-beside-absent-main-child shape the downstream incident reported.

The launcher now takes the same gate via `WithLaunchGate`, at the same position (argv and env final, no pane yet), with the same fail-closed shape. `PreLaunchRequest.Role` says which child is being judged, so worker and reviewer can never be silently conflated.

## Fourth commit: one config root, written and verified — the defect is now closed end to end

Head **`4bd58d8`**. The three earlier commits built the seam, made the resolved child environment visible to a gate, and let a gate take ownership of a variable the agent reads. This is the piece that uses them.

### Two roots is the whole bug

On a running install, `hasTrustDialogAccepted` was **true** in the operator's default Claude root for the exact worktree paths of four sessions — and the live child ran with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` pointing at a different root whose state file had none of those entries.

Every surface reported that the trust existed. The child still stopped at the prompt that trust was meant to answer, before its agent loop, and AO reported it as ordinary work in progress.

### `claudetrust.Gate`

Resolves **one AO-owned root per session**, writes the exact worktree's trust there, reads it back **from the same file the child will read**, and overrides `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` so the child cannot return to the root that lacks the entry. A worker and its reviewer resolve the same root — the incident was observed on a reviewer, and one session with two roots is the same bug wearing a different hat.

Details that are deliberate:

- **Verification reads the file** rather than trusting the write. A write that succeeded and a state the child can see are different claims — that difference is the entire incident.
- **Trust is keyed on the exact path.** A trusted parent must not confer trust on a nested worktree, or the gate would report a trust Claude does not apply.
- **Unrelated state survives.** Another session's entry and Claude's own keys are preserved; an unreadable or non-object state refuses rather than replaces, since it may belong to a live child.
- **A non-Claude launch is untouched**, and an unusable request refuses with a reason rather than writing somewhere unexpected.

### The regression is the incident

`TestWrongRootTrustIsNotEnoughAndTheChildIsRedirected` runs once per affected session id (61, 62, 67, 68). Each subtest first asserts the precondition that made the incident invisible — default root trusts the worktree, inherited root does not — so it fails if the fixture ever stops reproducing it. Then the gate must move the child to a root that trusts the exact worktree.

## Fifth commit: the gate is constructed and wired — installed behaviour now changes

Head **`48834a5`**. The previous commit added a gate that closes the two-roots defect and nothing constructed it, so nothing changed for a real install. This wires it.

**One gate, built once** from the daemon's own configured data directory, injected into **both** paths that create a Claude child:

- `sessionmanager.Deps.LaunchGate` — the session's own agent
- `reviewcore.WithLaunchGate` — its reviewer

Two gates, or one gate on only one of the two paths, would reintroduce exactly the split the gate exists to close.

### Where the root comes from, and why

`<dataDir>/claude-session-config/<sessionID>` — derived from what the daemon owns, deliberately. A home directory or a path taken from the environment is *how the writer and the child end up in different roots*, which is the defect itself. No `HOME` is read, no credential is copied or moved, and the gate writes only workspace-trust state for the exact worktree it was handed.

An empty data directory yields **no** gate, so embedders and focused tests that pass none keep the behaviour they had.

### Covered

The trust half of this issue, end to end in source:

- a pre-spawn boundary in `Manager.Spawn`, at the position the existing agent-binary check already established;
- the resolved child environment visible to the gate, because an agent whose config root comes from the environment cannot be pre-seeded without it;

### Not covered, explicitly

These are the parts of this issue's requested contract that remain open, so nobody reads the PR as more than it is:

- **Persisted lifecycle states.** `needs_input`, `launch_failed`, `resume_invalid` are not introduced. Process creation still leads to the same statuses it does today.
- **Readiness handshake.** Nothing binds readiness to `(session, launch, conversation)`, and nothing prevents a stale child from making a replacement launch look ready.
- **Post-spawn verification.** The gate proves the root is right *before* the child starts; nothing asserts afterwards that the child actually ran with it. A `launch_failed:config_root_mismatch` state would need the lifecycle work above.
- **Delivery.** `ao send` is unchanged; nothing refuses or queues a message to a worker that has not reached readiness.
- **Separate main/supervisor/reviewer liveness.** The gate now sees both children, but AO still reports their liveness as it did.
- **An intentionally configured custom config root.** The gate always takes ownership, so a deliberate operator choice is currently indistinguishable from the accidental inheritance that caused the incident. If custom roots should be supported, that wants a decision before code.
- **Worktree provenance.** The gate trusts the workspace path the daemon hands it rather than re-deriving that the worktree is AO-created.
- **No installed build, no canary.** Nothing here has been proven against a running daemon; there is no live evidence that a reviewer reaches readiness without a prompt.

## Follow-up: 00032 was not applying on existing envs (goose out-of-order guard) — fixed

Your friend was right: on any environment already migrated to v36, goose **aborts the whole run** with `found 1 missing migrations before current version 36: version 32: ...` and applies nothing — so 00032 never landed there and browser.fetch kept 422'ing. Fresh DBs were fine because they migrate the full chain in order.

### Root cause of the second failure
`postgres.Migrate` called `goose.UpContext` without `WithAllowMissing`. goose v3 treats a version gap below the current version as a hard error (protection against accidental out-of-order migrations), which is exactly what a restored-below-tip migration like 00032 looks like.

### Fix (pushed, head 94b90ee36)
One change in `cloud/internal/postgres/migrate.go`: pass `goose.WithAllowMissing()`. Both entry points (`ao-cloud-migrate` and control-plane startup) share this function, so both pick it up. This is safe here because 00032's Up is a pure constraint rewrite with a superset allowlist — applying it out of order only adds allowed kinds.

### End-to-end proof on scratch Postgres (all with real binaries)
1. Built an env at v36 **without** 00032 and with the old 00035 (the friend's exact state) → `browser.fetch` INSERT fails with the check-constraint violation (the DB-level cause of the HTTP 422).
2. Ran the **old** runner against it → aborts with the exact reported error, applies nothing (v32 stays unapplied).
3. Ran the **fixed** runner against it → applies `00032_browser_fetch_worker_requests.sql`, migrates cleanly.
4. On that same healed DB, `browser.fetch`, `interface.start`, and `terminal.open` INSERTs **all succeed** — the handoff kinds were not disturbed.

Following the RCA in [issue #4908](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/4908), there is one rare startup/recovery edge case that this PR appears to have missed.

### Missed sequence

1. The daemon starts and `WarmCodexAccounts()` begins the first device-global Codex account bootstrap.
2. That first attempt fails transiently—for example, resolving/launching `codex app-server`, its `initialize` handshake, `account/read`, the 10-second timeout, catalog cleanup, or the account-state store fails.
3. `codexAccountManager.bootstrap()` stores the error inside `bootstrapOnce.Do(...)` and closes `bootstrapDone`.
4. The underlying condition recovers while the same daemon remains alive.
5. The user retries ordinary Codex task creation.
6. `WaitCodexAccountBootstrap()` returns the cached failure forever; `sync.Once` prevents a second bootstrap attempt. Every Codex controller admission then returns `503 CODEX_ACCOUNT_MANAGEMENT_UNAVAILABLE` until the daemon is restarted.

This is why it is easy to miss in Electron development: the happy path normally succeeds on the first attempt using a working Codex binary and the established device account in `~/.codex`. Dev AO state is isolated under `~/.ao/dev`, but the device-global Codex home is still the normal Codex home. Frequent daemon restarts can also clear the poisoned in-memory `sync.Once` state before it is noticed.

The missing regression test is specifically **fail once, recover, and retry without restarting**. A fake account factory should fail its first `Open`/`Read`, succeed on the second, and verify that a later launch can complete. With the current implementation, the second factory call never happens.

This is not caused by the account-switch endpoint URI. Ordinary task creation reaches the shared controller-admission gate before launch; that gate waits for account bootstrap independently of `POST /api/v1/agents/codex/account-switches`.

One additional diagnostic problem: the underlying bootstrap error is replaced with the generic “Codex account setup did not complete” response and is not logged at the bootstrap boundary. Therefore, the reporter's exact initial transient trigger cannot be recovered from the screenshot/503 alone.

Suggested direction: replace the terminal `sync.Once` failure with a serialized/single-flight bootstrap state that permits a bounded retry after retryable failures, while preserving fail-closed behavior for permanent credential-safety failures and logging a sanitized classified cause.

Analyzed against `feef57bcba40d2e485dec53e9ea138db7277be22`.

## Additional clarification: why this is rare and easy to miss

This defect does not affect every Electron development run. It requires a specific **fail once, recover, retry without restarting** sequence:

1. The daemon starts and the asynchronous device-global Codex account bootstrap begins.
2. Its first attempt fails transiently—for example, while resolving/launching `codex app-server`, completing `initialize`, calling `account/read`, hitting the 10-second timeout, cleaning the account catalog, or reading account state.
3. `codexAccountManager.bootstrap()` stores that error inside `bootstrapOnce.Do(...)` and closes `bootstrapDone`.
4. The transient condition recovers while the same daemon stays alive.
5. A later Codex task launch calls `WaitCodexAccountBootstrap()`, but receives the original cached failure. `sync.Once` prevents bootstrap from running again, so launches continue returning `503 CODEX_ACCOUNT_MANAGEMENT_UNAVAILABLE` until a daemon restart.

Normal Electron dev usage usually never enters this path: the first bootstrap succeeds with an already-working Codex binary and established device credentials under `~/.codex`. AO's dev database is isolated under `~/.ao/dev`, but the global Codex account home remains the standard device home. Development daemon restarts can also clear the in-memory failed state and hide the symptom.

The missed regression case is therefore: make the account factory fail its first `Open`/`Read`, make the second attempt succeed, then retry task creation without restarting the daemon. The expected second call never occurs with the current `sync.Once` implementation.

This remains unrelated to the account-switch URI. Ordinary task creation is stopped by the shared Codex controller-admission bootstrap gate before launch; it does not need to call `POST /api/v1/agents/codex/account-switches`.

The precise initial trigger from the reported screenshot is unknown because the bootstrap boundary replaces the underlying error with a generic response and does not log a sanitized cause. The sticky lifecycle defect is confirmed; the one-time environmental trigger is not.

Pushed four more fixes, closing the remaining gaps from this PR's own "what is not verified" section and folding in the two defects found by other PRs.

**Stale status overwriting a newer one** (`79918e92c`) — `useUpdateStatus` requested the mount-time snapshot before registering the push listener and applied it unconditionally. A push landing in the gap was lost, and a slow snapshot walked the UI backwards over a newer push, leaving "Last checked" stuck until Settings was reopened. Listener registers first; the snapshot is dropped once any push has landed. Same defect as #4633, which fixes it by sharing one subscription across callers — that dedup is a worthwhile optimisation on its own and is not done here.

**Stalled downloads** (`c454fb125`) — a download that stops receiving bytes held the last percentage forever, kept the serialized updater queue occupied, and offered nothing to retry. A two-minute inactivity watchdog re-arms on every progress event, so a genuinely slow download stays alive while a dead one is caught, then cancels through the provider's cancellation token and publishes a retryable error. Cancelling matters as much as reporting: without it the queue stays blocked and even a manual retry waits behind the dead download. Same defect as #4832.

**Release notes had no source on either channel** (`0afa65d02`) — nightly never could have any: the direct feed is electron-updater's *generic* provider, which never populates `releaseNotes`, and `nightly-mac.yml` has no field for them. The tag lookup already calls the GitHub Releases API and that response carries the release body, so it is now kept and used as a fallback. On stable the pipe worked but the body was empty, so the publisher now asks GitHub to generate it.

**Two worktrees could not run the dev app** (`a7439b8b9`) — Chromium's singleton lock lives in the profile and every checkout resolved to the same `~/.ao/dev/electron`, so a second `npm run dev` exited with code 0 and no explanation. Hit repeatedly while testing this work. `AO_DEV_ELECTRON_DIR` overrides it; default behaviour unchanged, packaged builds deliberately not overridable.

### Still not verified by execution

- **The install step has never been run.** Unchanged from the original description, and still the item I would most want confirmed on a signed build.
- **The generated release notes may be overwritten.** Released bodies currently read `Automated <channel> release built from <sha>`, and nothing in this repository writes that text, so something downstream of the publisher replaces it. If that is still true after this lands, users see that one line and the generated notes never reach them.
- **The channel-switch window** still exists: between the switch and the replacement download finishing, the old build is armed and a quit installs it. Nothing in electron-updater or Squirrel.Mac can cancel a handed-over build.

**Root cause:** the TUI rebuild (`relaunchSessionWithPolicyAndGeneration`) re-derived the harness model from the project config (`effectiveAgentConfig`), discarding the model selected later in Chat UI — which only lived in conversation settings. The rebuilt TUI therefore resumed with the project default (e.g. 5.6 Full) instead of the Chat UI pick (e.g. 5.6 Luna).

- Chat UI model changes are persisted onto the session's durable metadata (`PersistChatModel`) before the next prompt routes.
- The TUI rebuild (and its target preflight) now refresh the model from the session metadata, so the choice survives the handoff.
- The model is forwarded into every harness restore command — Codex and Cursor already did; Claude Code was fixed at both the adapter and `agentruntime` layers (`--model` on `--resume`).
- The existing conversation is resumed via its native session id — no new session, history preserved.

**Follow-up (2026-09-05):** The reporter confirmed in Discord that manually deleting the app cache under `%APPDATA%` — after three reinstalls — resolved the problem. This reinforces the stale-install analysis: Electron uninstallers do not remove the app's profile folder, so stale state survived every reinstall and the cache deletion was the actual fix.

### Idempotency hardening for the `/etc/skel` harness link (`ln -sfn`)

> **Edited to correct overclaiming.** This comment originally called the change a build-blocker fix and floated upstream mutable-tag drift as the mechanism. Both were wrong: #4795 builds fine on a clean upstream base, and the reported failure came from a contaminated local base tag on one host. See the follow-up comment for the evidence and full retraction. The build results, reproduction and repo checks below are unchanged.

Applied the change reported from the Coder integration branch (equivalent to `a1e70b1c5`). `cloud/coder/Sandbox.Dockerfile` now uses `ln -sfn` for the `/etc/skel/.local/bin/claude` harness link, matching the convention already used in `cloud/nodeops/Sandbox.Dockerfile` and `cloud/nodeops/harness/claude-code.Dockerfile`. Nothing else from the combined integration branch was cherry-picked.

```diff
-    ln -s "$(readlink -f "$(command -v claude)")" \
-      /etc/skel/.local/bin/claude
+    ln -sfn "$(readlink -f "$(command -v claude)")" \
+      /etc/skel/.local/bin/claude && \
+    test -x /etc/skel/.local/bin/claude
```

The `test -x` is the narrow build validation: `-f` makes the link unconditional, so the build should still fail loudly if the link ever stops resolving to an executable harness rather than silently baking a dangling link into `/etc/skel`.

**Correcting my own argument, since it is on the record in this PR.**

This PR argued that a bare target is unsafe because it follows the session's *active* pane, and proposed `<id>:^.{top-left}` as a positional alternative. The first half is right. The proposed remedy is not — I re-tested it properly before closing and it fails two ways on tmux 3.7c:

```console
# zoom: user splits, then hits prefix+z on their pane
agent pane pid 60736 ; user pane pid 60741
$ tmux display-message -p -t 'z:^.{top-left}' '#{pane_pid}'
60741        # <- collapses to the ACTIVE pane; tmux skips panes failing
             #    window_pane_visible, and only the active pane is visible when zoomed

# window reordering: user runs new-window -b
agent lands in window 2, user in window 1
$ tmux display-message -p -t 'w:^.{top-left}' '#{pane_pid}'
61190        # <- the user's pane; `^` is the lowest-numbered window, not the agent's
```

So `^.{top-left}` is defeated by one keystroke after the split its own test builds, and by `new-window -b` / `move-window` / `renumber-windows`. It would have shipped the same class of bug it claimed to fix. Better that this closed than merged.

**The underlying concern is still live on `main`, though, and it is wider than this PR treated it.** Beyond `respawnPaneArgs` and `panePIDArgs`, these also target the bare session id: `sendKeysLiteralArgs`, `sendEnterArgs`, `sendInterruptArgs`, `capturePaneArgs`, `capturePaneStyledArgs`. With a user-opened second pane active, `SendMessage` types the agent's prompt plus `Enter` into the user's interactive shell — arbitrary text run as a shell command — and `GetOutput` returns the user's pane content to AO's state detection. That is a worse outcome than the respawn case.

The target that survives all of it is the pane id captured at `Create` (`#{pane_id}`, e.g. `%0`), which is stable across zoom, splits, window renumbering and index settings — unlike any positional token.

I would rather file that as its own issue with these reproductions than reopen this PR on a rewritten argument. Happy to do so, and equally happy to be told the user-opened-pane scenario is rarer than I think and not worth the change.

To check the new scheduler I ported the poll effect into a harness with a fake clock and a scripted network, so the numbers below are behaviour rather than a reading of the comments. It is a simulation of the effect, not the hook under a real renderer, so treat it as a strong hint rather than proof.

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Fresh TUI session, clears at 1.3s | 3 calls, settles at 2.1s, stops |
| #4122 session, never clears | 11 calls over 10.2s, stops |
| Readiness wait, backgrounded 3s to 30s | attempts survives the background, stops at 10 |
| Readiness wait, every other request times out | 21 calls, attempts reaches 10, stops |
| 404 mid-transition | stops in 15.4s |
| **90s outage mid-transition, then the network recovers** | **stops at 75s and never resumes** |

The readiness bound, the `readinessRef` keying, and the failure backoff all behave exactly as documented. The last row does not.

### The failure cap outlives the outage it was meant to survive

`interfaceTransitionNextPoll` consults `consecutiveFailures` before it ever looks at whether a transition is live:

```js
if (failures > 0) {
  if (failures >= interfaceTransitionFailureAttempts) return undefined;   // wins over the 300ms branch
  return failureBackoff[Math.min(failures - 1, failureBackoff.length - 1)];
}
return interfaceTransitionPollInterval(args.status, args.readinessAttempts ?? 0);
```

So a live handoff plus a network drop spends five requests over about 75 seconds (four backoff steps on top of `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` each) and then stops for good. Connectivity returning afterwards changes nothing, because there is no timer left to notice. The "Switching to Terminal UI · <phase>" banner stays frozen and `onSettled` never fires, so the board never refetches.

The escape hatch the comment relies on is not reachable in this state:

- `ChatSessionScreen.tsx` never calls `interfaceSwitch.refresh()`. Its only refresh is `conversation.refresh()`, a different hook.
- On the terminal screen the button is now `disabled={... || interfaceTransitionActive}`, so the tap recheck is unavailable during exactly the state that strands.
- What does recover it is navigating away and back, which remounts the hook — the symptom #4841 was filed about. The fix reintroduces a narrower version of the shape it set out to remove.

The case the cap targets is real and worth keeping: a session deleted mid-transition 404s at 300ms forever, and my harness confirms the cap stops that in 15.4s. But a 404 or 410 is a definitive answer about the session and a timeout is not, so the blanket cap over-reaches. Stopping immediately on a definitive gone, and letting transient failures keep retrying at the capped 8s backoff instead of giving up, gets the deleted-session win without the frozen banner. A Retry action on the transition banner would also make it recoverable on the chat screen, where nothing else can.

### The failure budget is not held the way the readiness budget is

`readinessRef` is deliberately a ref, keyed on the situation, so backgrounding cannot hand a spent window a fresh ten attempts — the harness confirms that works. But `let failures = fetchFailed ? 1 : 0` is a plain local re-seeded on every effect run, and `appActive` is in the dep list, so app switching silently refills the failure budget: the same stranded-transition scenario goes from 6 requests to 10 if the user backgrounds and returns.

That is inconsistent with the rationale written two lines above it, and right now it is the only thing that can restart a stranded poll — an escape hatch the user has no reason to discover. Worth either keying it the same way as the readiness budget, or writing down that the reset is deliberate.

### Checked and clean

For the record, so these do not get re-raised: the dropped `interfaceSwitchUnavailableMessage` re-export has no consumers outside the test; `interfaceTransition.ts` keeps its runtime imports pure, so it stays unit-testable per the convention in `connectionError.ts`; setting `mountedRef` inside the effect rather than relying on the `useRef` initialiser is strict-mode-correct; and `shellOnly` gates the button out entirely, so the `not-attempted` branch is only reachable with a null config.

## Review: infinite terminal ticket minting (#4668)

I reviewed this against issue #4668 and verified it by tracing the actual code paths (the frontend mux plus hook wiring and the backend SQL), building and vetting the cloud module, and reading the new tests. I also have independent staging evidence of this exact failure mode (a cloud terminal minting a fresh ticket roughly every 2 seconds with sub-second socket lifetimes), so the problem this targets is real and worth fixing.

### What the PR does
Two defenses for the failed-attach-retries-forever loop:
- Frontend: a `cloudConnectFailures` counter in the terminal-session runtime. In `scheduleReattach`, a cloud session that has never attached trips into an `error` state after `CLOUD_CONNECT_MAX_FAILURES` (8) failed cycles, and `TerminalPane` renders a dedicated `CloudConnectError` overlay with a Retry button instead of the generic banner.
- Backend (`worker_transport_store.go`): before `IssueTerminalTicket` refreshes the sandbox `interactive_until` lease, it counts unconsumed `terminal:%` tickets minted in the last 2 minutes; above `unconsumedTicketThreshold` (10) it skips the lease refresh so the idle scanner can eventually pause the sandbox. The paused-to-running wake still fires and the ticket is still issued, so the client still receives a normal 201.

### Use case it addresses
When the terminal WebSocket cannot attach (CSP block, proxy, firewall), the app used to loop mint-ticket forever with no surfaced error, and because every mint refreshed `interactive_until`, the sandbox never idle-paused and billed compute indefinitely. This PR is meant to both surface the failure and stop the billing leak.

### What I verified
- `cd cloud && go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` are clean.
- The backend defense is correctly targeted: it counts only unconsumed tickets, so a healthy viewer whose tickets get redeemed is never throttled, and it fails open (defaults to refreshing the lease) if the count query errors. At the observed rate of about 2 per second, the 10-ticket threshold is crossed in roughly 5 seconds, and `PauseIfIdle` gates on `interactive_until <= now()`, so the lease genuinely lapses and the sandbox pauses within about 2 minutes. This part is sound.
- i18n is complete: all 8 locale files carry the 3 new keys with real translations.

### Findings

**Blocker: the frontend breaker cannot tell "worker still provisioning" from "WebSocket permanently blocked", so it false-fires during normal slow cold starts.**
`useTerminalSession.ts` increments `cloudConnectFailures` on every not-yet-attached cloud "closed" event. But a still-provisioning worker returns 409 WORKER_UNAVAILABLE on the ticket mint, and `cloud-terminal-mux.ts` (around line 107) converts that 409 into the same `setConnectionState("closed")` that a real socket block produces. The hook has no way to distinguish them, so both increment the counter. At the flat 1s retry, the breaker trips at about 8 seconds. NodeOps and especially Coder cold starts routinely exceed that (the same file's own comment anticipates a worker ready at 17s). So a normal fresh or resumed cloud session whose worker takes longer than about 8 seconds to become ready shows a misleading "Cannot connect to terminal, check proxy, firewall, or CSP" overlay and stops the readiness poll the flat-retry path was explicitly designed to tolerate. Issue #4668 called out this exact distinction ("nothing distinguishes worker still provisioning from attach permanently failing client-side"), and the PR does not implement it. Suggested direction: have the mux signal "ticket minted (201) but socket failed" separately from "mint 409", and only count the former. That is the same consumed-versus-unconsumed signal the backend already keys on, so the two sides would agree.

**Major: the exponential backoff #4668 asked for is not implemented.** Only the hard cap is added; the never-attached cloud path stays at the flat `CLOUD_CONNECT_RETRY_MS = 1000`, so each attempt still mints roughly 8 tickets over about 8 seconds. Worth confirming whether the cap is intended to fully replace backoff.

**Major: the backend billing and SQL change has no test coverage.** `internal/postgres` has no test harness, so the threshold boundary (10 unconsumed freezes the lease, wake still fires, a healthy single-ticket session is not throttled) is unverified by anything runnable. Note also that the cloud module is not covered by CI at all (`.github/workflows/go.yml` triggers only on `backend/**` and `pricing/**`), so the passing "test" check does not exercise this file.

**Minor: the restore path re-enters `connect()` from the error state without resetting the counter** or `hasAttachedOnce`, so a single subsequent "closed" re-trips the breaker immediately. Only the Retry button, which routes through `attach()`, resets cleanly.

**Minor: the overlay detection couples to a hardcoded English substring** (`error?.includes("WebSocket cannot connect")` in `TerminalPane.tsx`, matching the literal in `useTerminalSession.ts`). Editing that message silently breaks the overlay. A typed error or flag would be more robust.

**Nits:** a "trasient" typo and a truncated comment ("Detect specific cloud WebSocket block error and for "), plus a couple of double blank lines that may trip the frontend lint.

### Recommendation
Good direction, and the backend defense is solid. But the frontend breaker as written would regress normal slow provisioning with a misleading network error, which is the specific case the issue warned about. I would request changes on the provisioning false-positive (the blocker) and the missing backend test before merge.

Related: #4792 (WebSocket keepalive) fixes a different terminal drop (the 60-second ALB idle timeout on connections that do attach), so the two are complementary rather than overlapping.

## Review: keep terminal WebSockets alive

I reviewed this and verified the concurrency-safety claim against the WebSocket library source, and built and vetted the cloud module.

### What the PR does
Adds a per-connection goroutine (`keepTerminalAlive`) that sends a protocol-level WebSocket ping every 20 seconds with a 5-second pong deadline on cloud terminal streams. A missed pong closes the stream cleanly, and the goroutine is tied to the existing terminal context.

### Use case it addresses
The public ALB has a 60-second idle timeout. An idle cloud terminal emits no traffic, so the ALB drops it at about 60 seconds (the PR cites an observed EOF at 60,005 ms). The 20-second pings keep the connection non-idle so the ALB does not tear it down. This is complementary to the never-attached ticket-minting churn (#4697): those connections die in under 2 seconds and never survive to the first ping, so this fix only helps connections that live past about 20 seconds of idle.

### What I verified
- The library is `github.com/coder/websocket v1.8.15`. The concurrency question is the crux here, since terminal output is written from another goroutine and the ping goroutine does not take the application-level `writeMu`. I confirmed by reading the library source that `Conn.Ping` and `Conn.Write` both funnel through `c.writeFrame`, whose first action is to lock a single per-connection `writeFrameMu`. So ping frames and output frames are serialized at the library level and the unsynchronized ping goroutine is genuinely race-free. Control frames may legally interleave with data frames per RFC 6455, so there is no protocol corruption either. The PR's risk note is accurate.
- Ping waits for the pong via the read path, and `readTerminalInput` reads continuously, so the required concurrent reader is always present.
- The goroutine lifecycle is clean: it exits on context cancel or ping error, the ticker is stopped, and `pingResult` is buffered so a send never blocks.
- `cd cloud && go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` are clean.

### Findings

**Major (process, not logic): no test, and no CI to run one.** The `internal/httpapi` package has zero test files, so `go test -race` exercises nothing, and the concurrency safety rests entirely on a library-internal invariant that a future library bump could regress silently. On top of that, `.github/workflows/go.yml` triggers only on `backend/**` and `pricing/**`, so the cloud module is never built or tested in CI on PRs or on main. The passing "scan" check is not a build or test gate. A minimal httptest test that opens a terminal, keeps it idle past one ping interval under `-race`, and asserts the socket stays open would lock in both the keepalive behavior and the concurrency safety.

**Minor: the 5-second pong deadline is shared with the ping-frame write and is a little aggressive.** If a large output write is holding `writeFrameMu`, the ping's write blocks on the lock and eats into the pong budget; combined with network jitter this can trigger a false disconnect. The impact is low (a clean close plus a client reconnect, not a hang), but a slightly longer window, for example 10 seconds, may reduce reconnect churn.

### Recommendation
The logic and the concurrency reasoning are correct, so this is safe to approve. I would ask, non-blocking, for a `-race` keepalive test and for the CI path filter to include `cloud/**` so this module is not shipping on manual review alone. It is also worth a line in the description noting this fixes the 60-second idle drop specifically and is independent of #4697.

## Review: remote capability broker write parity (#4718)

I reviewed this against issue #4718 and verified by building and vetting the cloud module, running gofmt, grepping the sentinel usage, and diffing the new remote-broker methods against the authoritative local `Service` implementation.

### What the PR does
- Phase 1: renames the unexported push-not-supported error to an exported sentinel and adds an `errors.Is` check in five worker handlers so an unsupported write returns 403 WRITE_NOT_SUPPORTED instead of 502, plus org, session, and worker fields on the error logs.
- Phase 2: implements the four remote-broker write methods (IssuePushGrant, RaisePullRequest, ClaimPullRequest, SubmitReview). It adds `RedeemRepositoryCapabilityForWrite` (a write-scoped mint using `repositoryWriteToken` with contents:write and pull_requests:write), registers a new `/control/github/capabilities/redeem-write` endpoint on the broker, extends the `RemoteCapabilityStore` interface with four store methods, and has the broker call GitHub REST directly with the write token and persist records locally.

### Use case it addresses
On environments where repositories are authorized through the remote capability broker (staging redeeming from production), workers could clone and read but never push or open a PR, because those methods were stubs returning a generic error that the handler mapped to a retryable 502. Per #4718, a staging worker spent about 6 hours retrying the PR step (243 error events in 12 hours), burning compute and agent tokens. The fix is meant to both stop the grind and deliver real write parity.

### What I verified
- `cd cloud && go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` are clean, so the store already satisfies the four new interface methods.
- Security of the write-token path checks out: `/redeem-write` is guarded by the same `brokerAuthToken` bearer check as the read `/redeem` and is only mounted when that token is set (production token-vending), workers cannot reach it (they hold session tokens, not the broker secret), the minted token is repo-scoped by the presented capability, and the token is never logged while the response is `no-store`. The one thing to flag is that the same broker secret can now mint write tokens rather than only read tokens, so its blast radius widens (still repo-scoped, so bounded).

### Findings

**Blocker: Phase 1's 403 safety net is dead code, so the 502 grind can recur.** The sentinel `ErrorRemoteWriteNotSupported` is defined and checked in the five handlers, but after Phase 2 replaced every stub, nothing returns it (grep-confirmed). So the five `errors.Is` short-circuits are unreachable. Any real failure in the new write path falls through to the generic 502 (SCM_BROKER_FAILED, PULL_REQUEST_FAILED, REVIEW_FAILED), which is the retryable code the incident retried on. Concrete recurrence: if staging ships this before production exposes `/redeem-write`, `IssuePushGrant` gets a 404, returns "repository write capability broker returned status 404", maps to 502, and the worker retries for hours again, reproducing the exact incident. Either keep a guarded terminal path that actually returns the sentinel when write is unavailable, or classify definitively-terminal broker failures as non-retryable. It is also worth confirming the worker and agent side treats 403 as terminal and 502 as retryable, since that assumption is load-bearing and is not in this PR.

**Major: `RemoteCheckoutBroker.SubmitReview` posts to GitHub before the ownership and status checks.** The local `Service.SubmitReview` validates the verdict, a non-empty body, that the run belongs to this session, and that the run is running, all before calling GitHub. The remote version fetches the review run, immediately gets a push grant and POSTs the review to GitHub, and only afterward does the store enforce session ownership and running status. So a same-org session can cause a real GitHub review comment to be posted for a run it does not own or that is already resolved, then receive a 403 or a no-op. The checks should run before the GitHub call.

**Major: remote `SubmitReview` never fails the run or closes the review terminal on error,** so a failed submission leaves the run stuck in running forever. The local path has explicit fail-and-close handling; the remote path just returns.

**Major: `triggerReview` is not wired on the remote `RaisePullRequest` and `ClaimPullRequest`.** The local paths auto-start a review run and review terminal, so remote-broker environments get PRs created and tracked but the automated reviewer silently never runs. That is a real parity gap.

**Major: the base-branch default is dropped.** Remote `RaisePullRequest` requires a non-empty base and returns invalid otherwise, but the local path defaults base to the repository default branch, and the worker handler does not require it. So a PR raised without an explicit base succeeds locally but returns a 400 only on remote-broker environments.

**Minor:** `SubmitReview` always posts the GitHub review as event COMMENT regardless of the verdict, so approve or request-changes semantics are lost on the GitHub side. `ClaimPullRequest` decodes the PR state but never sets it on the record and does not validate open or closed.

**Minor and hygiene:** gofmt flags 4 of the 5 files because the new code is space-indented and mixed with the surrounding tabs. The cloud CI gap (go.yml triggers only on `backend/**` and `pricing/**`) means the format failure and the absent tests are never caught, so the passing "scan" check is not a build, test, or format gate. The exported name `ErrorRemoteWriteNotSupported` also breaks the Go `Err...` convention (and the PR description calls it `ErrRemoteWriteNotSupported`), the error message has typos ("operation are", "thorugh"), and the comment above the sentinel is now stale.

**Test coverage: none.** A 436-line change on a write-capable token path has no tests for the write methods, the `/redeem-write` guard, or the 403 mapping.

### Recommendation
Phase 2 is a real and welcome implementation, and the write-token endpoint's auth and scope are sound. But the dead 403 safety net means the headline "stop the 502 retry loop" does not actually hold during rollout or on transient GitHub failures, and the review-submit ordering plus the missing review automation and base default are real parity and correctness gaps. I would request changes, and given the security sensitivity and the fact that cloud is outside CI, add unit tests before merge.

## Review: server-side WebSocket pings for ALB idle timeout (#4667)

I reviewed this against issue #4667 and verified it by checking out the branch, building and vetting the cloud module, running gofmt, and tracing the goroutine wiring. I also reviewed the very similar #4792 recently, so I can compare the two directly.

### Heads up: this overlaps PR #4792
#4741 and #4792 both fix the same problem in the same file (`cloud/internal/httpapi/terminal_handlers.go`): the ALB severs idle cloud terminal WebSockets after its 60-second idle timeout, so both add a server-side ping loop to keep the connection non-idle. Only one should merge. The differences are below, and I would consolidate on one before either lands.

### What the PR does
Adds `terminalPingInterval = 25s` and a `pingTerminalConnection(ctx, connection)` goroutine spawned in `connectTerminal`. Every 25 seconds it calls `connection.Ping(ctx)`, and it exits when the context is cancelled or the ping returns an error.

### Use case it addresses
The public ALB has a 60-second idle timeout. A healthy cloud terminal that sits idle emits no frames, so the ALB drops it at about 60 seconds and the user's terminal disconnects for no apparent reason. The 25-second pings put frame traffic on the wire well inside that window (about 2.4x headroom) so the ALB keeps the connection.

### What I verified
- Checked out the PR head. `cd cloud && go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/httpapi/...`, and `gofmt -l` are all clean.
- Concurrency is safe. The ping goroutine calls `connection.Ping(ctx)` without holding the application `writeMu`, but the library here is `github.com/coder/websocket`, where `Ping` and `Write` both serialize on a single per-connection `writeFrameMu`, so ping frames and output frames cannot corrupt each other or race. The PR's phrasing that Ping control frames "do not block application data frames" is slightly imprecise (they do briefly serialize on that lock), but the code is race-free.
- Goroutine lifecycle is clean: `Ping(ctx)` respects the session context, so when the handler exits and cancels the context, a blocked ping returns and the goroutine stops, and the ticker is stopped via defer. No leak.
- For a healthy connection the mechanism does what it claims: 25-second pings keep the ALB from idling out.

### Findings

**Major: this duplicates #4792, and #4792 is the more robust of the two.** Two concrete differences:
- No bounded pong wait. #4741 calls `Ping(ctx)` with the full session context, so on a half-open connection (peer gone, TCP not reset) the ping blocks until the session context is cancelled or another path errors out, rather than detecting the dead peer quickly. #4792 uses a 5-second pong deadline and closes the stream cleanly on a missed pong.
- The ping goroutine is fire-and-forget. `go s.pingTerminalConnection(...)` is not wired into the handler's select (which reads only `readResult`, `writeResult`, and `ctx.Done()`), so a ping failure just exits the goroutine silently and does not close the connection. #4792 sends its ping result into a channel the select reads, so a ping failure closes the connection and the client reconnects. #4741 relies on the read or write path to eventually notice a dead connection, which works but is slower and less deliberate.

Neither of these is a correctness bug for the primary goal (a healthy connection is kept alive correctly), but they are why I would prefer #4792's shape if the team consolidates, or fold the pong timeout and error propagation into this one.

**Major: the testing claim is not reflected in the PR.** The body says "Executed Go unit tests (`go test -v ./internal/httpapi`) confirming Ping control frames flow over TCP and context cancellation cleanly terminates the keepalive goroutine," and the checklist marks tests as added. But the diff adds no test, and `internal/httpapi` has no test files at all, so `go test -v ./internal/httpapi` reports "no test files" rather than exercising anything. For a concurrency-sensitive change, a committed httptest keepalive test run under `-race` would be worth adding, and it would be the only automated coverage (see below).

**Minor: the cloud module is not covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/go.yml` triggers only on `backend/**` and `pricing/**`, so this file is never built, vetted, or tested by CI on PRs or on main; the passing "scan" check is not a build or test gate. All the build, vet, and gofmt results above are from my local run.

**Minor:** 25 seconds versus #4792's 20 seconds is fine either way; both stay safely inside the 60-second window.

### Recommendation
The fix is correct and clean for the healthy-connection case, and unlike some sibling PRs it is gofmt clean and builds and vets cleanly. The main issue is that it duplicates #4792, which handles dead peers more deliberately (a bounded pong timeout plus error propagation that closes the connection). I would pick one PR to carry this fix, prefer #4792's shape or fold its two improvements into this one, and add a committed `-race` keepalive test since the cloud module has no CI coverage. Note also that #4741 correctly links the issue (#4667) while #4792 does not, so whichever one is dropped, keep that issue reference on the survivor.

Two things that could break after this change:

1. **Windows scripts can lose project variables.** The environment merge uppercases every variable name. For example, if a project sets `buildMode=production`, a Bash script reading `$buildMode` works today. After this change, only `BUILDMODE` exists, so the script gets an empty value. Can we compare variable names without caring about case, but keep their original spelling when passing them to the child process?

2. **Some custom installs could start agents with the wrong Node version.** If someone puts `ao` in `/usr/local/bin` alongside an older Node, moving that whole directory first also puts the older Node ahead of the newer one beside their NVM-installed agent CLI. A launcher using `#!/usr/bin/env node` can then pick the wrong runtime and fail. The normal desktop bundle avoids this because `ao` has its own directory. For shared-directory installs, could we use a directory containing only an `ao` shim so other tools keep their existing priority?

It would be good to cover both with regression tests. I checked these against head `6b4fd8167`: the Node selection change reproduces with fixture subprocesses on macOS. The variable-name change was checked by exercising the Windows merge logic locally and passing its output to Bash; I have not run that case on native Windows.
