Pushed `b63c2c751`. Thanks for running the harness again — the 183-requests row is the one I would not have found by reading.

### 1. The readiness bound now holds on a failing link

You are right that the increment rule should stay as it is: a run of timeouts teaches you nothing about whether the native session became ready, so it must not spend the window. That leaves the window unable to end a wait against a daemon that never answers, which is the bug.

So rather than change what spends the readiness budget, I took the sentence in your review that names the actual distinction — the two waits are not the same shape and should not share a retry policy — and made the failure policy read the shape:

| Poll is waiting on | Failure policy |
| --- | --- |
| A live handoff (`activePhases`) | backs off 1/2/4/8s, holds at 8s, never gives up while the screen is open |
| A readiness wait (`NATIVE_SESSION_*`) | same backoff, stops after 5 consecutive failures |
| A mount fetch that never landed | same as the readiness wait |
| Any of them, 404/410 | stops on that response |

Five is five requests with 1+2+4+8s between them, the fifth failure being the one that stops it: about 15s against a refused connection, about 75s when every request burns `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`. Your row is now a test that asserts both the request count and that it lands inside 90s.

I went this way rather than either option you offered because each has a cost the split does not. Letting failures consume the readiness budget contradicts the rule you just endorsed, and it means an outage spends the speculation window so the wait is over before the link returns. A wall-clock bound on the readiness wait regresses the row you verified in round 2 — the budget survives backgrounding — because 30s in the background would elapse the deadline and the effect would then schedule nothing at all on return, so the user comes back to a stale button and no fresh check.

The escape past a spent budget is the header recheck, and it is reachable precisely in the states that can strand: nothing is live, so `interfaceTransitionActive` is false and the button is enabled. Any request that lands clears the count and the loop resumes on its own.

**The 5xx case, decided rather than inherited.** "A 5xx is a fact about the link, not the session" was doing too much work. A daemon panicking in this one handler is a fact about the session too, so a persistent 5xx now ends a speculative wait — the same 79-requests-over-10-minutes you simulated. Under a live handoff it is still ridden out, because a restarting daemon is the common cause and the banner and its Retry are on screen. Both directions are tested.

**One consequence, stated because it is a real trade.** A spent failure count survives backgrounding, for the same reason the readiness window does: `appActive` re-runs the effect, so anything the effect owned would make app-switching the way to refill a budget. That does mean the two stops behave differently — foregrounding gives a 401 stop one fresh request but gives a spent speculative budget nothing. Deliberate: a password is re-paired outside the app, so returning is genuine news about a 401 and no news at all about the link. It is written down next to the constant.

### 2. The three smaller ones

- The already-active branch now fires `haptics.success()` before returning. The user asked for a switch to Chat and a switch to Chat is under way, so confirming it is honest, and the card still does the explaining. I stopped short of an alert — a modal for "the thing you wanted is already happening" seemed worse than the silence.
- Fixed in both, at the component. `InlineBanner` slots take `disabled={!onPress}` / `disabled={!onSecondary}`, so a label whose handler is withheld is not pressable and fires nothing. - `fetchFailed` has its own line in the dep array saying it is deliberately a dependency and deliberately unread, and that dropping it as unused would take cold-start recovery with it.

We hit this same root cause through a third trigger path: **auto-review launching a reviewer harness**, with no reboot involved.

Every auto-review attempt failed before the reviewer started:

```
launch reviewer: reviewer replace stale pane: tmux runtime: destroy session review-<session>:
runtime: liveness probe inconclusive: system tmux "/opt/homebrew/bin/tmux" could not inspect
legacy default-socket session review-<session>: exit status 1:
error connecting to /private/tmp/tmux-501/default (No such file or directory)
```

The reviewer pane never existed in the first place, so AO blocked on exactly the condition proving it could not exist: there was no legacy tmux server at all.

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| AO | 0.12.12 (also seen on 0.12.11), desktop app |
| OS | macOS 26.5.2 (build 25F84), arm64 |
| Bundled tmux | 3.5a |
| System tmux | 3.7c (Homebrew, `/opt/homebrew/bin/tmux`) |
| Reviewer harness | codex |
| Permission mode | auto |

### Two things that made this hard to diagnose

**1. `ao doctor` reports tmux as PASS.** It resolves the bundled binary and says so, which reads as "tmux is fine" while the failure message blames tmux. But the legacy default-socket probe will not use the bundled binary, so on a machine with no `tmux` on `PATH` the earlier failure is:

```
... cannot inspect legacy default-socket session review-<session> because system tmux is unavailable
```

Installing a system tmux only moves the error along to the socket-absent case above. Worth considering whether the doctor check should report the system slot separately, since one code path depends on it.

**2. The bug only bites when the default socket file has *never* existed.** If the socket file exists but its server has exited, tmux says `no server running on ...`, which the current code already accepts as definitive. Only a never-created socket produces `error connecting ... (No such file or directory)`. That is the normal state on a machine that never uses tmux interactively, and it explains why this can look intermittent or environment-specific.

### Workaround

Keeping any tmux server alive on the default socket resolves it, because probing a missing session then returns `can't find session: ...`, which is already handled:

```bash
tmux new-session -d -s ao-probe-keepalive 'while :; do sleep 3600; done'
```

We run that from a LaunchAgent at login so it survives reboots. Creating a decoy session named after the specific reviewer pane also works, but only for that one session name.

### On the fix

We independently traced this to `socketForSession` in `backend/internal/adapters/runtime/tmux/tmux.go` omitting the absent-socket matcher from its legacy-branch check, and were about to open a patch when we found #4859 already does exactly that, plus the equivalent branch in `IsAlive`. It looks correct for our case too, so we would rather see that land than add a competing PR. Happy to test a build if that helps.

One note for whoever merges: auto-review has a cap of 3 attempts per PR head commit, so a session that burned its attempts on this bug will not retry by itself even after the fix ships. Ours needed `ao review trigger <worker-session-id>` to recover.

Pushed `de0c6d4cc`. You are right, and I want to be precise about how I got it wrong, because I raised this race myself and then dismissed it.

I wrote that a late answer "cannot pollute the retention — it is recorded as *that* machine's list, and the next tick from this one replaces it". I had checked the wrong direction: whether A's list could be *read as* B's. It cannot. What I never checked is whether A's answer could *destroy* B's, which is what actually happens — and then B's next failed `/projects` finds nothing retained for B, goes unknown, and the filter I removed comes back. The retention guarantee was "the last list a machine gave us"; the race made it "the last list a machine gave us, unless another machine's answer arrived in between", which is not a guarantee.

### Two guards, because they close different windows

**`retainProjects` drops an answer whose machine is not the one the app is on.** That restores the guarantee to "the last list THIS machine gave us, until this machine gives us another".

**`projectsForMachine` gates the read**, and it is not redundant: the write guard cannot help in the window before the new machine has answered *at all*, because state still holds the old machine's list. Your spawn tracing is what convinced me this half has to exist rather than being belt-and-braces — the sheet re-checks its seed against the same value, so exposing A's list on B invalidates a legitimate pick and clears the model chosen under it. Unknown is the honest answer until this machine has spoken, and it is identity-stable in both branches so it costs no re-render.

**Scoped to the project write, as you suggested.** Guarding every write in `fetchAll` is what I had tried and abandoned before the first round — it also swallows the connection and loading state on a re-pair, because the `finally` still runs `setLoading(false)` while the early return skips `setConnection("open")`. ### Remaining correctness issues

1. **[P2] A failed first review fetch can still publish a known-looking `0`.** If a known PR has no prior review observation, metadata/CI changes successfully, and `FetchReviewThreads` fails, the observer preserves review rows but still fills a previously zero `ReviewObservedAt`. `ReviewPartial` remains false. The new summary gate therefore treats empty, never-fetched review storage as complete. Only successful review observations should establish completeness; metadata success must not manufacture it. See [observer timestamp/flag handling](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/observe/scm/observer.go#L1752-L1762) and [summary gate](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/service/session/pr_summary.go#L84-L90).

2. **[P2] The PR-claim writer does not populate the new completeness field.** `enrichClaimReviews` knows whether the fetch was partial and selects Merge/Preserve appropriately, but `claimRowsFromSCM` never assigns `ReviewPartial` and always assigns `ReviewObservedAt`. The full upsert then persists false, potentially overwriting an existing true value. A partial claim can publish an inaccurate exact count; a failed first claim-review fetch can publish zero. Update this producer too, including preservation of existing certainty on failure. See [claim enrichment](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/service/session/claim_pr.go#L166-L192), [claim row construction](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/service/session/claim_pr.go#L223-L258), and [new upsert assignment](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/storage/sqlite/queries/pr.sql#L57-L61).

3. **[P2] Upgrades incorrectly mark historical observations complete.** `DEFAULT FALSE` gives every existing PR a nonpartial flag, including old partial snapshots with nonzero review timestamps. Those immediately qualify for an exact count. A subsequent poll is not a reliable repair: the observer skips writes when semantic hashes are unchanged, and the review hash already included `Partial` before this commit. Initialize historical certainty conservatively and ensure certainty changes can persist even when provider content is unchanged. See [migration](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/storage/sqlite/migrations/0123_pr_review_partial.sql#L6), [unchanged-observation skip](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/observe/scm/observer.go#L579-L583), and [review hash](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/03d11d0a1589f264c8da58f64bb318df70b5d688/backend/internal/observe/scm/observer.go#L2015-L2022).

# PR #5170 — Manual Testing

## What are we testing?

Sometimes AO cannot confirm which Codex account the computer is currently using. Earlier, this could hide or disable all saved accounts and prevent new Codex tasks from starting.

This change should keep saved accounts and normal Codex tasks working while AO tries again in the background.

## Before starting

1. Add at least two Codex accounts in AO.
2. Confirm that one account shows **In use**.
3. Confirm that you can create a normal Codex task.

## Test 1: Open AO without internet

1. Close AO.
2. Turn off Wi-Fi.
3. Open AO.
4. Open **Settings → Subscriptions → Codex**.

Expected:

- Previously added accounts remain visible.
- AO may say that it cannot confirm the active account and is trying again.
- If AO cannot confirm the account, no account shows **In use**.
- **Add account** remains available.
- The page does not fail with `CODEX_ACCOUNT_MANAGEMENT_UNAVAILABLE`.

If AO can still confirm the account while offline, that is okay. Report that this condition could not be reproduced.

## Test 2: Restore the internet

1. Continue from Test 1.
2. Turn Wi-Fi back on.
3. Keep AO open without restarting or refreshing it.
4. Wait for about one minute.

Expected:

- AO recovers automatically.
- The correct account shows **In use**.
- The retry message disappears.
- No saved account disappears or changes unexpectedly.

## Test 3: Create a Codex task during the problem

1. While AO cannot confirm the active account, create a new Codex task.

Expected:

- It does not fail with `CODEX_ACCOUNT_MANAGEMENT_UNAVAILABLE`.
- If the internet is off, the Codex request itself may fail because there is no connection. That is acceptable.
- AO must not reject the task because of its account check.

## Test 4: Log out outside AO

1. Keep the accounts saved in AO.
2. Run `codex logout` in a terminal.
3. Return to **Settings → Subscriptions → Codex**.

Expected:

- Saved accounts remain visible.
- No account shows **In use**.
- AO does not treat the saved-account list as broken.
- Adding or signing into an account remains possible.

## Test 5: Change the account outside AO

1. Start with account A showing **In use** in AO.
2. Outside AO, log Codex into account B.
3. Return to AO and open Subscriptions.
4. Wait for AO to update.

Expected:

- Account B eventually shows **In use**.
- Account A remains saved.
- Existing Codex tasks are not restarted or removed.

## Test 6: Keep an existing task open

1. Start a Codex task and send a message.
2. Turn off Wi-Fi or change the Codex account outside AO.
3. Return to the existing task.

Expected:

- The task and its history remain present.
- AO does not restart or recreate the task.
- A temporary account-checking problem does not close the task.

## Report a failure with

- Test number
- Operating system
- AO version or build
- Output of `codex --version`
- Exact steps followed
- Expected result
- Actual result
- Exact error message
- Screenshot
- Approximate time of the failure

Additional macOS evidence for the termination/process-exit part of this issue, potentially relevant to #5173. This is an observed incident and cleanup result, not a reproduction of #5173 or proof of the same root cause.

**Environment (observed 2026-09-10):** macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), arm64; Agent Orchestrator desktop bundle 0.12.12; bundled daemon reports `dev`; Codex 0.153.4, Chat/app-server mode. The bundled daemon executable SHA-256 was `78ef9c6aabfdbd52aab01d0efe9a6f46ac15c49937dbf3811233d198c7ef085c`. We could not establish its source commit, so the bundle version is not proof of code ancestry.

**Observed state:**

- `ao session get scratch-14 --json` reported `isTerminated: true`, `status: terminated`, and activity `exited`, last updated `2026-09-08T15:00:28.066885Z`.
- About 45 hours later, its detached `ao chat-host scratch-14 ... -- codex app-server` was still alive (PID 69547, PPID 1), with Codex PID 69548 and three Node/REPL descendants (69553, 69554, 69559).
- All five had the old session workspace as their cwd. The host still listened on an ephemeral loopback TCP port. They were idle when inspected. The active replacement orchestrator was a separate session, `scratch-15`.

**Explicit cleanup did not match the reported result:**

1. Ran `ao session kill scratch-14 --project scratch`.
2. CLI returned `session scratch-14 killed` and the empty old workspace directory disappeared.
3. A subsequent `ps` check showed all five processes still alive with the same parent relationships.
4. `ao session exit-agent scratch-14 --project scratch --json` refused with `Session is terminated (SESSION_TERMINATED)`.

**Recovery performed:** revalidated the exact chat-host command/session identity and descendant parent links, sent targeted SIGTERM to those five PIDs, and verified all five exited. The main AO daemon PID remained unchanged and ready, and the live replacement orchestrator remained running. No daemon restart, database edits, source changes, or broad process kill was used.

The original event that marked this session terminated was not captured, so we cannot say whether replacement, startup reconciliation, or another path created the orphan. We understand live persistent Chat hosts intentionally survive daemon detach/restart; the discrepancy here is a durably terminated session whose explicit kill reported success while its owned host/provider tree remained alive.

Does #5173 cover this already-terminated persistent Chat host case, including retrying shutdown when its original controller is no longer registered? If not, this appears to need a separate regression: verify actual host/provider exit (or return a retryable cleanup failure) before reporting successful termination, including when the session was already marked terminated.

2. `ao session restore <owner-id>` made that owner live. Because restore runs an agent, I immediately sent an explicit observe-only instruction: do not resume original work; do not edit, merge, close, reopen, or publish anything.
3. Normal observer activity then updated the tracked PR to `merged` at `observedAt: 2026-09-10T12:42:00.16639Z`. The provider state had changed on 2026-09-07 at 13:00:24Z. No GitHub/source change, database edit, re-merge, daemon restart, bulk cleanup, or manual intervention was used to make that state change.
4. After confirming the workspace was clean and had no unique artifacts, the owner was terminated with `ao session kill <owner-id>`. `GET /api/v1/sessions/<owner-id>/pr` still reported `merged` afterward.

Mobile should refresh from the corrected backend state; I did not observe the mobile visual directly and do not claim that verification.

## Agent-collected evidence

Collected by a local AO worker session on the reporter's machine, 2026-09-11, using read-only
checks only (no switches, resumes, restarts, or writes to the affected session). Analyzed
against `origin/main` at `4ad71cc24d965ee42a812db83bbb9e3b0eda2353`. Reporter's installed build:

### Chronology (observed)

Source: `session_interface_transitions` and `sessions` rows for `agent-orchestrator-309`, read
via a read-only SQLite open of the daemon's database; plus the `session_meta` header of the
Codex rollout file. Times are UTC.

| When | Fact |
|---|---|
| 2026-09-10 21:09:11.814 → 21:09:16.334 | Transition `981051da-e030-41b6-8fc6-881a83d19a91`, chat → tui, policy `drain`, phase **completed**, `native_conversation_id = 01a077dc-1de6-7c81-af05-c88acfb7f1d5` |
| 2026-09-10 21:09:33.374 | Codex CLI creates a **new thread** `01a08d27-878b-7db0-9e84-9a921099f4a8` whose `session_meta` records `forked_from_id: 01a077dc-…`, `forked_from_ordinal_exclusive: 3362`, `originator: agent-orchestrator`, `source: cli`, `cli_version: 0.153.4` |
| (after) | `sessions.agent_session_id` and `sessions.provider_conversation_id` for `agent-orchestrator-309` both read `01a08d27-…`; `session_mode = tui` |

| 2026-09-11 04:41:13.958 → 04:41:15.072 | Transition `6c295206-…`, tui → chat, phase **failed**, `error_code = TARGET_RESUME_FAILED`, detail = the reported message |

So the two handles in the error message are: the handle the durable conversation branch owns
(`01a077dc`, the pre-switch thread) versus the handle the live session now carries
(`01a08d27`, the thread Codex forked 17 seconds after the Chat → Terminal switch completed).

### Where it is refused

`backend/internal/service/chat/service.go:417-421` (origin/main):

```go
if cfg.ProviderConversationID != "" && providerHandleOwnedByActiveBranch {
    if activeBranch.ProviderConversationID != "" &&
        activeBranch.ProviderConversationID != cfg.ProviderConversationID {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("active conversation branch provider handle %q does not match session handle %q",
            activeBranch.ProviderConversationID, cfg.ProviderConversationID)
    }
}
```

`providerHandleOwnedByActiveBranch` stays `true` because no provider scope is supplied on this
path. The scope that would open a new provider boundary is reserved by
`Manager.historicalChatProviderScopeID` (`backend/internal/session_manager/chat_spawn.go:492-538`),
which returns `""` unless the session `IsTerminated`, is in `SessionModeChat`, and its
**latest** interface transition is a *completed* TUI → Chat transition. A live TUI session whose
latest transition just failed matches none of those gates, so every retry takes the refusing
branch. That matches the reporter's "identical error both times".

This guard is covered today by `TestOrdinaryResumeRejectsProviderHandleOutsideActiveBranch`
(`backend/internal/service/chat/controller_test.go:705`), which asserts the refusal happens
before any provider launch. The refusal itself looks intentional and correct for a genuinely
unrelated handle; what appears to be missing is a path for a handle that is a *descendant* of
the branch's handle.

### What this supports, and its limits

**Supported by the evidence above:** the session handle and the active branch handle diverged
because Codex forked the thread on the Terminal side, and AO's Chat start path has no way to
accept a forked successor handle, so Terminal → Chat cannot succeed for this session.

whether `codex resume` forks by design in `0.153.4`, or whether it forked after failing to take
the thread-writer lock (`~/.codex/thread-writer-locks/<threadId>.lock`) while the outgoing chat
host was still exiting. The same session hit a hard `-32600 "already has an active writer"` on a
Chat → Terminal switch on 2026-09-08; whether that is the same mechanism with a different
outcome in this build is **not** established. Treat the fork trigger as open.

divergence reproduces on a clean install.

### Fix direction (not implemented)

AO already models provider-handle rotation as a chain of branches — this project conversation
has several historical provider-boundary branches, each carrying a different Codex thread id.
The missing piece is reserving such a boundary when a live TUI → Chat handoff presents a native
handle that descends from the active branch's handle, instead of refusing.

The ancestry proof is already available over the existing RPC: AO's generated Codex protocol
already carries `Thread.ForkedFromID`

`thread/read` of the new thread returns its fork parent.

**No patch is proposed here.** A fix has to distinguish a legitimate forked-successor migration
from a genuinely inconsistent identity, and it lands in the durable conversation-branch and
controller-generation logic. Getting that wrong risks rewriting conversation history, so it
needs an owner who can design the boundary semantics and cover both cases with regression

**[P1] The direct-copy fallback can return uncommitted, inconsistent browser data.**

Reviewed commit `9ccda34d7`. The diagnosis of the zero-page/missing-destination backup is sound, and validating the backup result plus preflighting rollback journals are useful changes. However, I would change the [raw-copy fallback](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/9ccda34d7d9f3a4ac76abb439824f9a72ddb7792/frontend/src/main/browser-profile-import.ts#L733-L747) before merging: it can turn the visible import failure into a successful import of incorrect data.

In rollback-journal mode, SQLite saves the **old** versions of modified pages in `History-journal`. It can then flush **uncommitted** changes into `History` itself, for example when its page cache fills. The exclusive lock prevents another reader from seeing this unfinished transaction. `copyFile` bypasses that protection, and omitting the journal prevents the staged database from undoing those uncommitted changes. This is why removing the journal can make the read succeed without making the data correct. SQLite explicitly documents the risks of [copying an active database or separating it from its journal](https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html).

I reproduced this using the PR's unchanged `snapshotSQLite`/preflight implementation and `better-sqlite3@12.11.1`, with a real locked synthetic database and **no mocked backup**:

1. Create a rollback-mode database with 1,000 history-like rows, each with `visit_count = 1000` and a roughly 2 KB title.
2. Set `cache_size = 10` and `cache_spill = ON` to force the relevant SQLite behavior with a small fixture.
3. Start `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE`, update all visit counts to `9999`, and leave the transaction unfinished.
4. Call this PR's `snapshotSQLite`, then read the returned snapshot.
5. Roll back the source transaction and compare.

Observed output:

```text
PR snapshot:
  visit_count 1000:  14 rows
  visit_count 9999: 986 rows
  PRAGMA integrity_check: ok

Source after ROLLBACK:
  visit_count 1000: 1000 rows
```

The snapshot returned changes that never committed, mixed with the previous state. Even adding `integrity_check` would not catch this example: structural validity does not establish transaction consistency. The small cache deliberately forces the failure; this demonstrates a valid failure scenario, not its frequency in normal browsing.

The added test correctly models the library's zero-page return, but uses an otherwise clean database and a text placeholder for the journal. It therefore verifies the fallback branch without verifying consistency during a real transaction. The shared helper also handles cookies and Firefox databases, so the impact extends beyond Brave history. Separately copying the main database and WAL can capture different moments during writes/checkpoints, and sidecars that appear or grow after preflight are copied without rechecking their size/budget. The catch-all also applies this fallback to non-lock backup errors.

My suggested change:

- Keep backup-result validation and journal preflight; retain SQLite's online backup as the mechanism that produces a consistent snapshot.
- Retry transient lock errors and the known zero-page/missing-output condition within a bounded, cancellable time budget. Preserve meaningful non-lock errors. The existing 5-second SQLite timeout should count toward that budget.
- If the source remains locked, return an actionable “Close Brave and retry the import” message instead of reading through the lock.
- Add tests with a real unfinished transaction, a lock that is released, and a persistent lock. Assert that no uncommitted data is imported and that unsuccessful attempts leave no staged data or destination profiles.

Retries will not guarantee import while the browser stays open: Chromium can [put its history database into exclusive locking mode](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/refs/heads/main/components/history/core/browser/history_database.cc), which can [retain locks beyond an individual transaction](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_locking_mode). If keeping the source browser open is a hard product requirement, that needs a separate design using browser cooperation or a coordinated snapshot of the database and required journals, with recovery confined to staging. Copying the files sequentially or switching SQLite backup commands does not solve a persistent exclusive lock.

This is also a concern with the raw-copy workaround proposed in #5155 itself. Following that proposed fix does not establish that the resulting snapshot is safe.

Reproduced on Linux x86_64 in the native Electron app at `13c73f197f88369b2a648dfde9691d13ab173791`, using installed CLI version `2.1.268`, an existing Pro subscription login, and isolated AO data.

**Reported by:** @Prasad-D-Ware | **Date:** 2026-09-11

Session `meetyou-26` (Claude Code, ACP) could not return to Chat. Eight consecutive attempts failed, each after ~46s, then rolled back to Terminal.

### New trigger: a *cancelled* prompt, days earlier

This did **not** come from "Stop now and switch". The poisoning fact was four days stale:

```
sessions.latest_user_prompt    = "Say hi to"
sessions.latest_user_prompt_at = 2026-09-07 14:35:15.607692
```

`conversation_turns` shows the turn requested at exactly that timestamp has `state = cancelled`. Claude Code never replays a cancelled prompt as a completed user message, so the latest-completed text match in `nativeHistoryCheckpoint.reached()` (`backend/internal/service/chat/controller.go:501`) can never be satisfied. The settle loop then burns the full 45s `nativeHistorySettleLimit` and fails `TARGET_HISTORY_UNSETTLED`, and `rollbackInterfaceTransition` commits the mode back to `tui`.

Note `captureAOHighWater` already refuses to anchor on non-completed turns (`controller.go:415-424`), with a comment saying that requiring one "would make every future switch time out" — that is exactly what happens here, because the hook-derived facts get no equivalent filter.

### Controlled before/after, from `session_interface_transitions`

| Time (UTC) | Phase | Error | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14:43:07 | failed | TARGET_HISTORY_UNSETTLED | 46.4s |
| 14:49:51 | failed | TARGET_HISTORY_UNSETTLED | 46.4s |
| 15:28:47 | failed | TARGET_HISTORY_UNSETTLED | 46.4s |
| **15:29:59** | **completed** | — | **2.6s** |

Between the last failure and the success, the only change was clearing that one field:

```sql
update sessions set latest_user_prompt='' where id='meetyou-26';
```

Same daemon process, same session, same provider transcript, 72 seconds apart. After the successful switch the daemon repopulated the field from the imported history with a prompt that *is* present in the replay, so the session stayed switchable.

### Ruled out

- **Not provider/account-wide:** `oddswell-24` and `meetyou-24` both completed `tui->chat` in ~4s at 14:19:01 and 14:19:12 — same minute, same daemon, same account, while `meetyou-26` was failing.
- **Not rate limits:** the account sat at 99% of its 7-day quota throughout, including during those successful switches.
- **Not a forked transcript:** one `.jsonl`, one session id, `bridge-session` rows consistent throughout.
- **Not the 45s budget:** the successful switch took 2.6s. Raising the limit would only make the failure slower.

### Note on #4770

[PR #4770](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4770) (merged 2026-09-02, in this build) made the ACP replay refreshable. It changed the error text from #4681's "snapshot is incomplete and cannot be refreshed" to `refresh ACP session history: context deadline exceeded`, but not the outcome — the retry loop now re-issues `session/load` against a checkpoint that can never match. Worth flagging so this doesn't read as already-addressed.

### Impact

Permanent loss of Chat for an otherwise healthy session, with no UI recovery path. On mobile it is worse than on desktop: the failure appears as a banner and the screen bounces back to Terminal, so nothing actionable is surfaced at all.

The workaround above needs direct `sqlite3` access to `ao.db`, which is not something a normal user can be asked to do — which is why the recovery action in [PR #4466](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/4466) matters as much as the checkpoint fix itself.

## Follow-up: fresh `claude setup-token` test

Tested on macOS 26.5.1 with Claude Code 2.1.268, at PR head `13c73f197f88369b2a648dfde9691d13ab173791` (`ao/credential-validation`). Used the native Electron app built from this checkout, an isolated Claude configuration directory, and isolated AO data/Electron profiles. Renderer: `http://localhost:5173`; daemon: `127.0.0.1:35212`.

This run actually generated a new token using `claude setup-token` and completed browser authorization. The new token was supplied through `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` unset. It did not rely on the previously saved Keychain login. No credential values are included below.

### Authentication and models: PASS

- `claude setup-token` exited 0 and reported `Long-lived authentication token created successfully!`.
- With the fresh token, `claude auth status` returned:

```json
{"loggedIn":true,"authMethod":"oauth_token","apiProvider":"firstParty"}
```

- Anthropic `GET /v1/models` accepted the token with HTTP 200 and returned 11 provider models.
- AO `GET /api/v1/agents/readiness` reported:

```text
authentication.state = authorized
authentication.freshness = fresh
authentication.reasonCode = authorized
effectiveReadiness = ready
```

- After refreshing the model catalog, AO returned `source: provider`, `stale: false`, and 12 picker entries: the 11 provider models plus the configured `opus[1m]` default entry.
- In native New Task, Claude Code was selectable without a login warning or another login prompt. Real model names appeared.
- Opus 5 exposed Low, Medium, High, Extra high, and Max, plus Agent default. Selecting an effort worked in the dialog. Switching to Sonnet 4.5 removed the effort control; switching back restored it.
- Created a native Chat session with Opus 5. Sent `Reply with exactly PR5208_SETUP_TOKEN_OK. Do not use tools or modify any files.` The provider replied `PR5208_SETUP_TOKEN_OK` and the turn completed. The daemon conversation response recorded `role: assistant`, `origin: provider`, `streaming: false`, and `settings.model: claude-opus-5`. This confirms actual inference with the newly generated setup token, beyond credential presence/readiness.

### Effort propagation on startup: FAIL

Reproduction with that same valid setup token:

1. Open Scratch → New Task.
2. Select Claude Code → Opus 5 → Low effort.
3. Leave task text empty and click Start task to create a Chat session.
4. Open the running chat's model/effort menu and read its configuration endpoint.

Expected: the running chat retains Low effort.

Actual: the native menu shows `Effort Default`. `GET /api/v1/sessions/scratch-1/conversation/config-options` returns:

```json
{"options":[{"id":"model","currentValue":"opus"},{"id":"effort","currentValue":"default"}]}
```

The chat still answers successfully. The failure is loss of the selected effort during startup, not setup-token authentication. This corroborates the previously reported [effort propagation issue](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/5208#issuecomment-5633419336), with Low becoming Default on this clean configuration. A screenshot of the native menu was captured during the run.

### Testing-guide correction

This checkout does not implement the guide's `ao new` command: `go run ./cmd/ao new --help` returns `unknown command "new" for "ao"` and exits 1. The native New Task flow above was used instead.

The build and focused automated checks reported earlier passed at this same SHA; this follow-up adds fresh-token and live-chat evidence. It does not clear the previously reported fake-key/preselected-agent spawn issue or the older-model startup issue.

I independently forward-ported this fix onto a newer AO base and exercised it on a real packaged Windows Desktop build. The core fix works: Codex account bootstrap succeeds, account_storage_unsafe disappears, account management reports supported, managed credential homes work, and real Codex sessions can spawn.

Two things came out of an adversarial review that may be worth tightening before merge:

1. Unknown effective ACE types should fail closed.
In the current account_home_windows.go, the managed-home loop has the equivalent of:

if !allowed || uint32(prefix.mask) == 0 {
    continue
}

That means an unrecognized effective ACE type can be silently ignored rather than causing the private-home check to fail. In my forward-port I changed the classification so known deny/non-granting ACEs remain non-granting, known allow ACEs are evaluated normally, INHERIT_ONLY remains non-effective, but an unsupported/ambiguous effective ACE type rejects the managed home.

2. Consider narrowing TrustedInstaller trust.
The PR currently adds TrustedInstaller to the general trusted owner/principal set. I kept it narrower: accepted where necessary for the actual Windows volume-root/ancestor case, while keeping the private vault/managed-home ownership rules strict. That avoids accidentally broadening trust beyond the system-owned ancestor that requires it.

Validation on the forward-port included real Windows ancestor-chain tests, managed-home admission through AccountFactory, unsafe-DACL negatives, reparse defenses, packaged Desktop install/startup, account bootstrap, direct Codex worker execution, and delegated orchestrator workers. No Windows ACL changes to C:\ were required.

Follow-up with end-to-end validation from another Windows machine/build.

The previously identified account_storage_unsafe path was indeed the blocker in my environment. After forward-porting the ancestor ACL fix plus the Windows managed-home fix from the work around #5108, the failure disappeared without modifying the machine-wide ACLs or ownership on C:\.

On a packaged AO Desktop build I verified:

Codex account bootstrap: PASS
account_storage_unsafe: absent
account management: supported
managed Codex credential home admission: PASS
fresh Codex session spawn: PASS
normal session resume: PASS

I then used the same build for real read-only Codex worker execution and AO orchestrator/delegated-worker execution, so this was not just an /accounts/ensure smoke test.

One additional bug was masked by the ancestor failure: AccountFactory.Open was checking info.Mode().Perm() == 0700 for managed homes. On Windows the directory reports POSIX-style mode bits such as 0777, so the managed account path still fails after fixing only the ancestor walk. #5108 addresses this with platform-specific Windows DACL/ownership validation.

So at least for this reproduction, #5108 is the correct implementation path for the account-management failure.

## Agent-collected evidence

Collected on 12 September 2026 from the affected macOS installation. The repository checkout was reset to `origin/main` commit `15e9ea971f1711ec8b50e157d6eb300db6cbe0d6`. The installed app reported version 0.13.0. Sensitive credential material and unrelated session data are omitted.

### Persisted switch state

Read-only SQLite queries against `~/.ao/data/ao.db` showed that credential activation completed, with `credentials_committed_at` populated. Seven session rows reached `restart_state = restarted`. Three Chat sessions reached `restart_state = failed` with only `restart_unconfirmed:<generation>` stored. The parent switch remained in `phase = recovery_required` with `failure_code = restart_unconfirmed`.

The relevant query shape was:

```sql
SELECT id, phase, failure_code, credentials_committed_at, created_at, updated_at
FROM codex_account_switches
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

SELECT session_id, interface_mode, stop_state, restart_state, error_code
FROM codex_account_switch_sessions
WHERE switch_id = ?;
```

The affected switch began at `2026-09-12 08:30:41 UTC`. The final unchanged recovery update was `2026-09-12 08:45:02 UTC`.

### Code evidence

The exact original per-session cause cannot be recovered from durable state. `restartCodexSwitchSessions` replaces every underlying worker error with `restart_unconfirmed:<generation>` in `backend/internal/session_manager/codex_account_switch.go`, around line 898. The wrapped cause is neither persisted nor logged there.

Chat restart is serial. Native history settlement may wait 45 seconds in `backend/internal/service/chat/controller.go`, around line 34. `restartCodexSwitchSessions` retries `ErrChatHistoryUnsettled` once, around line 881. This makes a multi-session switch slow and leaves the overall worker dependent on each serial restart.

The switch and recovery goroutines run on the daemon background context without an overall switch deadline, around lines 265 and 1178 of `backend/internal/session_manager/codex_account_switch.go`.

The confirmed recovery defect is around lines 1185 through 1192. After the HTTP handler accepts recovery and starts a goroutine, `recoverCodexAccountSwitch` silently returns when journal loading or session-operation acquisition fails. It does not persist a recovery attempt, update the failure, or log the cause. Deferred cleanup retains the global fence because the switch phase remains nonterminal. The UI therefore remains blocked in `recovery_required`, while the accepted recovery request appears to have succeeded.

An existing `codex_account_switch` operation can be reclaimed. A conflicting different operation can make acquisition fail. That failure is currently swallowed.

### Suggested verification coverage

1. A blocking Chat launcher is bounded by a switch-level deadline.
2. Several serial `ErrChatHistoryUnsettled` results cannot block indefinitely.
3. A conflicting session operation produces a durable, visible recovery result.
4. Failure to load the switch journal is logged and reflected in recovery state.
5. A recovery request never returns apparent success when its worker immediately exits without progress.
6. Sanitized per-session failure classifications are persisted without credentials or private conversation content.

The separate `CODEX_HOME` mismatch observed later was introduced during manual diagnostic relaunch and is not part of the original report.

### Why the fence never lifts

`domain/codex_account_switch.go:34-36` — only two phases are terminal:

```go
func (p CodexAccountSwitchPhase) Terminal() bool {
	return p == CodexAccountSwitchCompleted || p == CodexAccountSwitchFailed
}
```

`recovery_required` is neither, so `GetActiveCodexAccountSwitch` keeps returning it as the active switch, and `session_manager/codex_account_switch.go:165-169` rejects every new switch request:

```go
if _, active, readErr := store.GetActiveCodexAccountSwitch(ctx); readErr != nil {
	return domain.CodexAccountSwitch{}, readErr
} else if active {
	return domain.CodexAccountSwitch{}, ErrCodexAccountSwitchInProgress
}
```

The fence is also enforced in the schema, so nothing can work around it at the storage layer:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_codex_account_switches_one_active
ON codex_account_switches((1))
WHERE phase NOT IN ('completed', 'failed');
```

That is the "account switching doesn't work" symptom: the user is locked out of switching entirely, not just stuck on this one.

Retry recovery cannot escape either. `dispatchCodexAccountSwitch` at `recovery_required` (`codex_account_switch.go:591-604`) sees `active.AccountID == sw.TargetAccountID` (credentials committed at 06:23:33), so it advances to `VerifyingAccount` → `RestartingSessions` → `restartCodexSwitchSessions`, which retries the same two sessions. They fail again, and line 569 sends it straight back to `recovery_required`:

```go
case domain.CodexAccountSwitchRestartingSessions:
	if err := m.restartCodexSwitchSessions(ctx, store, sw.ID, sessions); err != nil {
		_ = m.advanceCodexAccountSwitch(ctx, store, sw, domain.CodexAccountSwitchRecoveryRequired, "restart_unconfirmed")
		return
	}
```

`recovery_required` → `restarting` → `recovery_required`, forever. `CodexAccountSwitchFailed` is only reachable through the rollback path, which needs `active.AccountID == sw.SourceAccountID` — and it is not, because the credential swap already succeeded. So no input the user can give reaches a terminal phase.

### Suggested direction

The state machine needs an operator-driven give-up edge: mark the unrestartable sessions abandoned, settle the switch `Failed` (or `Completed` with partial-failure detail), release the fence, and tell the user which sessions need a manual restart. Right now a partial restart failure is treated as retryable forever, but nothing about it is retryable once the credential is committed and the worker cannot resume.

Secondary: the banner says only "AO could not confirm that every session restarted." It should name `agent-orchestrator-2` and `agent-orchestrator-5` — the data is already in `codex_account_switch_sessions.error_code`.

Worth noting the trigger too: the switch was made 22 seconds after a `You've hit your usage limit` turn failure on `agent-orchestrator-12`, which is the normal reason to switch accounts. Hitting a usage limit and then being locked out of switching away from it is the worst case for this fence.

Filed separately from this: the failed Codex Chat turns in the same session store an **empty** `error_message`, so they render as a bare "The agent ran into a problem" with no cause.

Filed the empty-`error_message` half separately: [#5289](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5289). Different subsystem (`acp/conversation.go` error propagation, not the switch state machine) and it reproduces with no account switch involved, so it should not block this one.

Hey @nikhilachale, I have a concern regarding your requested change. I checked the actual launch path as well as #5000 . The `systemexec` wrapper added by that PR handles installer/capability commands, but Goose sessions are still launched through direct `exec.CommandContext` calls in the launch paths.

If this PR wraps only the `--help` probe, a Windows npm `goose.cmd` installation could pass detection and be reported as installed, BUT then fail when AO actually tries to start the session for that harness. That seems worse than the current explicit false negative.

Should this PR intentionally accept that detection/launch mismatch, or should `.cmd` remain excluded until #3409
provides one shared execution path for both probing and launching? If `.cmd` support is required here, I think both paths need to be covered and tested.

Basically, even if we go by the `cmd.exe /d /s /c` path for detection of Goose, it is not a good way to launch the actual session in Goose. Go preserves arguments cleanly for native executable like:
```
argv := []string{
    "goose.exe",
    "run",
    "--system",
    "line one\nline two & %PATH%",
}
```
where the child receives the fourth arg. 
But for a shim, we will have to flatten it into a command like:
```
cmd.exe /d /s /c "goose.cmd run --system "line one
line two & %PATH%""
```
With this, special characters(`\n`, `&`, etc) and environment variable expansions(`$something`) will happen which will be interpreted differently by the shell. Very brittle. 

So we can't use what #5000  did for launching Goose sessions even though it will solve the detection problem and avoid any false negatives. 

I feel we should merge this and accept the false negatives on windows using npm only install path for Goose until #3409 lands and we have a proper launching mechanism for shims. 
Because even if we cover the false negative via #5000, we still won't be able to launch it properly because its current wrapper is not sufficient for arbitrary interactive launch arguments.

The npm-only installation is not just undetectable; it is currently not launchable by AO. Adding `.cmd` support only to the identity probe would therefore create a false positive rather than restore a working installation. Supporting it correctly requires the shared Windows launch work tracked by #3409.

Nice find, this catches three real bugs (superseded epoch never closing the terminal, typing into an auto-paused box not waking it, and the reconnect backoff resetting on every open). Two of them are already event-driven and I would keep them as-is. One I would fix differently, and I want to flag it before we merge because we just shipped an overlapping state-driven terminal redesign and I would like these to stay consistent.

## The 2s staleCheck poll: fix the state at the source instead

The `staleCheck` ticker in `writeTerminalOutput` is polling to discover that the terminal's own state is lying. The output loop already re-reads terminal state on every iteration (the 50ms ticker plus the output NOTIFY), and it already returns on `state == "closed"` / `"failed"`. So it does not need a second liveness query; it needs the state to be truthful.

The root cause is exactly what your comment says: retiring an epoch updates `ao_worker_connections` and fails the old requests, but never touches the retired epoch's `ao_terminal_sessions` rows, so they stay `open` for the full session TTL. The state-driven fix is to close those rows in the same retire transaction (`sandbox_store.go`, right after "fail worker requests from superseded epochs"):

```sql
UPDATE ao_terminal_sessions
SET state = 'closed', closed_at = now(), updated_at = now()
WHERE org_id = $1 AND session_id = $2 AND worker_epoch < $3
  AND state IN ('opening', 'open')
```

This mirrors what `OpenTerminal` already does when it retires old agent terminals on re-open. Once the row is truthful, the existing `writeTerminalOutput` loop sees `closed` on its next tick (worst case ~50ms), returns, and the client re-attaches against the live epoch. That lets us delete `staleCheck`, `TerminalWorkerEpochCurrent`, and the 2s cadence entirely, and it fixes the root (the row not reflecting retirement) rather than adding a detector for the lie. It also avoids a per-open-terminal DB query every 2s across every replica.

We have implemented exactly this on our terminal branch and are deploying it, so if we take that approach here the two branches converge instead of fighting over the same file.

## Keep these (they are already event-driven, not polls)

- The `queueTerminalRequest` wake-on-input: it fires because input arrived, so it is a reaction to an event, good.
- Returning `ErrWorkerSuperseded` (fail fast) instead of retrying `ErrWorkerUnavailable` for the full `terminalReadyTimeout`: still worth keeping so a keystroke into a superseded terminal does not stall 20s.

## Frontend backoff (secondary)

`STABLE_CONNECTION_MS` is the one remaining wall-clock timer. Consider resetting the reconnect backoff on a real "worker is serving" protocol milestone (`ready` / `replay_complete` / first live output) rather than on `opened` (which fires before replay) or after a fixed stability window. That keys the reset off state, not the clock. With the CP change above the client gets a clean close and reconnects to the live epoch instead of looping into a dead one, so this is lower priority, but it is the same principle.

## One unrelated thing

The persistent-chat-host reconcile loop (`backend/internal/daemon/*`) is a good fix but is a separate concern from the terminal reconnect. Might be cleaner to split it into its own PR so this one stays focused on the terminal path.

Two things I would rather put up front than have you find them.

**1. The guard is a deliberate divergence from the desktop, not a copy of it.**

`frontend/src/renderer/lib/terminal-mux.ts:36` calls `atob` bare. The two files are otherwise the same shape: both drop an unparseable message with `try { JSON.parse } catch { return }`, and both call the decoder *outside* that guard — desktop at `:214`, mobile at `:207`. The difference is that mobile extends the same "drop what we cannot read" policy one level down, into the decode, where the desktop stops at JSON.

I went that way because the two hosts treat an exception escaping a socket callback differently, but it is a divergence and I would rather name it than let the body's "same shape as the desktop" imply otherwise. If you would prefer the two files match exactly, I will drop the try/catch — the daemon cannot produce input that reaches it either way.

**2. What the guard replaces is not a throw, it is silent corruption.**

The decoder being removed pre-filtered anything outside the standard alphabet and decoded whatever was left, so a malformed frame reached xterm as arbitrary bytes instead of failing. Running that implementation against the same inputs the new tests use:

|---|---|---|

| `"QQ="` (bad padding) | `[65]` | empty frame |
| `"QU-JD"` (base64url) | `[65, 66, 67]` | empty frame |

So on this path the choice is drop-versus-corrupt, not drop-versus-throw. Still unreachable from the daemon, for the reasons in the body.

## Reproduction

1. Open an orchestrator session in TUI mode (harness: `codex`, but see above).
2. Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> in the terminal pane to kill the agent process.
3. The pane shows `[process exited]` and the strip reads **TERMINAL ENDED — "This terminal process ended, but the session is not marked terminated yet."**
4. No recovery control is offered anywhere on that pane.

Resulting session state:

```
id: agent-orchestrator-309
role: orchestrator      harness: codex
status: exited          activity: exited
terminated: false
```

## Root cause

**The backend is fine.** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/resume-agent` recovers this state perfectly:

```
$ ao session resume-agent agent-orchestrator-309 --json
{ "ok": true, "resumeMode": "native", ... "status": "idle" }
0.136s total
```

`resumeMode: "native"` — it resumed the real Codex conversation, not a fallback restart from the saved prompt. Nothing was lost. This is purely a UI gap.

### The category error

`TerminalPane.tsx:966` decides whether a dead **process** can be recovered by asking whether the session **row** is alive:

```ts
const canRestoreSession =
    terminalTarget?.kind !== "reviewer" &&
    terminalTarget?.kind !== "shell" &&
    session !== undefined &&
    !isSessionActive;            // <- sessionIsActive(session)
```

and `workspace.ts:296`:

```ts
export function sessionIsActive(session: WorkspaceSession): boolean {
    return session.isTerminated !== true && session.status !== "terminated";
}
```

A Ctrl+C'd session has `isTerminated === false`, so `sessionIsActive` returns **true**, so `canRestoreSession` is **false**, so `TerminalEndedStrip` renders no button and falls through to the `terminal.sessionEndedNotTerminated` message — which literally describes the dead end it is stuck in without offering a way out.

Secondary problem: even when `canRestore` *is* true, the strip's only action is `useRestoreSession` → `POST /sessions/{id}/restore`, which relaunches a **terminated** session. The strip has no concept of "agent exited, session alive", so fixing the predicate alone would call the wrong endpoint.

### Three gates, three different answers

| Surface | Gate | Result for this state |
|---|---|---|
| `TerminalPane.tsx:966` | `!sessionIsActive(session)` | ❌ hidden — row isn't terminated |
| `command-palette.ts:156` | `!sessionIsActive(session) && !isOrchestratorSession(session)` | ❌ hidden — **twice**: same predicate, plus orchestrators are explicitly excluded from resume |
| `SessionInspector.tsx:1036` | `isTerminated === true \|\| activity?.state !== "exited" \|\| activeAgentSwitch` | ✅ should render |

So `ResumeAgentControl` in the inspector rail is the only surviving path. That matches the report: from the terminal pane — where you are when you press Ctrl+C — it looks completely unrecoverable, because on that surface it is.

## Workaround

```
ao session resume-agent <session-id>
```

Or the **Resume agent** button in the Session Inspector rail.

## Suggested fix

1. Introduce a predicate for *process* liveness distinct from *row* liveness — e.g. `sessionAgentExited(session)` = `activity?.state === "exited" && isTerminated !== true` — and stop using `sessionIsActive` to gate recovery affordances.
2. In `TerminalEndedStrip`, offer **Resume agent** (`/resume-agent`) when the agent exited but the row is alive, keeping **Restore** (`/restore`) for terminated rows. They are different operations and currently only one is reachable.
3. Drop `&& !isOrchestratorSession(session)` from the command-palette resume item. Orchestrators are resumable — the backend proves it — so excluding them removes the only keyboard-reachable path.
4. Consider making the strip's action a labelled button rather than a bare icon (see [#3300](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/3300)).

## Related

- [#3300](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/3300) — same strip; covers the case where `canRestore` is true but the button is a near-invisible 24px icon. This issue is the complementary case where the button is absent entirely.
- [#3875](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/3875) — another route into the same "unrecoverable exited/non-terminated orchestrator" state.

When running AO with `npm run dev`, macOS identifies the application requesting access as **Electron**, not **Agent Orchestrator**. To test Safari import locally:

Confirmed — this implementation writes `<Event>.ps1` PowerScript hooks on Windows so Cline's hook discovery actually runs them. On Windows, `GetAgentHooks` no longer writes the extensionless bash scripts (which Cline ignores on that platform); it writes `.ps1` wrappers under `.clinerules\hooks\` (e.g. `TaskStart.ps1`):

```powershell
# ao-managed-cline-hook
try { $input | ao hooks cline session-start 2>$null } catch {}
Write-Output '{"cancel": false}'
```

We did live Windows testing and verified it end-to-end:

- `GetAgentHooks` writes **only `.ps1` hooks** on Windows — `PreToolUse.ps1`, `TaskCancel.ps1`, `TaskComplete.ps1`, `TaskStart.ps1`, `UserPromptSubmit.ps1` (no extensionless files are left behind).
- Executed the generated hook exactly as Cline's discovery does (`powershell -NoProfile -File TaskStart.ps1` with a Cline payload piped on stdin) — it ran successfully and returned `{"cancel": false}` on stdout.

How we tested, and how to re-run it in the next round:

1. Install the hooks into a workspace — start a Cline session or call `GetAgentHooks` — which writes the `.ps1` hooks under `.clinerules\hooks\`.
2. Confirm the names end in `.ps1`: `dir .clinerules\hooks` should list `TaskStart.ps1` etc.
3. Execute one hook just like Cline does:
   `'{"event":"TaskStart"}' | powershell -NoProfile -File .clinerules\hooks\TaskStart.ps1` → expect `{"cancel": false}` on stdout.
4. Unit tests assert the naming and rendering on Windows CI: `TestClineHookScriptNameIsPlatformAware`, `TestRenderPowerShellClineHookScript`, `TestRenderClineHookScriptFollowsPlatform`, `TestGetAgentHooksWritesPlatformScriptNames`.

### The stale pill

`ao session get agent-orchestrator-328 --json` for the affected session:

```
5310  open    ci=passing  mergeability=blocked
5134  closed  ci=passing  mergeability=conflicting   <- drives the pill
```

`#5134`'s mergeability froze at `conflicting` at its last poll before closure (its
base branch had moved on), and closing it never cleared the field.

`frontend/src/renderer/components/SessionInspector.tsx:1419` then folds every PR on
the session into the timeline with no check on PR state:

```js
for (const pr of session.prs) {
    if (pr.ci === "failing") add("ci_failed");
    if (pr.review === "changes_requested") add("changes_requested");
    if (pr.mergeability === "conflicting") add("conflict");
}
```

The same hole applies to `ci_failed` and `changes_requested`: a closed PR that last
polled red would pin those pills too. Only the conflict case has been hit so far.

**Why the PR card directly above it looks right.** The backend already handles this,
but only halfway — `backend/internal/service/session/pr_summary.go:401`:

```go
func mergeabilityReasons(pr domain.PullRequest) []string {
    if pr.Merged || pr.Closed { return nil }    // reasons cleared for a closed PR
```

while `summarizeMergeability` three lines above still returns
`State: mergeabilityOrUnknown(pr.Mergeability)` with no such gate. So a closed PR
reports no *reasons* but keeps its raw *state*, and the timeline reads the raw state.
Either side alone would remove the symptom.

### The placement

`SessionInspector.tsx:1321-1345` builds the timeline's "now" row as one composite
line: the agent-activity pill, then an optional `no_signal` pill, then the SCM pills
from `scmTimelineStates`. They share a single timestamp:

```js
const activityAt = session.activity?.lastActivityAt ?? session.updatedAt ?? session.createdAt;
```

So the SCM pills have no time of their own and inherit the agent's last-activity time.
That is where "just now" comes from in the screenshot — it describes the agent going
idle, not the conflict, which in this case belongs to a PR closed earlier and has no
current moment at all.

This supports the reporter's second point structurally, not just visually: the row
merges two different subjects (a live agent process; a pull request) onto one line
with one timestamp, and the SCM pills carry no PR identity, so on a session with more
than one PR they cannot say which PR they mean.

Hypothesis, not verified: fixing only the staleness would leave the confusing
composition in place, and any session with a genuinely conflicting PR would still read
as "Idle Conflict" with a misleading timestamp.

## Agent-collected evidence

Collected 2026-09-13 by a local coding agent at the reporter's request, reading
`origin/main` at `ce4fa7c78`. Read-only; nothing was changed.

### The timeline already works this way — the SCM row is the exception

`frontend/src/renderer/components/SessionInspector.tsx:1259` (`ActivityTimeline`)
pushes discrete events, each sorted on its own timestamp:

| Event | Timestamp source | PR-associated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Created workspace | `session.createdAt` | — |
| Draft PR #N | `pr.stateChangedAt` | yes, via `PRTimelineLink` |
| Opened PR #N | `pr.createdAt` | yes |
| Merged PR #N | `pr.stateChangedAt` | yes |
| Done | `latestMergedTimestamp(prs)` | — |
| agent activity + `no_signal` + SCM pills | `activityAt`, shared | **no** |

The last row (`SessionInspector.tsx:1321-1345`) is built as one composite entry whose
timestamp is:

```js
const activityAt = session.activity?.lastActivityAt ?? session.updatedAt ?? session.createdAt;
```

so the SCM pills have no time of their own and no PR identity, on a surface where the
adjacent entries have both. `PRTimelineLink` — the association primitive this proposal
needs — already exists and is already used by the neighbouring rows.

### What is missing to implement it

`SessionPRSummary` (generated schema) exposes `observedAt`, `ciObservedAt` and
`reviewObservedAt`, but **no mergeability timestamp at all**, so a "Conflict detected"
event has no time to render today.

More importantly, those `*ObservedAt` fields record *when AO last polled*, not *when
the state changed*. Driving timeline events from them would re-stamp an unchanged
conflict as "just now" on every poll — reproducing the misleading timestamp in
[#5316](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5316) rather than
fixing it.

There is also no durable event store to source transitions from: `ao events` does not
exist in the current CLI (verified against the installed
`0.13.1-nightly.202609121623` binary — the command is absent). Earlier triage notes
referencing an `ao events` subsystem describe an older build and no longer apply.

So this needs the daemon to persist SCM **transitions** (state, PR, changed-at) rather
than only current state plus last-observed. That is a data-model change, not a
renderer change — which is why it is filed separately from #5316 rather than folded
into that fix.

### One design question worth settling first

Conflict, CI-failure and changes-requested are conditions (intervals), not instants.
As timeline events they become start/end pairs, which raises a product question this
issue should probably answer explicitly: should a resolved condition stay in the
history as a pair, or should the timeline show only currently-open conditions and drop
them on resolution? Note also that "conflicts resolved" is normally inferred from the
absence of the conflict on a later poll rather than observed directly, so its
timestamp would be an upper bound.

- [#5316](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5316) — the stale Conflict pill; the correctness bug that prompted this.
- [#5081](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5081) (closed) — loader spinning next to a green "Mergeable" label; same agent-state/SCM-state conflation on the board surface.

Filed [#5317](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/issues/5317) for the second half of this report — giving SCM state its own timeline events with their own timestamps and PR association, instead of stacking it onto the agent's current activity row.

Kept separate so this issue stays closeable by the correctness fix (a closed PR should stop driving the pill). #5317 needs the daemon to persist SCM transitions, which is a data-model change and a longer piece of work; the stale pill shouldn't wait on it.

The gate applied to **every** adapter with an auth checker, not just command-backed ones. Claude Code's catalog is static — `discoverClaudeCatalog` returns a fixed list and never spawns anything — but its probe returns a real `Unauthorized` when `loggedIn: false`. So a signed-out Claude Code user would have lost their model picker entirely, to prevent a browser sign-in that could never happen for them. Muse was in the same position. Claude Code is probably the most-used harness in AO, so this was the most damaging part of the change and it had nothing to do with Kiro.

`AgentModelDiscoverer.RunsAgentCommand` now decides, and the gate consults it first:

| | gated | why |
|---|---|---|
| claude-code, muse | no | static catalog; Discover never spawns |
| codex | yes | catalog comes from the app-server, which starts the agent |
| kiro, cursor, devin, and the other command-backed adapters | yes | run their CLI by definition |
| config-derived (qwen, goose, cline, …) | no | read files only |

Config-derived catalogs are deliberately left ungated: under-reporting just preserves today's behavior, while over-reporting withholds a list that was never at risk.

I reviewed this implementation against the intended direction for standalone and imported sessions.

The recommended model is one session type with optional project ownership:

- If AO can verify that an imported Codex or Claude session belongs to a repository, attach it to the registered project and use the normal Git worktree flow.
- If the repository cannot be verified, no longer exists, or the user chooses standalone, create a projectless session with `project_id = NULL` and an AO-managed per-session directory.
- Store source identity separately, such as `provider` and `provider_session_id`, so imports can be deduplicated without overloading the AO session ID or display title.
- For readable standalone folders, use an immutable initial-title slug plus the stable AO session ID, for example `release-quality--standalone-41`. A title-only or `hi-2` scheme is unsafe because titles can repeat across providers and users can rename sessions.

The current PR has the right foundation: nullable project ownership, a plain-directory workspace adapter, projectless routes, restart preservation, and removal of the old global Scratch bootstrap. Reviewed on Linux x86_64 at PR head `b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2`, with Go 1.26.5 and installed CLI version 2.1.270. This is a static review of the diff plus targeted verification, not a repeat of the manual test matrix already posted above.
