Findings are ordered by confidence and impact. Each states what I verified rather than what I suspect.

---

### 1. The selected effort is dropped whenever the model is untouched or equals the project default

[`TaskComposer.tsx`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/frontend/src/renderer/components/TaskComposer.tsx#L339-L368) computes `requestedModel` as `undefined` unless `modelTouched` is set *and* the cleaned model or mode differs from the resolved project default. The submit payload then sends `effort: requestedModel ? effort : ""`.

Two common paths lose the selection:

1. The user never opens the model picker, accepts the default model, and picks an effort level. `modelTouched` stays `false`, so `requestedModel` is `undefined` and the effort is blanked.
2. The user changes the model, changes it back to the default, and picks an effort level. `cleanModel === defaultModelForSelectedAgent`, so `requestedModel` is again `undefined`.

The control stays interactive in both cases. It is disabled only on `isSubmitting || selectedAgent === ""`, and its option list is read from `model` rather than `requestedModel`, so the dropdown renders a populated list of levels that never reach the spawn. This is the same class of failure as the effort bug reported earlier in this thread, moved from the backend to the submit path.

Suggested fix: send `effort` whenever the level is non-empty and the currently displayed model advertises it, decoupled from whether `requestedModel` was set. Add a test that submits with an untouched default model and asserts the effort reaches `createTask`.

### 2. `Validate` collapses a rejected credential into `StateUnknown`

[`agentcreds.go`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/pkg/agentcreds/agentcreds.go#L226-L245) sets `StateUnknown` for every error returned by `requestFor`, with no `errors.Is` check.

That defeats an explicit intent stated one file over. [`vertex.go`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/pkg/agentcreds/vertex.go#L174-L180) wraps `ErrInvalidCredential` on a 400 or 401 from the service-account token exchange, under the comment "A rejected key exchange is a rejected credential, and it must surface as such rather than as an unknown transport failure." Because the wrap happens during request construction, `Validate` swallows it and reports unknown.

The consequence compounds: [`local.go`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/pkg/agentcreds/local.go#L62) guards its CLI retry with `!errors.Is(result.Err, ErrInvalidCredential)`, and that guard can never be false, so a Vertex key the exchange already rejected still pays a full CLI fallback attempt.

Suggested fix: in `Validate`, check `errors.Is(err, ErrInvalidCredential)` and set `StateInvalid` with the wrapped error before falling through to `StateUnknown`. A table test over `requestFor` error shapes would pin both arms.

### 3. `ao doctor` shares one 2s budget across the CLI subprocess and the provider round-trip

[`checkClaudeAuth`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/cli/doctor.go#L447-L492) derives a single `reqCtx` from [`probeTimeout = 2 * time.Second`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/cli/status.go#L17) and passes it to both `claude auth status` and `ValidateLocal`.

The validator's own client is built with [`DefaultTimeout = 3 * time.Second`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/pkg/agentcreds/agentcreds.go#L171-L173), documented as sized for measured round-trips of roughly 350ms. Under doctor it never gets that budget: the shared deadline is 2s total, already reduced by CLI startup and, with `AllowKeychain: true`, by a keychain subprocess. When it expires the result is `StateUnknown`, and doctor prints the WARN "claude reports credentials configured, but AO could not validate them" for a perfectly healthy credential. That inverts the purpose of the check.

Suggested fix: give the provider probe its own `context.WithTimeout(ctx, agentcreds.DefaultTimeout)` derived from the parent, so the subprocess and the round-trip do not compete for one budget.

### 4. Mobile was not taught the new `configured` auth state

The backend adds [`AgentAuthStatusConfigured`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/ports/agent.go#L35-L41), and the desktop schema and UI handle it in several places, including `CreateProjectAgentSheet.tsx` and `HarnessSettingsSection.tsx`. Mobile did not follow.

[`packages/mobile/lib/api.ts`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/packages/mobile/lib/api.ts#L464) still types `authStatus` as `"authorized" | "unauthorized" | "unknown"`, and [`agentPicker.ts`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/packages/mobile/lib/agentPicker.ts#L29-L37) falls through to `auth-unknown` for anything that is neither `authorized` nor `unauthorized`.

This matters because `configured` is the *expected* steady state here, not an edge case. The desktop test at `CreateProjectAgentSheet.test.tsx` records that a signed-in Claude Code "reports `configured`, never `authorized`". So a normally signed-in user now sees "Auth unknown" on mobile where they previously saw an authorized agent.

Suggested fix: add `"configured"` to the mobile union and treat it as authorized-enough for availability, matching the desktop `["authorized", "not_applicable", "configured"]` set.

### 5. Unused import fails `tsc --noEmit`

[`TaskComposer.test.tsx`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/frontend/src/renderer/components/TaskComposer.test.tsx#L91) imports `agentReadinessQueryKey as realAgentReadinessQueryKey`. It occurs exactly once in the file, the import itself. The line below hardcodes `["agent-readiness"]` as a duplicate.

`frontend/tsconfig.json` sets [`"noUnusedLocals": true`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/frontend/tsconfig.json#L18) and its `include` covers `src/**/*.tsx`, so `npm run typecheck` should report TS6133. Flagging as high confidence rather than confirmed: I could not execute `tsc` (no `node_modules` in this checkout), and an earlier comment in this thread reports typecheck passing at an older SHA, so this may be newly introduced.

Suggested fix: drop the import and use it in place of the hardcoded key, or remove it outright.

### 6. `acpAuthRejectionPhrases` includes the bare word `unauthorized`

[`acp/driver.go`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/adapters/chatdriver/acp/driver.go#L614-L636) documents the list as "deliberately narrow and phrase-based rather than keyword-based", specifically to avoid catching "a tool echoing an HTTP status from the user's own code". Twelve lines later the list contains `"unauthorized"`, which is exactly such a keyword.

The blast radius is wider than the message text alone: `acpErrorMentionsAuthRejection` also scans every string value in `RequestError.Data`. A turn that fails on a registry `unauthorized: authentication required`, or a GitHub 403 surfaced through a tool result, matches. Since this path calls `OnAuthRejected`, a false positive wipes the auth cache and shows the user a reauth banner for a session whose credential is fine.

Suggested fix: replace the bare keyword with the specific phrases that actually appear in provider rejections, and add a negative test using a tool-sourced 403 payload.

### 7. Chat-start preflight runs a subprocess and a network probe before the cache is consulted

[`AuthVerdict`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/adapters/agent/claudecode/auth.go#L64-L151) runs `claudeCLIAuthReport` (bounded at 3s) before `probeVerdict` reaches its cache lookup, then a provider probe bounded at another 3s. This is reached synchronously from the ACP driver's chat-start `Probe`, so a session start can absorb roughly six seconds in the worst case.

Two aggravating details: a `StateUnknown` result returns before `authCache().Put`, so an inconclusive probe is never cached and a flaky network re-pays the full cost on every session start. And `cache.go` states that "validation never runs on the render path: it runs asynchronously and writes here", which chat-start preflight does not honor.

I want to be explicit that the ordering is deliberate and documented: the CLI report supplies `apiProvider`, which decides whether a first-party probe is even the right thing to send, and the cache key is the credential fingerprint, which needs the resolved provider. So simply moving the cache lookup earlier is not free and would risk the exact provider misdirection the comment warns about. Raising it as a latency and caching concern rather than prescribing that fix.

Suggested direction: cache inconclusive verdicts under a short TTL so repeated failures are not re-paid, and consider warming the verdict off the session-start path entirely.

### 8. The Anthropic probe sends OAuth tokens with no beta or client headers

[`setAnthropicAuth`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/pkg/agentcreds/providers.go#L102-L120) sets only `anthropic-version` and `authorization: Bearer` for `KindOAuthToken`. Subscription logins reach this path: [`readKeychain`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/pkg/agentcreds/keychain.go#L47-L56) classifies a claude.ai credential as `KindOAuthToken`, and `kindForToken` routes any `sk-ant-oat*` value the same way.

If `/v1/models` declines an OAuth token that arrives without the Claude Code beta and client headers, the result is a *verified* `StateInvalid`, which becomes `AgentAuthStatusUnauthorized`, which [`authPreflightError`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/adapters/chatdriver/claudeacp/driver.go#L35-L50) turns into `ErrChatAuthRequired`, blocking session start outright. That is the lockout the preflight comment says is strictly worse than staying quiet.

Stated as a risk, not a defect: I could not exercise a real subscription token against the endpoint, and I want to correct something before it propagates. I initially believed a prior validator set these headers deliberately and that this PR dropped them. That is wrong. Grepping `anthropic-beta`, `oauth-2025-04-20`, and `claude-code-20250219` across the whole repository at this SHA and on `main` returns zero matches, so there is no prior behavior being regressed here.

Suggested fix: if the endpoint does require them, key the beta and client headers off `KindOAuthToken` and cover it with an integration test against a live credential, since a unit test with a stub server cannot catch this.

### 9. Minor: `ProviderModels` cannot see a provider configured through settings rather than env

[`ProviderModels`](https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/blob/b9e6427422de1d97d9225268a2cadabeabeccdc2/backend/internal/adapters/agent/claudecode/auth.go#L399-L405) passes an empty reported provider, so resolution falls back to the environment gate.

The code comments this and accepts it, and the reasoning holds: the gate either identifies a provider or declines, and declining yields an error that makes the caller fall back to the static catalog. The residual case is a machine configured for Bedrock or Vertex through `settings.json` that also carries a working first-party credential in the keychain. There the first-party probe succeeds and the picker offers first-party model identifiers for a runtime that wants provider-prefixed ones.

Narrow enough to be a follow-up rather than a change request. Noting it because it is adjacent to the model-identifier mismatch already reported in this thread.

## How the Activity section relates to the Kanban status

The **Kanban status** (`kanbanColumn` + `displayStatus`) always reflects the session's **current, single, latest** state — nothing more.

The **Activity section** in the Session Inspector is not a duplicate of that pill. It's a **running history log** of the session's journey through the board's columns (Building → Validating → Needs Review → Ready), built the same way the existing "workspace created / PR opened / PR merged" entries already work.

**Rule of thumb:**
- Granular, in-progress detail (e.g. "Fixing CI failures", "Reviewing") is shown **only for the column the session is in right now** — that's the only column whose status can still change.
- For every column the session has **already moved past**, the Activity log shows just the **one result** of that column (e.g. "Validated", "Approved") — not every intermediate back-and-forth (CI failing → fixing → passing) that happened while it was there.
- So as a session moves through the columns, its Activity history accumulates one result entry per completed column, plus a live, detailed entry for whichever column it's currently sitting in.

### Sample: session currently in Validating
```
● Fixing CI failures        just now   <- live detail, current column
  Opened PR #482            40m ago
  Workspace created         2h ago
```

### Sample: session currently in Needs Review
```
● Needs human review        just now   <- live detail, current column
  Validated                 55m ago    <- result of Validating
  Opened PR #482            2h ago
  Workspace created         3h ago
```

### Sample: session currently in Ready
```
● Mergeable                 just now   <- live detail, current column
  Reviewed: Approved        30m ago    <- result of Needs Review
  Validated                 1h ago     <- result of Validating
  Opened PR #482            3h ago
  Workspace created         4h ago
```

This keeps the Activity log readable — a clean trail of "what stage was this in, what came of it" — while the current column still carries the same fine-grained detail the Kanban card itself shows.

StopAll now closes every controller even if an earlier Close burns the shared shutdown context. Added a two-controller regression test (stuck + healthy).

**Relay review: migrations, telemetry, and one production blocker**

**Migrations:** none. `AppendTerminalOutputAt` reuses the existing `ao_terminal_output` schema, so no schema change and no collision with the in-flight `00037` migrations.

**Telemetry:** too loud on the hot path. Three INFO lines per output frame (`forwarded` / `delivered` / `mirrored`) plus one per input chunk, gated only by `logger != nil`. A streaming session writes thousands of frames, so this floods CloudWatch and adds work on the data path. Suggested:
- Move the three per-frame INFO lines to DEBUG, or sample them.
- Keep `terminal relay durable mirror failed` (Error).
- Keep `saturated_clients`, but as a counter, not a per-frame INFO line.

**Single-replica is a production blocker, not a testing one.** The live fan-out is in-process (`clients map[string]map[chan terminalRelayOutput]struct{}`, delivery tagged `mode=local_same_replica`). It only bridges a browser and its worker when both WS connections land on the same CP task. The PR is safe to run and test today, but only at `desired-count=1`, which is how staging is pinned for the relay test right now. At two or more replicas the ALB can split worker and browser across tasks, and the browser silently falls back to the durable Postgres mirror (correct, but poll latency, not the live path). So the blocker is scaling the CP past one task, not merging or testing.

**Mitigation (pick one):**
1. Cross-replica bus (preferred, no new infra). Add Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` on a per-terminal channel. Every frame is already written to the mirror table, so NOTIFY only has to wake the replica holding the browser to read frames after the last sequence. Reuses what is here and keeps the same-replica path as the fast path.
2. Replica affinity. Route a session's worker-WS and browser-WS to the same task via a layer that consistent-hashes on session or terminal id. ALB cookie stickiness alone does not solve this, since the worker and browser are separate clients and would not share a cookie.
3. Split the terminal data plane into its own service kept at count=1 (or sticky) while the API scales. Smallest change, least elegant.

**Test the mitigation before pushing it:**
1. Reproduce first. Scale staging CP to `desired-count=2`. Force worker and browser onto different tasks (temporary log of which task served each WS, or pin each connection). Confirm the split falls back to mirror latency.
2. Behind a flag (for example `AO_CLOUD_TERMINAL_RELAY_CROSS_REPLICA`), deploy the `LISTEN/NOTIFY` path to staging at count=2. Repeat the split. Assert live frames arrive with single-digit ms added latency, sequence stays gap-free, no dupes, ordering intact.
3. Load and failure test. Stream a heavy output burst across the split, watch DB CPU and NOTIFY volume. Kill the browser's task mid-stream, confirm reconnect resumes from the last sequence via the existing durable replay.
4. Only after that passes on staging at count=2, raise prod `desired-count` above 1.

Net: fine to keep deployed and merged behind its flag at count=1. Hold multi-replica until the cross-replica path lands and passes the test above.

The language icon uses `group-focus-within:opacity-0` (in `SessionFileTabs.tsx`), tied to the same `.group` wrapper the tab's activation button lives in (`TerminalTabFrame.tsx`). Clicking a tab leaves that button focused (normal browser behavior), and unlike `:hover`, `:focus-within` doesn't clear on its own so the icon stays hidden until focus moves to something else entirely.

The fix drops the focus-within trigger and keeps only the hover-based fade, which self-corrects when the pointer leaves. Also added a regression test that clicks the tab, confirms it retains focus, and asserts the icon is never tied to that sticky state.

@illegalcall, thank you for the detailed review. The comments were useful because they exposed places where the implementation had mixed together local account ownership, provider authentication, usage checks, and recovery.

We have now simplified the design and addressed the seven remaining threads in commit `f89e2be97`.

Here is the final model in simple terms.

### 1. The device credential decides which account is in use

The device-global Codex `auth.json` is the source of truth.

AO does not use a database pointer to decide which account is active. This is intentional. A database pointer can become stale when somebody logs in, logs out, or changes the Codex account outside AO.

Reconciliation now reads the local credential and matches it with an AO account. It does not contact Codex or the provider. A network failure, expired token, or provider outage cannot change which account is marked as in use.

If reconciliation has not verified the local credential yet, the UI shows no account as `In use`. It no longer preserves an old active badge while checking.

### 2. Switching is a local credential transaction

Account switching only works with local credential files.

Before changing the global credential, AO stores safe source and target checkpoints and creates a durable journal. It then atomically installs the selected credential and reads it back locally.

Recovery now classifies the device state as one of four clear results:

- the target credential is installed;
- the source credential is still installed;
- the credential is missing;
- another external credential is installed.

A temporary file or database read failure is not treated as a completed failure. AO keeps the journal, staging files, and Codex operation fence, then retries with capped backoff.

A confirmed target completes the switch. A confirmed source, missing credential, or external credential safely cancels the old switch and reconciles the actual device state. AO never overwrites an unrelated external login.

### 3. Startup recovery protects Codex without blocking the daemon

The Codex operation fence is now acquired before the first fallible journal read.

If the switch journal cannot be read, AO keeps that fence and retries after 1, 2, 4 seconds, up to a maximum delay of 30 seconds. New Codex launches and account mutations wait while the credential state is uncertain.

The rest of AO still starts and remains usable. Existing sessions, the UI, and unrelated agents are not stopped by a Codex recovery problem.

### 4. Delete is owned by the backend

The frontend now sends one DELETE request. It no longer decides whether it should call logout first.

The backend handles the complete workflow:

- an already signed-out account is deleted directly;
- an account that still has credentials is logged out through native Codex logout first;
- if logout fails, the credential and account descriptor are preserved;
- if logout succeeds but catalog deletion fails, the signed-out account remains available for a safe retry.

The explicit Logout button remains a separate user action.

### 5. Inactive logout does not depend on the global device account

A known inactive account is logged out through its own isolated AO Codex home. A temporary failure reading the device-global credential cannot block that operation.

AO reconciles first only when the selected account is the verified device owner, the last-known device owner, or ownership has never been determined safely. This prevents native logout from being sent to the wrong global account.

### 6. Re-login is protected against external account changes

AO now reconciles locally before opening every re-login terminal.

At that moment, it keeps the exact starting global credential and whether the selected account was active. These values stay only in memory and are never sent through the API or written to logs or SQLite.

When login finishes:

- the new credential must belong to the selected account;
- the global credential must still match the starting snapshot;
- an active account is updated through a compare-and-swap of both global and private credentials;
- an inactive account updates only its private credential.

If the global credential changes during login, AO preserves the pending credential and returns a retryable result. It does not overwrite either the external device credential or the previously saved account credential.

We intentionally did not restore the durable active-account pointer suggested in the older contract. The later product decision makes the device-global `auth.json` the only ownership proof, which avoids split-brain state after an external Codex login or logout.

### 7. Authentication and capacity are separate again

Capacity checking no longer refreshes OAuth credentials, retries a protected request, marks authentication as verified on success, or turns temporary capacity failures into authentication failures.

A successful capacity call updates capacity only. Network, timeout, and provider failures leave the existing authentication state unchanged.

There is one narrow exception required by the final product behavior: if a protected capacity endpoint definitively rejects the OAuth credential, capacity reports that typed evidence to the authentication owner. The authentication coordinator then marks the account as `Login expired`. This handles the real case where an account is logged out externally after the earlier authentication check but before the next usage check.

### 8. Session restart behavior remains outside this PR

This PR now covers only:

- adding and managing Codex accounts;
- local reconciliation;
- local credential switching.

It does not stop or restart existing Codex sessions. Session propagation or an idle-session restart policy can be added separately without coupling it to this credential transaction and recovery model.

We added focused regression coverage for backend-owned delete, inactive logout, re-login races, all switch settlement states, startup fencing, capacity and authentication separation, and the unverified active-row UI behavior.

Thanks again for pushing on these boundaries. The resulting implementation is smaller conceptually: local files decide account ownership, provider calls decide authentication and usage, and neither one is allowed to silently control the other.

Reproduced, and the cause is on the daemon side rather than in the app. Fix in #5445.

**What changed between 0.12.10 and 0.12.12.** #4727 moved new Linux sessions from tmux onto the native PTY host (macOS got the same host in #4473). That host answers every attach with a ring of the last 1000 output lines. A full-screen TUI prints its alternate-screen / mouse-tracking / bracketed-paste handshake once, at startup, so it is the first thing the ring forgets. A client that attaches after that renders the replay in its normal buffer with mouse reporting off, and its scrolling never reaches the program. tmux re-sends those modes on every attach, which is why 0.12.10 worked and why sessions created *before* the upgrade (they keep their tmux handle) still scroll.

**Reproduction** on macOS against a daemon built from `main`: Qwen Code 0.23.0 in a shell terminal, attaching over `/mux` the way the phone does.

| Attach | First frame |
|---|---|
| 2 s after launch | carries `?1049h ?1003h ?1006h ?2004h` |
| after ~220 keystrokes of repaints | exactly 1000 lines, no private-mode sequence at all |

Feeding those frames to headless xterm.js 5.5 (what the phone's WebView runs): the second one lands in the normal buffer with mouse tracking `none`, so `TerminalSessionScreen.tsx`'s gesture router pans local scrollback instead of sending wheel reports to Qwen. The desktop pane uses the same rule, so a relaunched desktop pane should be affected the same way (not exercised).

Qwen Code does draw on the alternate screen with SGR mouse tracking, so no screenshot needed. If a maintainer can move this to `comp/daemon`, that is where the fix lives.

### Security: GitHub PAT can be sent to arbitrary repository hosts

`probeRepositoryAccess` sets Basic auth with the saved GitHub PAT, but `validProjectInput` accepts any `https` URL. That means a repository URL such as `https://attacker.example/repo` receives `git:<PAT>` during validation and project creation.

Please restrict authenticated probes to approved GitHub hosts before attaching credentials (and ensure redirects cannot forward them), or validate access through GitHub’s API instead.

the main cause appears to be acp history replay backpressure during resume.

when ao resumes an opencode conversation, it calls acp `session/load`. opencode replays a large number of `session/update` notifications. ao currently normalizes each replay update synchronously on the sdk notification handler. the acp sdk has a bounded notification queue of 1024 items; for large replays, that queue fills, so the sdk closes the connection with `notification queue overflow`. ao then surfaces the follow-up generic error `peer disconnected before response`.

the fix is to keep replay notifications lightweight: buffer the raw `session/update` payloads while `session/load` is running, return quickly from the sdk callback, and normalize/process the buffered updates after `session/load` returns. replay capture should remain active until the buffer is fully drained and then switch to live updates atomically, so events are not lost or reordered. this is the approach proposed in pr #5372.

the failure is therefore in acp replay handling and backpressure, not the sidebar ui or sqlite data. the current main branch is still exposed while pr #5372 remains unmerged.

### 1. Security Fix: GitHub PAT SSRF Mitigation

* **Removed `git-receive-pack` probes:** The backend no longer sends the user's PAT to arbitrary user-provided hosts via Git Smart HTTP.
* **Strict host enforcement:** Implemented `parseGitHubRepo` to validate that repository URLs belong exactly to `github.com` or `www.github.com`.
* **GitHub API validation:** Reworked `probeRepositoryAccess` to query `https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}` directly. Credentials are now only sent to the official GitHub API.
* **Push permission checks:** The implementation correctly evaluates `permissions.push`, supporting both personal and Organization repositories.
* **Canonical clone URLs:** The backend constructs and persists a strict canonical clone URL (`https://github.com/owner/repo.git`) from API-validated components, preventing downstream injection through malformed or untrusted URLs.
* **Edge cases audited:** Verified concurrency safety through idempotency keys and ensured missing or revoked tokens return a `422` response, prompting the user to provide a valid token.

### 2. Frontend CI & Test Suite Resolution

* **Updated test mocks:** Updated `CreateProjectFlow.test.tsx` and `cloudMocks` to support the new `validateSavedRepositoryAccess` flow and the refactored UI states.
* **All onboarding tests passing:** All **45 onboarding tests** now pass successfully.
* **Error recovery mechanism:** Added an **"Update Token"** fallback button to the Cloud Credentials UI. If a saved token is revoked during the flow, the backend safely maps the `401` response to a `repository_unreachable` state, allowing users to provide a fresh token without getting permanently blocked.
* **i18n support:** Re-added missing translation keys and typecast test dictionaries to satisfy strict TypeScript type-checking jobs in CI.

**Review: onboarding + GitHub PAT**

Good news first: no secrets, no migrations, and no local-app regression. The PAT/probe flow is fully gated behind `cloudEnabled && offering === "cloud"` (`CreateProjectFlow.tsx:739,1146`), and the local create path is unchanged. Cloud module builds/vets/tests clean. Findings below are cloud-side.

**1. HIGH: `.git` canonicalization breaks the GitHub App checkout path.**
`createProject` now stores `https://github.com/owner/repo.git` (`resource_handlers.go:208`). Two App-checkout sites read the same `project.repository_url` and assume no `.git`:
- `githubapp/service.go:462` compares it to GitHub `HTMLURL` (no `.git`): `github.com/o/r.git` != `github.com/o/r` -> `ErrForbidden`.
- `githubapp/remote_broker.go:170` appends `.git` itself: `github.com/o/r.git.git` -> invalid grant.

Base branch stored the URL verbatim, so the contract was no-`.git`. Fix: canonicalize without the suffix (`https://github.com/owner/repo`). That satisfies both sites and still clones fine.

**2. HIGH: repo probe fails closed on a GitHub blip, with a misleading message.**
`probeRepositoryAccess` maps any non-200 to unreachable (`resource_handlers.go:738`), so a 429 (rate limit) or 5xx (outage) blocks project creation with "repository unreachable, may be private". The token-validate path already handles this correctly (`agent_credential_validator.go`: 429 -> valid, 5xx -> distinct 502). Mirror it: 401/404 -> token/private, 429/5xx -> transient retry.

**3. MED: create checks reachability, not push.** `reachable, _ := probeRepositoryAccess(...)` (`resource_handlers.go:202`) drops writeAccess, so a read-only token creates the project and the worker fails at push time later. That is the opaque failure this PR set out to prevent. Push is only a UI warning today.

**4. MED: dead code + contradictory intent.** `probeRepositoryReachable` (fail-open, docstring says fail-open is correct) is never called; the used function fails closed. Remove it or wire it.

**5. MED: test cleanup.** `resource_handlers_repository_probe_test.go:151-160` has left-in dev notes ("Wait... Oh, the original test was for..."), and `TestProbeRepositoryReachableFailsOpenOnConnectionError` actually tests `probeRepositoryAccess` and asserts fail-closed. Name says the opposite of the test.

**Low / defensive:**
- Non-github hosts now hard-rejected (GHE/GitLab). Fine if github.com-only is intended. Upside: token only ever reaches `api.github.com` (SSRF/exfil closed, covered by `TestCreateProjectRejectsNonGitHubURLs`).
- `owner`/`repo` not charset-validated (`..` segments reach the api path, normalized to a 404).
- `createProject` calls `secretCipher.Decrypt` without the nil guard the other two handlers have.
- 502 provider_unavailable in the UI looks identical to an invalid token (no retry affordance).
- PAT state uses 3 non-cross-invalidating query keys (`cloud-user-providers`, `cloud-user-provider-connections`, `cloud-provider-connections`), so a token saved in Settings shows stale in an open onboarding card.

## Follow-up: owner-character rules now match GitHub's documented semantics

The first revision accepted `_` in an owner segment. That was checked against GitHub's actual rule rather than assumed, and it was wrong.

Source — GitHub's [username considerations for external authentication](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/managing-iam/iam-configuration-reference/username-considerations-for-external-authentication):

> Usernames for user accounts on GitHub can only contain alphanumeric characters and dashes (`-`).
> GitHub will normalize any non-alphanumeric character in your account's username into a dash.
> Normalized usernames also can't start or end with a dash. They also can't contain two consecutive dashes.
> Usernames […] must not exceed 39 characters.

Since every non-alphanumeric character normalizes to a dash, **no real login contains an underscore** — accepting one was a deviation with nothing on the other side of it. `7949fb94b` removes it, with `owner-underscore`, `owner-dot`, and `owner-plus` rejection cases.

### The one remaining deviation, deliberate and tested

**Two consecutive dashes are tolerated** (`some--org` → `some--org`, pinned by `consecutive-dashes-tolerated`). GitHub states that constraint for names it normalizes at signup; whether it was applied retroactively to accounts predating it is not something this code can establish, and I could not confirm it either way — a `"--" in:login` search returns 0, but GitHub's search tokenizer almost certainly strips the dashes, so that is inconclusive, not evidence of absence.

The errors are not symmetric. Wrongly rejecting a real owner silently loses exactly the attribution this PR exists to recover; letting `a--b` through costs nothing, because by that point the host is already confirmed `github.com` and the first path segment is the owner by construction. The filter's job is rejecting path noise (`..`, `%2e%2e`, spaces, over-length), not re-implementing the signup form.

Rule-by-rule, the parser now is: alphanumeric and dashes only ✅ · no leading dash ✅ · no trailing dash ✅ · ≤39 characters ✅ · no consecutive dashes ⚠️ deliberately relaxed, documented in `isGitHubLogin` and tested.

The 39-character limit is the `github.com` one. GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency lowers it to 30, which does not apply here — enterprise hosts are out of scope and rejected outright.

I traced the current reviewer flow and confirmed the mismatch goes beyond the CLI definition.

`--reviewer` is configured as repeatable and validation accepts multiple values, but the actual review path consistently consumes only `Reviewers[0]` (including `ResolveReviewerHarness()` and the reviewer selection in `review.go`).

Before implementing a fix, I think we should clarify the intended semantics:

1. **Support multiple reviewers**  define whether they should run sequentially/concurrently and how their results are handled.
2. **Make `--reviewer` single-valued** reject multiple values at CLI validation time and align the config/help text accordingly.

I’d lean toward deciding this behavior first rather than simply replacing the `[0]` access with iteration, since that could introduce ambiguous review lifecycle/aggregation behavior.

Once the expected semantics are confirmed, the implementation and tests should be straightforward.

Thanks for tracing and confirming this.

My preference is option 1: support multiple reviewers. The cross-provider review case is the main reason I noticed the repeatable flag, and reducing it to a single value would remove that capability rather than merely correct the mismatch.

Suggested semantics:

- Every configured reviewer evaluates the same PR head independently.
- Execution may be sequential initially; concurrency can remain an implementation or scheduling choice and should not change the result.
- A new commit invalidates the aggregate result and requires each configured reviewer to evaluate the new head.
- Any `changes_requested` result keeps the review unresolved.
- The PR is considered fully reviewed only after every configured reviewer has completed successfully for that head.
- Reviewer failure or timeout is surfaced as incomplete/failed, never treated as approval.
- Individual verdicts remain attributed and visible rather than being collapsed into one anonymous result.

That would give the configuration meaningful, predictable behavior without requiring concurrent execution in the first implementation.

Reproduced and root-caused. The screenshot above is a second, distinct failure in the same switch flow (the DRAIN_DRAFT_PRESENT false positive from the original report is also fixed, same branch). Repro (deterministic): Create a fresh orchestrator session (Terminal mode). Switch to Chat — completes. Send nothing. Switch back to Terminal → NATIVE_SESSION_MISSING — "The agent has not exposed a native conversation that can resume in the other interface". Root cause (verified against the session's durable state): Entering Chat reserves a provider_conversation_id, but the durable conversation row is materialized only when the Chat controller starts — i.e. on the first turn. Until then the session has: a reserved id, NativeConversationExists() == false (Claude Code creates the transcript only once there is content), and no conversation row at all. The Chat → Terminal handoff runs the intentional-fresh-handoff proof (nativeConversationNotStarted). Its Chat branch demands a durable empty root conversation row; ConversationForSession errors on the missing row, the proof fails, and the switch is refused with ErrNativeConversationMissing. So a session that has never been messaged in Chat — the freshest possible state, nothing to resume and nothing to discard — can never reach Terminal. Fix: the Chat emptiness proof now accepts domain.ErrNoConversation (the Chat lifecycle never began), while generic history read failures and every other guard (prompts, checkpoint facts, transcript evidence, turns) stay fail-closed. Both fixes on the same branch: fix(session): stop provider chrome from failing interface switches as drafts — Claude Code 2.1.273 paints non-dim provider chrome into the region the drain parser reads as a draft (a bare Claude Code product label on the prompt row between the composer rules, and a multi-line statusline below the lower rule). The draft refusal now also requires repeated stable samples instead of aborting on a single capture. fix(session): allow a never-messaged Chat session to switch to Terminal — this fix. PR to follow.

#3707 added the TLS path for exactly this case — `tailscale serve` on the MagicDNS name, so the app never has to send cleartext to a 100.x address — and the desktop now enables it on its own when Connect Mobile is opened on a tailnet machine. But the endpoint list the phone races (the v2 code and `GET /api/v1/endpoints`) is built by `mobilebridge.Endpoints`, which only knows LAN addresses, the plaintext Tailscale address and the Cloudflare tunnel. The proxy is never in it. So on iOS the tailnet entry is the one ATS rejects, and the phone only reaches the Mac through the tunnel, if cloudflared is installed.

The workaround in the report also undoes itself: the hand-typed `<magicdns>:443` entry is stored under the `tailscale` kind, and the daemon's list replaces that kind with the plaintext address on the first successful connect.

Fix in #5485: advertise the proxy as the tailnet endpoint whenever it is actually serving, in both the code and the refresh. Daemon-only, no ATS exception — the same direction #3707 took over `NSExceptionDomains`. Already-paired phones pick it up on their next connect.

**1. Foreign `.ShipIt` selection.** Confirmed. `macShipItDir()` now builds the exact path from the bundle id (`${AO_BUNDLE_ID}.ShipIt`, imported from `stale-app-copies.ts`) and returns it only if it exists, so a stalled AO stage falls through to the no-signal cap instead of reading another Squirrel app's growing cache. The real folder name `dev.agent-orchestrator.desktop.ShipIt` is confirmed against the repair-installer test fixtures.

**2. Verification plateau tripping the inactivity timeout.** Also real. Once `ditto` finishes, the staging bytes plateau while Squirrel runs its read-only signature check, and a plateau past 90s would have been called a stall the old three-minute cap tolerated. The inactivity trip is now gated behind a verification grace (`STAGE_VERIFY_GRACE_MS`, 3 min): a plateau is only a stall after both 90s without growth and 3 minutes total elapsed. A genuinely wedged stage still trips on the no-signal cap (6 min) and the absolute cap (15 min).

**3. Hardcoded 2 GiB floor.** No measurement was behind it. The requirement is now derived from the archive size electron-updater reports in the manifest (`info.files[].size`): roughly 3x the archive, with a 512 MiB floor for margin and 2 GiB kept only as a cap. When the manifest carries no size, it falls back to that 2 GiB cap.

One related fix while I was in here: the watchdog captured the staging directory once, at the start of `beginNativePreparation`. Since electron-updater emits `update-downloaded` before the `checkForUpdates()` call that makes Squirrel create the `.ShipIt` directory, that directory did not exist yet at capture time, so the growth signal never engaged and every stage fell back to the flat no-signal cap. The directory is now re-resolved each poll until it appears, so real progress on a slow disk keeps the stage alive through the full window. Covered by a new test.

Independent reproduction of the same root cause from a downstream fork, plus three gaps this shape still leaves. All measured today against the packaged `claude-agent-acp` 0.70.0 and `upstream/main` @ 28c68a08a.

### Where it comes from

`buildAvailableModes` gates `auto` on `modelInfo.supportsAutoMode`, and `set_config_option model=...` recomputes `availableModes` and clamps the session's current mode when the new model invalidates it (its own comment says "today: auto on Haiku").

Per-model, zero-token `session/new` + `session/set_mode auto`:

| model | `set_mode "auto"` | `effort` option |
|---|---|---|
| `default`, `opus[1m]`, `sonnet`, `claude-fable-5-1[1m]` | `{}` | 6 values |
| `haiku` | `Mode auto is not available in this session` | empty |

Because `applyTurnSettings` runs `set_mode` **before** the model config option, session creation succeeds and the **first turn** is what dies — which is why it surfaces as `deliver prompt: send turn` / `SPAWN_DELIVER_PROMPT_FAILED`, not as a session/new failure. Every failed conversation in our chat table was `claude-code/haiku`.

### Gaps in this patch

Ported the diff verbatim onto our tree and drove it through the existing `fakeAgent`:

**1. Raising the approval mode still fails the turn.** `ErrACPSetterUnsupported` is tolerated at `driver.go:253` (`Start`) and `:395` (`Resume`) only — `conversation.go:383` (`SendTurn`) returns it to the caller. With a session that never offered `auto` (haiku from the start) and approval going `default` → `auto`, the `!= currentPermission` short-circuit doesn't fire and the turn fails with:

```
ACP agent does not support runtime session configuration:
session/set_mode "auto" not offered by this session
```

**2. `!= currentPermission` skips the session's *first* `set_mode`.** `conv.start` sets `c.permissionMode = initialPermission = cfg.Permissions`, and `Start` then calls `applyTurnSettings` with that same `Approval` — so the whole mode block is skipped at session start. Measured: **0** `session/set_mode` calls at `Start` where `main` makes 1. For a provider whose mode only reaches the agent through the setter (`claudeacp` — `claudeSessionMode` has no launch-flag equivalent, unlike kimchi's `--auto`/`--yolo`), AO's permission mode silently stops reaching the agent and the session runs the agent's own default.

**3. Skipping the call leaves AO's bookkeeping saying something the session isn't doing.** `RequestPermission` (`client.go:61`) hands `c.permissionMode` to the provider's `PermissionPolicy`. If it still reads `bypassPermissions` while an agent built without `ALLOW_BYPASS` runs `default`, the policy approves every prompt the agent raises — the exact behavior the agent refused. Inverting `modeFor` against the session's current mode id, and falling back to the strictest mode when nothing maps, keeps the two in step.

### Note on the `legacyMode &&` gate

It holds for Claude Code today only because `session/new` returns **both** a legacy `modes` state and a `mode` config option, so `legacyMode` is true. An agent that publishes `mode` only as a config option would be unguarded. Treating an absent `mode` option (rather than absent legacy modes) as "ask exactly as before" covers both.

## Review: Manual PR Review Sessions

The overall structure looks good, especially the separation of review state handling, durable cancellation before terminal teardown, and reuse of the existing review presentation for cloud sessions.

I found a few correctness and authorization issues that should be addressed before merge, along with some test coverage gaps worth closing.

### 1. HIGH: Cancelled reviews permanently block re-triggering on the same commit

**Files:** `review_run_store.go`, `00016_pull_requests_and_review_runs.sql`

The unique constraint on `(pull_request_id, target_sha)` remains active for terminal states, while `CreateReviewRun` uses:

```sql
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (pull_request_id, target_sha) DO NOTHING
```

This creates the following failure path:

1. A review is started for a commit.
2. The review is cancelled.
3. The user attempts to run the review again on the same commit.
4. The existing `cancelled` row conflicts with the unique constraint.
5. `CreateReviewRun` returns `created = false`.
6. The handler returns successfully, but no new review is started.

As a result, the commit cannot be reviewed again unless a new commit is pushed.

Please update the idempotency/uniqueness logic so that cancelled and failed runs can be retriggered. A partial unique index limited to active runs, or an explicit transition/reuse of terminal rows within a transaction, would address this.

Please also add a store-level test covering:

* Create a review run.
* Mark it as `cancelled`.
* Create another run for the same PR and target SHA.
* Verify that a new active run can be created.

### 2. HIGH: Cancelling reviews does not enforce session-level ownership

**Files:** `pull_request_handlers.go`, `review_run_store.go`

`cancelSessionReviews` invokes `CancelRunningReviewRunsBySession` through `withOrg`, which provides the organization context but does not carry out a principal/session-level access check.

Although the subsequent payload read uses `withSessionAccess`, that check happens after the cancellation write and therefore does not protect the mutation itself.

This means an organization member who knows another session’s ID may be able to cancel its running reviews even without write access to that session.

Please enforce session ownership/write access before calling the cancellation operation, using the existing `withSessionAccess` pattern or a dedicated `requireSessionWrite` helper.

Please add handler-level authorization tests covering at least:

* A session owner/member can cancel its running reviews.
* A read-only project member cannot cancel reviews.
* A member without access to the session cannot cancel reviews.
* A user from another organization cannot cancel the session.

### 3. HIGH: Partial failure can leave previously started reviews orphaned

**File:** `pull_request_handlers.go`

When a session contains multiple eligible PRs, the handler starts reviews sequentially. If an earlier PR has already created a running review and opened a terminal, but a later PR fails during `OpenReviewTerminal`, the handler returns `502 REVIEW_FAILED`.

This leaves the earlier review running even though the overall request is reported as failed. The frontend only receives the error and may not have enough information to reconstruct or manage the already-started review.

Please choose and document an explicit behavior for multi-PR failures. Given the current single-button UI flow, rolling back reviews started during the current request before returning the error seems the safest option. Alternatively, return a structured partial-success response so the client can represent the successfully started reviews.

Please add a handler-level test for:

* Multiple PRs where the first review starts successfully.
* A later PR fails to open its review terminal.
* Verify that the response and persisted review/terminal state match the chosen partial-failure behavior.

### 4. MEDIUM: Avoid deriving `reviewerHandleId` from an immediate follow-up database read

**Files:** `review_run_store.go`, `pull_request_handlers.go`, `SessionInspector.tsx`

`OpenReviewTerminal` performs related updates across separate transactions. `triggerSessionReviews` then immediately calls `sessionReviewPayload` to reconstruct the response.

This introduces a window where the review may have started, but the subsequent read can still return an empty `reviewerHandleId`. The frontend then falls into the `"already ran for commit"` branch and does not open the reviewer terminal, even though the review is actually being launched.

Please return the reviewer terminal ID directly from the result already produced by `TriggerReview`/`OpenReviewTerminal`, or construct the response from the returned run values instead of relying on an immediate re-read.

Please add a frontend test covering a successful trigger response with a reviewer handle and verify that the reviewer terminal is opened. Also cover the case where the review is running but the handle is temporarily unavailable, so the UI does not incorrectly display the “already ran” message.

### Additional test coverage requested

These are not necessarily blocking individually, but the new handler paths should have coverage before merging:

* `triggerSessionReviews` handler success and error paths.
* `cancelSessionReviews` handler success and error paths.
* Trigger authorization and session ownership.
* Cancel behavior when no running reviews exist.
* Frontend cancel flow and cancellation errors.
* Frontend “already ran” state.
* Polling activation while a review is running.
* Local terminal behavior to ensure the cloud-specific terminal changes do not regress local sessions.
* Multi-review sessions, including how multiple reviewer handles are represented.

The overall approach is sound, but the cancellation/idempotency interaction and mutation authorization need to be fixed before this is ready to merge.

Collected read-only on 2026-09-16/17 PDT from the affected packaged installation (`0.13.1-nightly.202609161752`, packaged commit `bd388d6a42c`) and its loopback daemon.

- `GET /api/v1/sessions/agent-orchestrator-341/conversation` reported controller `ready`, while durable turn `020341ea-ec17-4f42-b046-db173abb54a8` remained `running` from `2026-09-16T01:43:56Z`.
- The turn emitted its last assistant text and usage events at approximately `2026-09-16T02:07:46Z`; the native Claude transcript then recorded a successful `stop_hook_summary`. No subsequent `message.completed` or `turn.completed` event exists.
- The turn had started a Monitor task. Its final cycle was triggered by a `<task-notification>` reporting that the monitored CI job passed. Five later AO messages remain queued behind the unresolved turn.
- The persistent ACP host and Claude adapter processes remain alive but sleeping at approximately 0% CPU. Its prompt journal has not changed since `02:07:46Z`.
- A read-only SQLite query found no other visible `running` conversation turns in this installation.

The pinned packaged dependency is `@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp@0.70.0`. In its long-lived consumer, results with origin `task-notification` take the `isAutonomousResult` early-return path. That path calls only `settleDeferredIfDrained()`, which is a no-op unless the active turn already has `deferredSettle`. In this incident the task-notification follow-up was the terminal cycle for the still-outstanding user prompt, so the active prompt was never resolved and AO never received `turn.completed`.

There is a secondary reconnect inconsistency: `Controller.restoreLiveTurnOwnership()` restores `busy`, but the ACP adapter's queued initialization `controller.state=ready` is later applied unconditionally by `Controller.afterProject()`. This explains `controller=ready` alongside the durable running turn, but the UI timer itself correctly derives from the durable `running` row.

Related issue #3749 has the same visible symptom but a different already-fixed projection/interrupt desynchronization mechanism.

Evidence limitation: the ACP SDK result object itself is not persisted in the Claude transcript. The `task-notification` origin is supported by the recorded notification-triggered cycle and by the exact adapter branch that can leave the prompt unresolved; a focused adapter regression test should confirm the sequence deterministically.

## RCA (agent-collected, 2026-09-17)

**Causal chain, link by link:**

1. **Foreign skills enter via the shared user tier.** Superset distributes its agent skills by installing `superset-*` into `~/.agents/skills/` — the cross-tool shared tier. Wmux uses the parallel MCP channel (auto-registration into the user's agent MCP config). AO never writes to either (its only user-global write is the additive per-workspace trust key in `~/.claude.json`).
2. **AO sessions spawn harnesses with no capability masking.** Chat launches return nil env overrides (`chatdriver/kimiacp/driver.go:33-41`); session env only *adds* AO vars (`session_manager/manager.go:4407`). Grep confirms zero use of `--strict-mcp-config`, `--bare`, `safe-mode`, `--skills-dir`, or any skill/MCP disable anywhere in harness launch paths.
3. **The one isolation AO has doesn't cover the shared tier.** `KIMI_CODE_HOME=<dataDir>/kimi` (`kimi/kimi.go:60-65`) relocates kimi's own state, but per the official docs `~/.agents/skills/` "stays under the real OS home so it can be shared across tools" and is always scanned. (Kimi MCP *is* isolated this way — `mcp.json` follows `KIMI_CODE_HOME`.)
4. **The model picks the registered skill over AO's prose.** All skills' `name`/`description`/`whenToUse` are visible to the model; auto-invocation fires on trigger match. `superset-browser`'s trigger ≈ "open a URL / preview a web app" — an exact match for "open x.com". AO's `using-ao` reaches the model only as a prose pointer appended to the system prompt (`manager.go:4230`), a pointer that has to compete with a first-class registered skill.
5. **For claude sessions the MCP channel is wide open by design.** The claude ACP driver documents its intent: "login, subscription, settings, MCP configuration, hooks … remain the user's own" (`chatdriver/claudeacp/driver.go:3-6`) — so auto-registered foreign MCP servers (Wmux) are live tools in AO claude chats.

**Root cause:** AO's "never touch user config" hygiene is only half a defense. It makes AO a good citizen of the shared user tier, but nothing shields AO sessions from what *other* products write there — and AO's only in-session countermeasures (the `using-ao` pointer, the "do not use a browser MCP" sentence at `manager.go:4241`) are prose, not enforcement. The shared `~/.agents/skills/` convention is simultaneously every product's distribution channel and every product's attack surface.

**Per-harness isolation levers verified against official docs (2026-09-17):**

| Harness | Foreign skills | Foreign MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Kimi | `--skills-dir <dir>` replaces all auto-discovered skill dirs for the session (verified: overrides doc). `~/.agents/skills` cannot be excluded individually. | Already isolated via `KIMI_CODE_HOME` (mcp.json follows it). |
| Claude Code | No per-session disable of `~/.claude/skills` (`--bare`/`--safe-mode` kill AO's hooks too). | `--strict-mcp-config` (with no `--mcp-config` ⇒ zero MCP) — unused by AO; passing it through the ACP adapter layer is unverified. |
| Codex | No documented per-session skill disable. | No strict flag; `CODEX_HOME` relocation is the only full isolation (AO already manages codex auth in data-dir slots, so seeding a managed home is feasible). |
| Gemini | `~/.agents/skills` alias tier, no documented disable. | `mcp.allowed` server-name allowlist in settings. |

## Proposed solution (layered)

**Layer 1 — close the kimi hole + parity for `using-ao` (small, surgical):**
- Pass `kimi --skills-dir <AO-managed dir>` on chat and TUI launches; the managed dir contains only AO's `using-ao` (plus optional user-allowed entries). This removes the `~/.agents/skills` tier from kimi sessions entirely. Flag position on the `acp` argv needs one verification pass.
- Register `using-ao` as a *real* skill for kimi (`$KIMI_CODE_HOME/skills/using-ao/`), claude (worktree `.claude/skills/using-ao/`, reusing the proven opencode sentinel+gitignore pattern from `opencode/hooks.go:188`), and codex (repo-scope skill, location to verify). opencode already gets this treatment — the other three never did (`skillassets` installs to `~/.ao/skills`, which no harness scans).
- Strengthen the system-prompt rule from "do not use a browser MCP" to an explicit priority rule: AO-owned surfaces (browser panel, preview, spawn) are handled only via `ao` commands; foreign orchestrator skills/MCP (Superset, Wmux, cmux-style) must not be used inside AO sessions even when installed.

**Layer 2 — per-project session capability policy (the real fix, ties into #2195/#2844):**
- Add a project/user setting `sessionCapabilities: inherit | isolated`.
- `isolated` applies, per harness: kimi `--skills-dir`; claude `--strict-mcp-config` (plus AO's own `--mcp-config` for AO-managed chat MCP — the plumbing exists at `ports/chat.go:337`); codex seeded `CODEX_HOME` (mirroring the kimi managed-home pattern, credentials from AO's existing codex account slots); gemini `mcp.allowed` allowlist.
- Precedent already exists in-tree: the reviewer gateway overrides HOME/XDG (`reviewgateway/gateway.go:65-71`) and reviewer adapters use `--allowedTools` allowlists — the mechanism philosophy just hasn't been applied to normal sessions.
- Default is a product call (cf. the naked-by-default debate in #2844); shipping as opt-in first avoids silently breaking users who legitimately want their MCP in AO chats.

**Layer 3 — detect and warn:**
- Extend the system check to scan `~/.agents/skills/` and user MCP config for known foreign orchestrator integrations (`superset-*`, `wmux`, cmux/multica-style entries) and surface a settings warning with a one-click "exclude from AO sessions" that flips the Layer-2 policy.

**Layer 4 — convention-level (upstream):**
- Propose skill-frontmatter metadata for the `.agents/skills` convention (e.g. an `origin`/`orchestrator` field and an opt-out marker) so orchestrators can filter foreign skills without excluding the whole tier. Until that lands, Layers 1–2 are the only reliable defense.

**Caveats:** claude skills have no documented per-session disable short of `--bare`/`--safe-mode` (which break AO's hooks), so claude's foreign-`~/.claude/skills` exposure needs either managed-settings (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` with credential seeding) or the Layer-4 convention; kimi's config seeding (`kimi/hooks.go:194`) may copy a user's `extra_skill_dirs` into the managed home and should be filtered when `isolated`.

**Another reproduction on packaged Windows desktop v0.13.0 (stable), Claude Code orchestrator session — with a verified trigger and the one-field DB fix**

Environment: Windows 10, agent-orchestrator v0.13.0 (stable channel), harness `claude-code`, session kind `orchestrator`, `session_mode = tui`, `session_permissions = auto`.

Symptom: identical to the report above. Seven consecutive `tui -> chat` transitions failed with `TARGET_HISTORY_UNSETTLED` after ~46s each (`session_interface_transitions`), both `drain` and `interrupt` policies:

```
switch interface bsms-1: resume chat: wait for settled native conversation history: chat conversation history is not settled: refresh ACP session history: context deadline exceeded: {"code":-32603,"message":"Internal error","data":{"error":"context deadline exceeded"}}
```

**Trigger (verified against the DB and the native transcript):**

- `sessions.latest_user_prompt` = the last `[from <worker>]` message injected by `ao send`; it *is* present in the transcript `.jsonl` as a completed user message at the same timestamp (`latest_user_prompt_at`).
- `sessions.latest_assistant_update` = a short French sentence that appears **nowhere** in any transcript on the machine (grep over all `~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl` and every file under `~/.ao/data`). It is the *human's* Terminal reply to the assistant's last question, typed right before a switch attempt; the prompt never reached Claude (no `user` entry, no `UserPromptSubmit` effect on `latest_user_prompt`), yet it was persisted as the *assistant* checkpoint.
- The session has **0** rows in `conversation_turns` / `conversation_messages` (never been in Chat), so `dropUnsettledHookFacts` has no evidence to retire the fact.
- With that field non-empty, `nativeHistoryCheckpoint.reached()` (v0.13.0 `backend/internal/service/chat/controller.go:533`) can never match the latest replayed assistant message, so the loop burns the full 45s `nativeHistorySettleLimit`.

Note that v0.13.0's `hookConversationFacts` (`backend/internal/cli/hooks.go:260`) accepts `last_assistant_message` / `assistant_message` aliases from any hook event, whereas current `main` gates them to `stop` only — so this trigger may already be closed on `main`, but v0.13.0 stable users still hit it and have no recovery path in the UI (PR #4466 is not in v0.13.0).

Thanks for both catches. Addressed in 4081a3c09 (https://github.com/Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator/pull/5480/commits/4081a3c09).

**P1 (surface racing completion).** The surface and settle paths are now serialized by a dedicated `idleMu`, and each one re-checks turn state under `c.mu` before acting. `surfaceIdleStall` only emits the started event when the stall isn't already open and the turn is still the active, non-settling turn; `settleIdleStallIfOpen` only emits the completed event when a stall is actually open. **Deterministic repro + fingerprint for the dominant 503 class**

I can reproduce the 503 pattern from this issue's telemetry deterministically: it is a wedged desktop (Electron) main process with the runtime socket still attached.

**Repro** (isolated dev instance, desktop+daemon built from main as of 2026-09-19, macOS):

1. Launch the desktop app, spawn a session, confirm `GET /api/v1/browser/status` → `connected: true`.
2. `kill -STOP <electron-main-pid>` — a deterministic stand-in for a busy event loop, wedged network stack, or mid-navigation system sleep.
3. From the session, `POST /api/v1/browser/commands` with `{"action":"open","args":{"url":"https://example.com/"}}`.
4. The request hangs for **60.00 s** and returns `503` `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` ("The service is momentarily unavailable, please retry."). Daemon log: `status=503 duration=1m0.001s error="context deadline exceeded"`.
5. During the whole window `GET /api/v1/browser/status` keeps returning `connected: true`.
6. `kill -CONT <pid>` → the next command succeeds in ~2 ms. No restart, no reconnect — the runtime "recovers on its own".

**Why (code paths as of main):**

- The 60 s / 503 is the REST request timeout (`DefaultRequestTimeout = 60s`) expiring in `Broker.Execute` (`ctx.Err()` → `context.DeadlineExceeded`) and mapped by the envelope as transient. In telemetry these land as `ao.http.5xx` on `/api/v1/browser/commands` with `duration ≈ 60000 ms`.
- `Broker.Status()` is literally `conn != nil` — a frozen-but-attached runtime stays "connected". There is no liveness probe, so neither agents nor the desktop UI get any degraded signal while every command is burning 60 s.
- Commands are serialized per session in the Electron link (each request chained onto the previous one). The daemon's cancel frame fired at the 60 s timeout aborts the `AbortController`, but the queued chain keeps waiting on the underlying operation — so one wedged execute (e.g. `entry.ready = loadURL(...)` never settling, or a CDP call with no deadline) blocks every subsequent command of that session, producing bursts of back-to-back 60000 ms 503s like the ones in the PostHog data here.

**Fingerprint proposal** (for the diagnostic-gap section): distinguish two 503 families on this route:

- `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` with `duration ≈ 60000` — request timeout over a connected-but-unresponsive runtime (this repro);
- `BROWSER_RUNTIME_UNAVAILABLE` et al. — fast failures when the runtime is genuinely not attached.

On one local installation the first family alone produced ~100 events over Aug 26 – Sep 16, always `duration = 60000±2 ms`, matching the "503s dominate and come in bursts" pattern above.

Possibly related: #5437.

Pushed 75402bdbc, which answers the `external_directory` / `doom_loop` question by removing the premise behind it.

The tiers were AO's invention. They are now what OpenCode itself does, so a mode leaves a session behaving the way the same session behaves outside AO:

| Mode | What it is |
|---|---|
| Default approvals | no rules; your configuration decides |
| Accept edits | `edit: allow` — the one grant OpenCode has no mode for |
| Auto-approve | OpenCode's `--auto`: everything not explicitly denied |
| Bypass permissions | `permission: "allow"`, its own full-access setting |

**Auto.** The Terminal UI now passes `--auto` and lets the provider decide what "not explicitly denied" means, instead of AO enumerating tools. Chat has no flags, so it assembles the same policy: allow everything, then restore every explicit deny AO can see — global config, repository, `.opencode`. That settles the guards: `--auto` approves permissions that merely *ask*, so `external_directory` and `doom_loop` are approved natively, and allowing them was right.

One divergence I had to close explicitly: a blanket allow on the agent would outrank OpenCode's built-in deny on reading `.env` files, which `--auto` keeps. The auto tier repeats that default, so secrets stay unreadable.

**Accept edits** drops the invented `ask` rules for shell, network and subagents. Those made the mode stricter than OpenCode would be, which is not what the name promises.

What AO now writes, in a workspace whose repository denies `rm *`:

```
ao-default       null
ao-accept-edits  {"bash": {"rm *": "deny"}, "edit": "allow"}
ao-auto          {"*": "allow", "bash": {"rm *": "deny"},
                  "read": {"*": "allow", "*.env": "deny", "*.env.*": "deny", "*.env.example": "allow"}}
```

Measured against #5632's run, the only change being the package order:

| | sqlite listed 161st | sqlite listed first |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Test step | 785s | 746s |
| `internal/storage/sqlite` | 556.4s | 686.4s |

39 seconds, and the package itself got 130s slower. The premise was wrong: its 556s was not a fixed cost that merely started late, it was 556s *because* it ran in the tail with three cores idle. Starting it at t=0 makes it compete with three other packages for cores and memory bandwidth, and it stretches to 686s. The ordering relocated the idle time rather than removing it.

It also costs all log streaming. `go test` emits in list order, so with the longest package first and finishing last, every other package's output buffers behind it — all 169 results printed at a single timestamp, leaving the step silent for 12m26s.

The useful result is the contention measurement, which strengthens the case for the separate job that this PR was trying to avoid: 556s uncontended versus 686s contended means a dedicated runner is the only way to give the package headroom, for roughly `max(556s + setup, 1574/4 + setup)` ≈ 10m30s against 13m26s today. That remains open under #5116, priced at a branch-protection change for the renamed required check plus a second runner.

## Proposed fix plan

**Root cause:** `ao send --steer` can only deliver into a "chat conversation"; the orchestrator session was created in Terminal UI where no conversation object exists → `SESSION_MODE_MISMATCH`. Meanwhile ao already has a mechanism for injecting a message into a live claude-code session: workers correctly receive incoming `[from <session>]` turns on the orchestrator→worker path. The fix is in the delivery transport, not in demanding a chat.

1. **Minimal bug fix:** in the `ao send` handler, when the target session is in Terminal UI, do not fail with `SESSION_MODE_MISMATCH`; deliver via the existing incoming-turn mechanism (pty console injection while the REPL is live) or a queued prompt picked up on the next idle. "No chat conversation" is a reason to pick a different transport, not to refuse delivery.
2. **Discoverable orchestrator address:** `ao session orchestrator --project <id>` (or a field in `ao session ls`) so workers stop guessing addresses (observed guesses: `hhru-80`, `hhru-580-10`).
3. **Sub-session address hygiene:** reviewer sub-sessions (`<worker>-10`, uds `/tmp/cc-socks/<pid>.sock`) should not resolve for foreign `SendMessage` calls without an explicit reference — otherwise the "reviewer sub-session replied as the orchestrator" collision will recur (observed: `hhru-580-10` answered worker `hhru-580`'s report in an orchestrator tone, and the worker accepted it as owner confirmation).

The minimal change that removes the pain is №1.

I found one concurrency edge in the attach path that seems worth addressing before merge.

`handleConn` takes the ring snapshot under `h.mu`, but `pumpPTY` updates the ring and `modes` before acquiring `h.mu` for `broadcast`. This permits the following ordering:

1. `handleConn` reads the old replay.
2. `pumpPTY` appends a new `?1049h` chunk and advances `modes`, then blocks in `broadcast` on `h.mu`.
3. `Restore(oldReplay)` observes the newer alternate-screen state and prefixes `?1049h`.
4. The client receives `?1049h + oldReplay`, followed by the real `?1049h` chunk after registration.

That paints pre-TUI shell output into the alternate buffer, contrary to the early-attach/no-prefix invariant described here. I was able to force this interleaving deterministically in a package-level diagnostic test.

Could the ring append, mode update, and client broadcast/registration be serialized through one output-ordering boundary (for example, `h.mu` plus a `broadcastLocked` helper), and covered with a test where output advances during attachment? The underlying mode-tracking approach otherwise looks solid and matches xterm.js 5.5 well.

## macOS manual testing report (2026-09-21)

Tested the real Electron app on macOS against exact PR head `a54c18b1fa34afb8c182f4e044e6e801f0c564c8`, using isolated data under `~/.ao/dev/pr-5604/data` and the dev daemon on `127.0.0.1:3002`.

### Result

The new standalone Chat flow is not passing reliably on this machine. When Chat creation fails, the dialog offers **Create as Terminal UI**; accepting that action intentionally creates a TUI session and should not be interpreted as Chat succeeding.

- **Prime Agent 0.9.1 — reproducible code-path failure.** The daemon reports: `default Chat unavailable; falling back to TUI`, because `prime-agent` lacks `[approvals resume]`. Prime is documented by this PR as bypass-only, but `createStandaloneTask` in `frontend/src/renderer/components/TaskComposer.tsx` does not include `approvalMode` in `POST /api/v1/sessions`. Therefore the standalone UI cannot communicate the explicit bypass needed for Prime Chat, and the backend falls back to TUI.
- **Kilo Code 7.4.17 — failed.** A fresh Chat launch failed because `~/.ao/dev/pr-5604/data/chat-hosts/standalone-5/host.json` was never created. An earlier Chat-mode session started, but turns completed without assistant output. The PR verification used Kilo 7.7.5, so the installed version is older than the verified version.
- **Cline 3.0.61 — failed.** A fresh Chat launch timed out during ACP initialization. An earlier Chat-mode session started but reported that Cline requires re-authentication. The PR verification used Cline 3.0.62.
- **Vibe 2.24.0 — mixed/flaky.** One Chat session worked end-to-end before restart; a later fresh launch timed out during ACP initialization. The PR verification used Vibe 2.25.5.

## How weekly changelog publishing will work

The process is intentionally semi-automated: automation prepares a complete draft, and a human editor decides what is ready to publish.

1. Every Sunday at 16:00 UTC, the workflow reads every merged PR since the previous published boundary. It follows GitHub pagination, removes PRs already referenced by older entries, and collects titles, descriptions, labels, authors, changed-file counts, and attached media.
2. The generator excludes internal-only work and classifies the remaining PRs into major features, smaller improvements, and bug fixes. It proposes up to four highlights and groups the other items by product area.
3. It creates or updates `changelog/YYYY-MM-DD`, writes `content/changelog/YYYY-MM-DD-weekly-update.mdx`, runs changelog tests, validates the content, and runs the production build.
4. It opens or updates a pull request. It never merges or publishes by itself.
5. A human reads every collected PR, removes unavailable, duplicated, reverted, superseded, or feature-flagged work, combines related PRs, rewrites the headline and explanations in customer language, verifies every link, and previews desktop and mobile layouts.
6. After CI passes, merging the PR publishes the weekly entry, its permanent detail page, and the RSS update through the existing website deployment.

Useful labels:

- `changelog:skip` — exclude a PR.
- `changelog:include` — include something the default filter would skip.
- `changelog:highlight` — prioritize a major feature.
- `changelog:credit` — explicitly allow rare contributor credit.

If a week contains no customer-facing PR after filtering, the current workflow opens no draft. If we want exactly one article every calendar week, including quiet weeks, the generator should be extended to create a short Maintenance entry instead.

## Adding screenshots and videos

Every weekly update must include exactly one high-quality image or video showing that week's most important user-facing feature. Place it directly below the major feature it demonstrates and before the Improvements section. The media must show the real product clearly and should not be used for routine fixes or small UI changes.

### Screenshot

1. Capture the real product state at a readable size.
2. Attach the image to the changelog PR to obtain a stable GitHub user-attachment URL, or add an optimized asset under the landing site's public assets.
3. Add it below the relevant major-feature explanation:

```mdx
![Project onboarding from repository selection to the ready board](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/IMAGE_ID)
```

The image is rendered responsively, and the alt text is displayed as its caption. The alt text should explain what the screenshot shows rather than repeat the feature heading.

### Short product video

The changelog MDX renderer already supports the `Video` component:

```mdx
<Video
  src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/VIDEO_ID"
  title="Creating a project and reaching the ready board"
/>
```

Use a short MP4 or WebM demonstration, without autoplay. The player renders with controls, inline playback, and metadata-only preloading. Add a descriptive title and keep the written explanation complete so the video is optional rather than required to understand the update.

The current automated rule only enforces a maximum of one image. It should be extended to require exactly one primary media item per weekly entry and count Markdown images and `<Video>` components together, so every future update consistently includes one high-quality product visual.

Further protocol tracing narrows the failure:

- This was **not general message loss**. AO durably received the provider's streamed command/activity events and final assistant text through `07:00:59Z`.
- The Claude turn is one long-lived ACP `session/prompt` JSON-RPC request. AO marks the turn complete only when that request returns a `PromptResponse`; `finishPrompt()` then emits `turn.completed` and `controller.state=ready`.
- At `07:00:45Z`, during the still-running prompt, the provider emitted `Reconnecting to Claude, attempt 1 of 10`. More command output and final answer deltas arrived afterward.
- No response resolving the outstanding `session/prompt` request appears in AO's normalized provider history. Consequently the persistent relay continued to regard the prompt as active, and AO had no terminal boundary to project.
- The relay deliberately does not infer completion from final-looking text: text may precede tools, approvals, or resumed work. Controller cleanup also runs only when the provider event stream ends; here the ACP/Claude processes remained alive.

Most likely trigger (not yet proven from provider-side raw logs): Claude Agent ACP resumed streaming after its internal reconnect but failed to resolve the original `session/prompt` request. AO's confirmed bug is the absence of a bounded recovery/reconciliation path for this live-process/unresolved-prompt state.

This evidence argues against broadly unreliable Claude→AO delivery: payload delivery continued successfully; the terminal RPC response alone was missing or never surfaced.
